# Chapter Two That night, the lodge felt smaller. JT sat at the long pine table while his father ladled stew into chipped bowls, and the kerosene lamp threw shadows that didn't quite behave themselves. He'd watched the wall behind the stove for a while—watched the way his father's silhouette stretched and bent across the logs—until he realized his father hadn't moved in nearly a minute. Just stood there with the ladle hanging over the pot, dripping, staring at the dark window above the sink. "Dad?" His father blinked. Set the ladle down. "Eat up. Long day tomorrow." That was it. That was supper conversation. Mike ate like a machine, methodical, jaw working in slow circles. JT pushed a piece of carrot around his bowl and worked up his nerve the way you'd work a splinter out of your thumb—slow, wincing. "That buck today," he said. "In the clearing." The spoon stopped halfway to Mike's mouth. His father didn't look up. "What buck," his father said. Not a question. There was no question mark anywhere in it. It was flat as a closed door. "The big one. You were—" JT's throat tightened. *You were reaching out to touch it like it was a dog you'd raised from a pup. You looked like you were about to kiss it.* "You had a shot." "Didn't see any buck." His father's eyes came up then, and JT wished they hadn't. They were ordinary eyes, brown and tired, set in the ordinary weathered face JT had known his whole life. But there was something *behind* the ordinariness, the way you'd sense a fish moving under the skin of a pond. "Eat your supper, JT." Mike resumed chewing. The lamp hissed. Outside, the wind moved through the spruce trees with a sound like a long, slow exhale. JT ate his supper. --- He woke at some black hour with his bladder aching and the woodstove ticked down to embers. The lodge had two bedrooms; he and Mike shared the back one, two cots and a window with a crack in the corner that whistled when the wind came from the north. The wind was coming from the north now. Mike's cot was empty. JT lay there for a moment, telling himself the obvious thing—*he's in the outhouse, dummy, same place you're headed*—but the obvious thing felt thin, like ice you wouldn't trust your weight to. He got up. Pulled his boots on over bare feet. Padded through the main room, past the rifles racked by the door, all three of them present and accounted for, which should have been comforting and somehow wasn't. The front door stood open about four inches. Cold poured through the gap like water. JT stepped onto the porch and the night hit him full in the face, vast and still and silvered with moonlight. And there, maybe forty yards out where the trees began, stood Mike. Barefoot in the frost. Wearing nothing but his long johns, arms loose at his sides, facing the treeline. Facing the caribou. There were five of them. Six. JT's eyes kept finding more, the way you find faces in wallpaper once you start looking—pale shapes standing among the black trunks, motionless, antlers branching up into the dark like things grown rather than worn. They were watching Mike. Or Mike was watching them. The distinction felt important and JT couldn't hold onto which way it ran. "Mike." His voice came out a husk. "*Mike.*" His brother didn't turn. But one of the caribou did—swung its head with a slow, hydraulic smoothness, and fixed JT with eyes that caught the moonlight and gave nothing back. Flat eyes. Patient eyes. JT thought of the first one of the season, the one that had waited for the bullet like it was waiting for a bus, and his skin tried to crawl off the back of his neck and head south for the winter. He made himself cross the yard. The frost crunched under his boots, absurdly loud, and the whole time the animals just *watched*, and the worst part—the part he knew he'd never say out loud to anyone, not ever—was that the closer he got, the more he could hear it. A sound under the wind. Under everything. A low, droning hum, almost like voices, almost like a hymn sung in a church three towns over, the words worn away by distance until only the wanting remained. It wanted him to keep walking. Past Mike. Into the trees. JT grabbed his brother's arm instead. The skin was cold as stovepipe in January. "Mike. Hey. *Hey.*" Mike turned his head, and for one terrible second his face was as empty as the clearing had been, a face with the furniture moved out of it. Then he blinked, and Mike came back into it the way water fills a footprint. "JT?" He looked down at his bare feet. At the frost. "What the hell. What the—why am I—" "You were sleepwalking." The lie came out smooth and instant, and JT understood, hearing himself, that this was what his father had done at the supper table. Built a door and shut it. "Come on. You'll freeze." When he glanced back at the treeline, the caribou were gone. Not fled—*gone*, the way a thought is gone, leaving the woods standing innocent and empty under the moon. The hum was gone too. Mostly. If he held very still he thought he could feel the bottom edge of it, a vibration in his back teeth. --- In the morning his father was already up, already dressed, sitting at the table with his coffee and his rifle broken open in front of him, running an oiled patch through the barrel over and over. The patch had been clean for a long time, JT thought. He was just doing it to do it. "Caribou came right up to the lodge last night," JT said, watching his face. His father's hands didn't stop moving. "That so." "Whole bunch of them. Just standing there." "They'll do that." Patch through the barrel. Out. Through again. "Tame as anything, this far north. Always have been." "That's not—" JT stopped. *That's not true. You taught me yourself, you said a caribou will run from its own shadow.* But his father was looking at him now with those ordinary brown eyes, and underneath them the fish moved, slow and certain, and JT heard himself say, "Yeah. Sure." "Get your gear," his father said, sliding the bolt home with a sound like a lock turning. "They're waiting on us." He was halfway to the door before the words landed wrong. *Waiting on us.* Not *we're burning daylight.* Not *the season won't last forever.* *They're waiting.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This continuation chapter successfully sustains the King-style blend of grounded realism and creeping surrealism. The domestic dinner scene is well handled—the father's non-question "What buck" is an excellent beat, and the narrator's interiority ("worked up his nerve the way you'd work a splinter out of your thumb") echoes King's conversational simile style authentically. The nighttime scene with Mike sleepwalking among the caribou builds tension effectively toward the payoff, and the "hum" under the wind is a nice concrete manifestation of the threat. The dialogue is generally strong: terse, plausible, and doing double duty as characterization and menace. "They're waiting on us" landing wrong in JT's mind is a clean, chilling chapter-end payoff that fulfills the instruction to build tension toward a payoff. Weaknesses: the narrator's King-isms occasionally shade into pastiche ("his skin tried to crawl off the back of his neck and head south for the winter," "the way you find faces in wallpaper")—a few of these stacked close together feel like a writer performing King rather than being one. The "fish under the skin of a pond" image is reused twice, which may be intentional motif work but reads slightly repetitive. Some of the sentence fragments and italics for emphasis are a bit stock. The unreliable-narrator ambiguity is maintained but leans heavily on a familiar trope (the sleepwalking family member, the gaslit denial), so the plot beats are competently executed rather than surprising. Word count is on the short side of the 1000-word target, though not egregiously. Overall, prose flows naturally, imagery is vivid without becoming purple, the dread accumulates steadily, and the psychological ambiguity (is it real or in JT's head?) is preserved. There are no unearned transformations—Mike's return to himself is handled with ambiguity. The ending is darkly inconclusive, consistent with the genre. Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. # Hell is Other Demons The ash began falling at six, as it always did, which in Hell meant nothing because six was a committee decision rather than a fact of astronomy. Lucifer Morningstar watched it drift past the window of his office and thought, not for the first time, that it looked almost like snow, if snow were the cremated remains of broken promises. Which it was. The promises burned hottest in the furnaces below, and what went up had to come down. He was reviewing the morning's intake figures. Four hundred thousand souls, give or take. Heavy on tax attorneys and people who clapped when planes landed. He signed the manifest with a flourish of his left hand, which still smoked faintly when he was bored, and noticed he had drawn a small heart in the margin without meaning to. He scratched it out. Then he scratched out the scratching-out, which only made it more obvious, the way these things do. "Belphegor," he said to the demon dozing in the corner, "has anyone called?" Belphegor opened one of his eyes. He had several, all of them disappointed. "Called, my lord?" "Visited. Sent word. Hurled anything through a window." "Lady Lilith has not been by since Tuesday, if that's what you mean." "It is not what I mean," said Lucifer, in the tone of someone for whom it was precisely what he meant. "I was asking generally." "Generally, then: no. The damned scream a great deal, but none of them ask for you specifically anymore." Lucifer found this depressing, and then found his own depression depressing, which created a sort of feedback loop he resolved by setting fire to the intake figures. A junior demon scurried in with replacements. The ash outside thickened agreeably, as it tended to do when he sulked. The weather here was, embarrassingly, somewhat mood-dependent. --- At what passed for noon, Lilith arrived. She did not knock. She had never knocked, not in six thousand years, not even back when they were married, or whatever the word was for what they had been before there were words. She simply appeared in the doorway in a coat made of night and owl feathers, holding something wrapped in waxed paper. "I brought you a heart," she said. "Whose?" "Does it matter?" "It matters to the protocols. If it's a sinner's heart it goes through processing. If it's an innocent's heart, that's a whole thing with the Upstairs office, there are forms—" "It's a *gesture*, Lucifer." She set it on his desk, where it beat once, hopefully, and stopped. He looked at it. It was, he had to admit, a thoughtful gift. The last time she'd visited she had thrown a screaming wraith at his head and called him a vain little candle-flame who had mistaken falling for flying. The time before that she had rearranged his torture schedules out of spite, and the Envy department had spent a week processing Gluttons, who frankly enjoyed it, which had ruined the quarterly numbers. A heart in waxed paper was, by their standards, a courtship. "Tea?" he offered, carefully casual. "Is it the kind made from tears?" "Regret of the recently deceased. Single estate." "Fine." They drank tea while the ash drizzled down outside, settling on the parapets and the gibbets and the small failed garden Lucifer kept on the balcony, where he had been trying for nine centuries to grow a single ordinary rose. It came up black every time, or screaming, or both. He suspected the soil. "You look thin," Lilith said. "I look exactly as I choose to look." "You *choose* to look thin, then. And tired. Asmodeus says you've been signing damnations until three in the morning." "Asmodeus should mind his own circle." He paused. "You've been asking Asmodeus about me?" "I've been asking *around*," she said, in the way one might confess to a misdemeanor rather than the felony of caring. --- The afternoon brought business. A delegation from the Eighth Circle arrived to complain about a zoning dispute—the Flatterers wanted to expand into territory traditionally held by the Sowers of Discord, and the negotiations had collapsed for reasons everyone agreed were ironic. Lucifer adjudicated. Lilith stayed, perched on the windowsill like something heraldic, occasionally offering suggestions of such elegant cruelty that the delegation took notes. "You're good at this," he said, when they'd gone. "I know." "You could be good at it more often. There's an office down the hall. It has a window. The ash is very scenic from that side." "Lucifer." "I'm only saying the office exists." "You offered me a *job*. We were married before the invention of marriage and you're offering me a corner office." "It has a very good view of the Pit," he said, wounded. She stared at him for a long moment. Outside, the ash fell harder, then softer, then settled into an uncertain drizzle, the meteorological equivalent of a man not knowing what to do with his hands. "The first man wanted me to lie beneath him," she said. "You at least want me beside you. I'll grant the trajectory is improving." "At this rate of improvement, in another six thousand years I'll be tolerable." "Don't oversell yourself." But she was smiling, the way she did, with too many teeth and all of them sincere. --- In the evening they walked the battlements together, not touching, in the precise and practiced way of two people not touching on purpose. Below them, Hell went about its eternal business: the screaming, the paperwork, the long queues. The ash dusted Lilith's dark hair grey, and Lucifer thought she looked, briefly, like a glimpse of some old age they would never be permitted, and found his ancient unbeating heart doing something architecturally inadvisable. "Same time Tuesday?" she said, at the gate. "You could stay." "I could," she agreed, and left anyway, which from Lilith was very nearly a yes. Lucifer went back inside, put the heart she'd brought him in a jar on the mantelpiece, and noticed it had started, very quietly, beating again. Outside, the ash kept falling, soft and grey and endless, on the just and the unjust alike—though here, of course, it was mostly the unjust.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece that hits nearly every note the prompt requested. The day-in-the-life structure is cleanly handled through four movements (morning, noon, afternoon, evening), each escalating the Lilith relationship while interleaving the bureaucratic absurdity of Hell administration. The Gaiman influence is evident in the dry, understated narration and the matter-of-fact treatment of the fantastic. Strengths: The understated irony is consistently excellent. Details like the ash being "the cremated remains of broken promises," the heart drawn in the manifest margin and then scratched out twice, the mood-dependent weather, and the "meteorological equivalent of a man not knowing what to do with his hands" all land precisely. The dialogue is sharp and character-revealing—Lilith's "I've been asking *around*" as a confession of caring is a genuinely good line, and Lucifer's wounded "It has a very good view of the Pit" captures the comedy of a devil trying to be domestic. The Lilith characterization is well-sourced (the "lie beneath me" reference to her legend is deployed with wit and earns real emotional weight). The ending is earned: the heart quietly beating again is a small, restrained symbol rather than a grand reconciliation, and the final line's echo of Matthew 5:45 inverted for the damned is a fitting close. Weaknesses: The piece is somewhat safe and familiar in its conception—bureaucratic Hell with a lonely Lucifer is well-trodden territory (Pratchett, Gaiman himself, various TV adaptations), and the story doesn't transcend its influences so much as execute them competently. Some jokes are slightly over-explained: "which only made it more obvious, the way these things do" and "the meteorological equivalent of..." both spell out ironies that were already working. The "people who clapped when planes landed" joke is a bit of a non-sequitur that gestures at humor without quite landing. The middle section (zoning dispute) is the weakest stretch—functional but the least specific and least funny of the four. Lilith's dialogue occasionally tips into being too aphoristic ("Don't oversell yourself") in a way that feels written rather than spoken. The prose is elegant but occasionally self-admiring, admiring its own cleverness a beat too long. None of these flaws are serious. The piece is coherent, tonally consistent, emotionally complex without sentimentality, and the relationship arc—loneliness, tentative courtship via gift, the office offer as commitment proxy, the non-touching walk—is genuinely moving in a restrained way. The transformation (heart beating again) is small enough to be earned. Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. Model Output:
# The Weight of Iron The smell of barley porridge woke me before the light did. It always did—that and the coughing of Brixus in the cell beside mine, his lungs ruined by some fever he caught two winters past and never fully shed. I lay on my pallet listening to the ludus come alive around me: the scrape of the cook's ladle against the great bronze pot, the creak of the water cart's wheels in the courtyard, the low murmur of men who had learned long ago that mornings were not for talking. I rose and pressed my palms against the cold stone wall, feeling the rough mortar between the blocks. Eleven years I had touched that wall each morning. Eleven years since the slave market at Capua, since the lanista Decimus Otho ran his thumb along my teeth and squeezed my shoulders like a man buying a horse. "Thracian," he had said, though I was Dacian. To Romans, all of us from beyond the Danube were the same. In the courtyard, the morning light came down honey-thick between the colonnades, and the sand—raked smooth by the boys before dawn—glowed almost white. I took my place in the line for porridge, and Verus the Gaul handed me a wooden bowl without a word. The porridge was thick with beans and ash-flavored, as it always was. They fed us well, the way a farmer feeds his oxen well. *Hordearii*, the city folk called us. Barley men. There was contempt in it, and envy too, which is the particular Roman talent: to despise a thing and desire it in the same breath. I ate sitting against the eastern wall where the sun struck first. Across the courtyard, two new men—*tirones*, soft-handed, one of them a citizen who had sold himself to pay his debts—were practicing footwork at the palus, their wooden swords clacking against the post in arrhythmic, hopeless patterns. The debtor moved like a man underwater. I gave him until autumn. That was a thing I did not used to do, measure men's lives in seasons. I learned it the way I learned everything here: without wanting to. After the meal, Doctore Pugnax called my name, and I went to the armory to see to my equipment, for I was to fight in six days at the games Senator Quinctius was giving—funeral games, supposedly, for his father, though everyone knew they were truly for the voters. The old man had been dead eight months. His body was ash, but his usefulness lingered. Even Roman corpses worked for the family. The armory smelled of leather oil and rust and the faint vinegar tang of the wine they used to clean wounds in the corner that served as the medicus's station. Old Felix, the armorer, had laid my gear on the table: the high greaves, the manica of layered linen and leather for my sword arm, the broad-brimmed helmet with its griffin crest. And the sica. I picked up the curved blade and felt its weight settle into my hand like a remembered word. The sica is a small thing, shorter than my forearm, bent like a reaping hook near the tip. The Romans gave it to me because I was sold as a Thracian and Thracians fight with the sica—their theater demands it, the way it demands that the murmillo wear a fish on his helmet and the retiarius cast his net. We are costumes to them, characters in a play about the world Rome has conquered. But here is what the Romans do not know: my grandfather carried a blade like this one. I saw it hanging by our door when I was a boy, in the village above the river before the legions came under Trajan's eagles and made our country into a province and our people into property. The curve of it was the curve of the falx, the great war-scythe of the Dacians, the weapon that frightened Rome so badly they reinforced their helmets against it. So when they put the sica in my hand and called me by the wrong nation's name, they handed me, without knowing it, a piece of home. Every time I oiled the blade, I was tending my grandfather's memory. Every time it caught the arena light, something of Dacia flashed in the heart of Rome. The crowd cheered the Thracian. I fought as something else entirely. Felix watched me test the edge with my thumb. "Quinctius is paying for fights *sine missione*, I hear," he said quietly. No mercy. To the death. "I heard the same." "The Senate frowns on it. The Emperor frowns on it." He shrugged his old shoulders. "But senators need votes, and the plebs are hungry this year. The grain ships from Alexandria came late." He didn't need to explain further. When bread is short, blood must be plentiful. The arithmetic of the city was simple and ancient. I set the sica down. Through the armory's narrow window, I could hear Rome beyond our walls: the cries of vendors, the rumble of carts forbidden by day but rumbling anyway, a flute somewhere, a woman laughing. A whole city of free people going about their morning, eating their bread that came from Egypt, drinking their wine that came from Gaul, wearing their silver that came from the mines of my country, dug by men who had been my neighbors. Three more victories and I would have the money for my freedom. Decimus had named the price, and Decimus, whatever else he was, kept his word. Three victories. I had stopped letting myself imagine what came after—the road north, the river, whatever remained of the village. Hope is a wound you reopen yourself. Felix began wrapping the manica around my arm to check the fit, his fingers quick despite their age. "Six days," he said. "Six days," I agreed, and flexed my hand around the grip of the curved blade, feeling my grandfather's ghost settle along my arm like armor.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with skill. The scene avoids combat entirely, focusing instead on a morning in the ludus—waking, eating, preparing equipment—which is exactly the "slice of life" requested. Sensory details are abundant and well-chosen: the smell of barley porridge, the scrape of the ladle, the vinegar tang in the armory, honey-thick light on raked sand. The prose is controlled and evocative without tipping into purple excess. The narrator's interiority is the piece's greatest strength. His Dacian identity mislabeled as Thracian, and the sica as an unwitting link to his grandfather's falx, is a genuinely inventive emotional conceit—Rome handing him "a piece of home" while erasing his actual nation. This is nuanced, layered characterization: a man who has learned to measure lives in seasons, who suppresses hope ("Hope is a wound you reopen yourself"), who observes Roman hypocrisy with clear-eyed bitterness rather than melodrama. The political and social context is woven in organically: funeral games as electoral theater, the grain supply from Alexandria, the silver from Dacian mines, the economics of "when bread is short, blood must be plentiful." These touches feel researched and integrated rather than info-dumped. The dialogue is spare and effective—Felix's exchange about sine missione fights carries menace economically. The voice is consistent throughout: reflective, hardened, occasionally aphoristic ("their theater demands it"), with a rhythm that suits a man who has spent eleven years in silence and observation. Minor criticisms: some aphorisms ("the particular Roman talent: to despise a thing and desire it in the same breath") flirt with being too polished, slightly authorial rather than diegetic. The piece is somewhat short of the requested 1000 words, though not drastically. The ending, while resonant, is a touch neat—the grandfather's ghost settling "like armor" is a satisfying but expected closing beat. The tirones and Brixus are sketched but the piece is deliberately a fragment, so this is acceptable. Nothing here is amateurish, meandering, or overwrought; the piece shows genuine craft. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper --- **14 March 1953** Dear Mam, Arrived Tuesday on the supply boat. The crossing was rough and I was sick twice over the rail, which gave the boatman a good laugh at my expense. Skerryvane is smaller than I imagined — you can walk the whole rock in four minutes if the tide's out and you don't mind wet boots. The Principal Keeper is a man called Davidson, near retirement, says about six words a day and four of them are about the weather. The other assistant, Charlie Munro, is away on his shore leave so it's just the two of us for a fortnight. The light itself is a beauty though. You'd not believe the lens, Mam — taller than me and cut like a great diamond. Tell Da the pay came through and I've sent the first portion by postal order. Your loving son, Ewan --- **2 April 1953** My dear Ewan, Your Da says to tell you any fool can be sick on a boat and it's no shame. I say it's no shame either but I laughed all the same, God forgive me. I am sending with this letter a tin of shortbread and your gran's wee brass compass — the one your grandfather carried on the trawlers. She wanted you to have it before she passed and I have been holding it for the right moment. The needle sticks a bit at north-northwest but your grandfather always said that was the compass having opinions. Mind you eat properly. Tinned meat is not a vegetable. Your Mam --- **29 May 1953** Dear Mam, The compass arrived safe and I keep it on the shelf by my bunk. It's a strange comfort, that wee thing. The casing's worn smooth where Granda's thumb must have rubbed it, and there's a scratch on the back — looks like he started to carve initials and gave up halfway. An "A" and the start of something else. I find myself turning it over in my hands of an evening more than I'd care to admit. I'll be honest with you, Mam, because you'd see through me anyway. The nights are long here. Davidson and Munro are decent men but we've said everything there is to say to each other by Wednesday and then there's just the wind. Last week I caught myself talking to the gulls. One of them I've named Hector. He has a bad leg and steals from the others. Don't tell Da about the gulls. Ewan --- **18 June 1953** My dear Ewan, I told your Da about the gulls. He says he once spent three weeks in hospital with his leg and by the end he'd named all the pigeons on the windowsill, so you come by it honestly. Son, I'll say this once. Your Uncle Tam went to the merchant navy at your age and came back a stranger to himself because he kept it all bottled like ginger beer. You write me the truth of things and I'll not fret — it's the silences that fret a mother. Mrs. Galbraith asks after you. So does her Aileen, though she pretends she doesn't. Your Mam --- **3 October 1953** Dear Mam, A hard month. There was a wreck — a fishing boat out of Mallaig caught on the reef in the storm on the 19th. We did what we could with the line but we lost one man before the lifeboat reached us. He was about my age. I keep seeing his face in the water. Davidson sat up with me after, said nothing, just sat. I understand now why he doesn't talk much. He's seen four wrecks in thirty years and he keeps them all somewhere quiet. I don't know if I'm made for this, Mam. That's the truth you asked for. Ewan --- **20 October 1953** My dear Ewan, I read your letter three times and then I sat in the kitchen a long while. You ask if you're made for it. Son, you saved the others. The light was burning and the line was thrown because you were there. Nobody is made for watching a man drown. The day a keeper feels nothing is the day he should come ashore. Your Granda lost his brother off the trawlers in '21. That unfinished carving on the compass — "A" was for Alasdair. He never could finish it, and he never could throw the compass away either. He carried his brother with him to every fishing ground for forty years. Now you know why your gran wanted you to have it. Grief is just love with nowhere to go, Ewan. Give it somewhere to go. Your Mam --- **11 December 1953** Dear Mam, Your letter is folded in my breast pocket and has been since October. The corners are going soft. I finished the carving. Took me three evenings with Munro's penknife — Alasdair's full initials, and beneath them the date of the wreck here, and the lost man's name. His name was Robert Weir. I wrote to his mother in Mallaig. She wrote back. We are two strangers but we understand each other better than most. Something settled in me when I did it, Mam. I can't explain it grandly. The light still needs trimming and Hector still steals from the other gulls and the wind is still the wind. But I sleep now. I've signed on for another year. Davidson says I've the makings of a Principal one day, which from him is practically a poem. Home for Hogmanay on the relief boat, if the weather allows. Tell Da to get the good whisky down from the press. Tell Aileen Galbraith — well. Tell her I'll be at the kirk hall dance on the 2nd, and that a man who can keep a light burning through a Force 10 can surely manage a waltz. Your loving son, Ewan *P.S. — The compass needle still sticks at north-northwest. I've decided Granda was right. It's not broken. It just has opinions. So do I, now. That's what this rock has given me.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary piece succeeds on nearly every requirement: distinct Scottish working-class voices, a months-spanning correspondence, a gradually unfolding plot (isolation → wreck → grief → resolution), and a satisfying final letter. The mother's voice is warm and wry without sentimentality; Ewan's is restrained and believable. The compass is an excellent recurring object — its unfinished carving becoming the vehicle for grief and inheritance, resolved without being over-explained. The wreck is handled with restraint ("I keep seeing his face in the water"). The Aileen subplot is lightly seeded and pays off with a charming, in-character flourish. The P.S. about the compass's "opinions" is a well-earned callback. Minor criticisms: the "Grief is just love with nowhere to go" line edges toward a familiar aphorism (a near-cliché now widely circulated). The mother's letters occasionally run slightly too polished/writerly for her station, though plausible for a literate woman. The emotional arc resolves perhaps a touch quickly — the December letter's "something settled in me" arrives with only one letter of gap — but the carving and correspondence with Robert Weir's mother ground it enough to feel earned. The pacing is tight; nothing meanders. No purple prose, no overwrought moments, dialogue (within letters) is natural and characterful. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It Okay. Okay okay okay. He's sitting down. Marcus is sitting down at my lab table because Ms. Okafor said "partner with whoever's adjacent," and I am adjacent. I am the adjacent person. This is happening. Say hi. Just say hi. That's a normal word that normal people say. "Hey," he says. "Hi." Good. One syllable. Delivered without incident. Although—did it come out too fast? Like I'd been waiting for him to speak first, which I was, but he doesn't need to *know* that. Maybe I should have said "hey" back instead of "hi." "Hey" is casual. "Hi" is what you say to your dentist. He's pulling out the lab packet. *Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration: A Comparative Investigation.* I read the whole chapter twice last night, not because of this, obviously, I read it before I knew about the adjacent thing, but the point is I know this material cold. I could explain the electron transport chain right now. I could draw the Calvin cycle from memory. What I cannot do, apparently, is form a sentence about it out loud. I've rehearsed three openers. Option one: "So I was thinking we could split it—you do the diagrams, I'll do the written analysis?" Confident. Organized. But what if he thinks I'm bossy? What if he wanted the diagrams to be a joint thing? Option two: "Did you understand the part about the mitochondria?" Self-deprecating, invites him to explain, except I *do* understand the mitochondria, and if he explains it wrong I'll have to either correct him (disaster) or agree with wrong science (worse disaster, somehow). Option three: a joke about the powerhouse of the cell, which is either perfectly timed internet humor or the single most predictable thing a person could say, and I genuinely cannot tell which, and the not-knowing is going to kill me. "So, uh," he says, "do you want to split it up, or—" "Yeah." Too fast again. TOO FAST. "I mean. Sure. Whatever works." *Whatever works.* Fantastic. I have the vocabulary of a thesaurus inside my skull and what comes out of my mouth is *whatever works,* like I'm a customer service hold message. He's writing his name on the packet. His handwriting is bad in a nice way. Is that a thing? Can handwriting be bad in a nice way? I'm staring. Am I staring? I redirect my eyes to the packet with what I hope reads as scholarly focus and not as a person frantically recalibrating her own face. What does my face usually do? I've lost track of my baseline expression. Resting state: unknown. I attempt "pleasantly neutral" and immediately worry it looks like "smelling something bad." Speaking of which— What *is* that? Ammonia. Sharp, chemical, crawling up the back of my nose. They must have cleaned the lab tables during lunch. It smells like a swimming pool had a fight with a hospital. Great, now I'm thinking about whether I should mention it. "Smells like they cleaned in here" is an objectively safe observation. Weather-tier small talk. But what if he says "I don't smell anything" and then I'm the girl with the weirdly powerful nose who comments on smells? That's a *trait* now. That's a thing people remember at reunions. "Oh, her? She smelled stuff." I will not mention the ammonia. "It reeks in here," Marcus says. "RIGHT?" Oh no. Volume. The volume was wrong. Two tables over, Priya glances at us. I physically feel my soul attempt to exit through the ceiling tiles. "Like—yeah. Ammonia. Probably." *Probably?* I know it's ammonia. I hedged on a fact to seem less intense, which is its own kind of pathetic, a counterfeit casualness, and now I'm spiraling about my spiral, which is spirals all the way down. But he laughed. A small laugh, an exhale-laugh, but real. I'm cataloging it. I hate that I'm cataloging it. I can already see myself tonight, lying in bed, replaying that half-second laugh and analyzing it like game footage. *Was it a laughing-with or a laughing-at?* My brain will convene a full tribunal at 11:47 p.m. and the verdict will change four times before sleep. "Okay, so light-dependent reactions," he says, tapping the diagram. "This part confuses me." This is it. This is my moment. I know this. I know this *so well.* The words are right there, queued up in perfect order: thylakoid membrane, photosystem II, water gets split, electrons get excited— "It's like—the light hits the, um—the membrane part, and then the electrons sort of... go." *The electrons sort of go.* Somewhere, my internal voice—the one that wins arguments in the shower, the one that composes flawless comebacks six hours after they're needed—is screaming. She had a whole presentation prepared. Slides. Laser pointer. And the mouth department delivered *the electrons sort of go.* But Marcus nods. He's actually following along, drawing little arrows where I pointed. "Okay, that actually makes sense," he says. "You're good at this." You're good at this. Do not smile too big. Do not smile too big. A normal-sized smile. What is a normal-sized smile? I've never once measured. I deploy something I hope is in the acceptable range and say, "It's just—I read the chapter," which technically downplays it, except now maybe I sound like I'm bragging about reading, which— You know what? No. Stop. He said I'm good at this. He's labeling the diagram with my words, *my* explanation, badly-nicely handwritten across the thylakoid membrane. The ammonia is fading, or I'm getting used to it, and the next forty minutes stretch out ahead of us, terrifying and full of conversational landmines, and I have approximately nineteen rehearsed sentences left in reserve. I'll probably use two of them. Badly. But he's still sitting here. Adjacent. And for one entire breath, I let that be enough.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a sharply executed piece of internal monologue that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt. The 8th-grade voice is convincing: articulate and self-aware internally, garbled and over-hedged aloud. The gap between the narrator's inner eloquence ("thylakoid membrane, photosystem II, water gets split") and her spoken output ("the electrons sort of go") is the emotional engine of the piece, and it's dramatized rather than merely stated. The rehearsed-conversation cycling (three openers, each picked apart for social risk) directly answers the prompt's request, and the self-monitoring of volume, facial expression, and word choice is rendered with specificity and humor. Strengths: the comedy is character-driven, not grafted on ("I am the adjacent person," "the girl with the weirdly powerful nose," "a swimming pool had a fight with a hospital"). The internal tribunal at 11:47 p.m. is a genuinely funny and true detail. The dialogue, though sparse, is naturalistic and does its job—Marcus reads as a real, mildly awkward kid, not a prop. The ending resists the trap of a fairy-tale connection: no confession, no triumph, just "for one entire breath, I let that be enough," which is proportionate and earned. Weaknesses: the piece leans on a familiar anxious-overthinker template (the "shower comebacks" line, the "smile too big" panic) that a seasoned reader has seen before; the observations are well-executed but not surprising in kind. The ammonia subplot is a nice grounding device but its payoff is modest. Occasionally the wit is a touch too polished for a 13-year-old ("counterfeit casualness," "spirals all the way down")—the voice is consistent, but it's the voice of a very literary 8th grader, which is a minor believability stretch. The prose is clean and rhythmic without tipping into purple. Structure is tight; nothing meanders. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 85.7
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection She's going to end it today. That's why she suggested coffee instead of dinner. Coffee is the exit-interview beverage. Dinner means commitment, lingering, wine, maybe her hand finding mine under the table the way it did three weeks ago. Coffee means: *I have somewhere to be in forty-five minutes, and that somewhere is away from you.* I've already written her speech. *Maya, I think we moved too fast. I value our friendship too much to risk it.* And I'll say—I've drafted this part carefully—I'll say, *Funny how you valued it enough to risk it three weeks ago.* Cold. Surgical. She'll flinch, and I'll feel terrible, and I'll also feel armored, which is the point. You can't be ambushed if you've already filmed the ambush from every angle. She took six hours to answer my text on Tuesday. Six. I counted. I know she had her sister's thing, she *told* me she had her sister's thing, but people make time. People who want you make time. When she finally replied it was warm—*sorry!! chaos here, miss your face*—and I read it eleven times and felt the warmth flood in like blood returning to a sleeping limb, and then, almost immediately: *miss your face* is what you say to anyone. It's what you say to coworkers. The exclamation points are guilt punctuation. I catch myself in the hallway mirror. Shoulders up around my ears, jaw set like I'm already mid-argument. I look like someone bracing for a car crash that hasn't happened. Hasn't happened *yet*, I correct, and then I hear how that sounds, and I think: *this is the thing Dr. Okafor talks about. The rehearsal. The pre-grieving.* I know what this is. I can name it. Naming it does absolutely nothing. It's like reading the warning label while you swallow the pill. I turn away from the mirror. If she says she's been distant because of work, I'll say I understand, and I'll mean it for four seconds, and then I'll think: work is the alibi people use when the truth is unkind. If she says she's been distant because she's scared of what we started, I'll say—what will I say? I'll want to say *me too*. I'll probably say something sharp instead. Something that punishes her for making me feel this, this dangling, this hanging by the wrists over my own history. She's already there when I arrive. She stands up. She *stands up*, like I'm someone worth standing for, and she hugs me long enough that I can feel her exhale against my neck, and the relief is so enormous it's almost nausea. "I got you the lavender thing," she says. "I know you pretend you don't like it." She remembered. She ordered before I came. She— *Or she ordered ahead to speed this along. Pre-purchased mercy. The condemned ate a lavender latte.* Stop. Stop it. "I've been a ghost lately," she says, "and I hate it. Dani's divorce blew up and I've been on the phone with her every night, and I kept thinking, I should tell Maya, but then it's eleven p.m. and I'm wrung out, and—" She reaches across the table and takes my hand. Takes it. Holds it in the middle of a coffee shop where anyone can see. "I didn't want you to think I was pulling away. Especially now. Especially after." There it is. The thing I needed. The exact transfusion. And I feel it land, I do, warm and real, her thumb moving over my knuckles, and for one whole breath I am a person who is loved and knows it. Then: *especially after.* What does that mean? After—does she regret the after? Is this the buttering before the blow? People hold your hand when they're about to hurt you. It's a restraint technique. "You okay?" she asks. "You went somewhere just now." I went to your funeral, I want to say. I've attended it nightly. Lovely service. You said terrible things about me in the eulogy and I had devastating comebacks for all of them. "I'm good," I say. "I missed you." "I missed you so much," she says, and her eyes do the thing, the shine, and she means it, she visibly *means* it, and I watch myself receive it like water poured into cupped hands with the fingers slightly spread. Holding it. Losing it. Holding it. She talks about Dani, about us, about a weekend trip she wants to take—*wants to take with me*, future tense, plural pronoun, evidence, evidence—and I am collecting these proofs even as some night-shift clerk in my head stamps each one INSUFFICIENT. She said *trip* but didn't name dates. She said *us* but looked at her cup. I am cross-examining a witness who is testifying entirely in my favor. I know this is the disorder talking. I know it the way you know a fact about a country you've never visited. The knowing lives in one room and the fear lives in all the others, and the fear pays the rent. When we leave, she kisses me on the sidewalk, unhurried, her hand at the back of my neck, and I think: *real, this is real, let it be real,* and underneath, already, quietly, the clerk is drafting tomorrow's case. *She'll text less this week. Watch. The trip won't materialize. Watch.* I am pre-resenting her for crimes she has not committed, building the wall brick by brick while she's still holding me, so that when she finally leaves—and they always finally leave—I'll have somewhere to stand. "Text me when you're home?" she says. "You won't answer for six hours," I say, and I make it sound like a joke, and she laughs and says, "Try me," and I walk home rehearsing both outcomes: the reply that comes in minutes, and the silence I've already, lovingly, furnished.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision. The internal monologue dominates; the imagined confrontations and drafted comebacks are vivid ("You can't be ambushed if you've already filmed the ambush from every angle"). The actual events are warm and validating—standing up, the lavender latte, the hand-holding, the kiss—while the narrator immediately reframes each as suspicious. The "night-shift clerk stamping INSUFFICIENT" metaphor is a standout, as is "reading the warning label while you swallow the pill." Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The temple's broken roof let moonlight fall in silver columns across the cracked stone floor. Around its edges, forty spectators pressed against toppled pillars, their breath fogging in the cold air, money already changing hands in whispers. Takeshi Murakami stood at the eastern end of the hall, beneath the headless statue of a forgotten guardian deity. His bokken—the duel's single concession to survival—rested high above his right shoulder in the *hassō* posture of Jigen-ryū, his left foot forward, his whole body coiled like a drawn bow. The red-and-black armband on his left bicep caught the moonlight. His school taught one truth: the first strike ends everything. There would be no second. Twelve paces west, Wei Liang rolled his shoulders in slow, loosening circles, arms hanging like ropes weighted with stone. His own armband, red and black, was knotted at his right arm—a deliberate mirror, a deliberate insult. Piguaquan lived in his joints, in the whip-crack relaxation of a body that struck like a flail. He had heard the Jigen-ryū boasts all his life: *one cut, one kill*. Tonight he would teach the samurai's heir what street fighters knew—that the man who commits everything to one strike has nothing left when it misses. "Begin," croaked the old bookmaker from atop a fallen lintel. Takeshi exploded forward. The famous Jigen-ryū charge—a shrieking *kiai* tearing from his throat, three lunging steps devouring the twelve paces, the bokken descending in the *kesa* cut that had split helmets in the Satsuma wars. The blow came down the diagonal, right shoulder to left hip, fast enough that the spectators flinched. Wei did not block. Blocking that strike was suicide. He slipped left—a single sliding step off the line of attack—and the bokken's tip cracked into the flagstone where his collarbone had been, throwing chips of granite. In the same motion Wei's right arm whipped horizontally, a backhand *gua* strike scything toward Takeshi's exposed temple. But Jigen-ryū trained recovery as ferociously as attack. Takeshi let the missed cut's momentum carry him into a forward roll of the wrists, the bokken sweeping back up and across to intercept. Wood met forearm—Wei pulled the strike short, taking only a glancing blow above the wrist rather than a broken arm. He spun away clockwise, circling toward Takeshi's right, putting a cracked pillar between them for half a heartbeat. The crowd roared. Coins clattered. Takeshi pivoted to track him, resetting the bokken overhead. He did not pursue around the pillar—he cut the angle instead, stepping to its far side to meet Wei's circle head-on. Smart. Wei reversed direction mid-stride, his footwork a stuttering shuffle that ate distance sideways, and now they faced each other across four paces in the open center of the hall, moonlight pooling between them. Wei attacked first this time. He flowed in low, arms churning in alternating vertical circles—*pi* and *gua*, chop and upswing—a wheel of limbs offering no single target. The first downward chop Takeshi deflected with the bokken's flat; the second, rising from below, grazed his ribs and stole his breath. Wei was inside the sword's effective range now, too close for a full cut, his palms hammering at Takeshi's body from impossible angles. Takeshi did what his masters had drilled into him since childhood: he attacked through the pain. He slammed the bokken's pommel down toward Wei's skull. Wei ducked, but the strike clipped his shoulder, staggering him back two steps—and that was all the space Jigen-ryū needed. The bokken rose and fell like lightning. Wei threw himself into a backward leap, landing on the raised dais where the altar had once stood, one step higher than the floor. The bokken's tip whistled past his shin. Takeshi pressed forward, cutting upward at the elevated target, and Wei leapt *over* the strike, off the dais entirely, landing behind Takeshi's left shoulder. The whipping backfist caught Takeshi across the back of the head. He stumbled forward onto the dais, vision whitening, and the crowd's scream told him the follow-up was coming. He spun blindly, sweeping the bokken in a flat horizontal arc at waist height—the desperate, instinct-bred counter of his school. Wei, lunging in to finish, took the strike across his left thigh. The crack of wood on muscle echoed off the broken walls. He buckled, catching himself on one palm against the cold stone. Both fighters froze, three paces apart—Takeshi on the dais, blood trickling down his neck, breath ragged; Wei below him on one knee, leg trembling. The hall went silent except for the wind through the shattered roof. Takeshi raised the bokken overhead one final time. His school had no word for retreat. He screamed and leapt down from the dais, the cut falling with his full descending weight behind it—unstoppable, unanswerable. Wei did not rise to meet it. He collapsed sideways, rolling under the strike's arc, and as the bokken smashed into the flagstones beside his head, his right leg—the good one—swept Takeshi's forward ankle. The samurai's heir, all his weight committed, had no base left. He crashed onto the stone, and Wei was on him instantly, forearm whipping down across Takeshi's wrist. The bokken clattered free. Wei's palm stopped one inch from Takeshi's throat. They stared at each other, both bleeding, both shaking, the moonlight cold on their faces. Around them the temple erupted—triumph and fury, money flung down, oaths screamed. Wei pushed himself upright, favoring his battered thigh, and extended a hand downward. Takeshi looked at it for a long moment. Generations of contempt pressed on his shoulders. Then he gripped the offered forearm and let his enemy pull him to his feet. "Next month," Takeshi said quietly, beneath the crowd's noise. "Same place." Wei's split lip curved into a grin. "I'll bring liniment for your ribs." Above them, the headless guardian kept its silent watch, and the blood debt between the schools grew one duel deeper—and, perhaps, one grudging respect lighter.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tight, well-structured duel narrative that fulfills the prompt's core requirements with notable competence. The Jigen-ryū fighter is characterized through the hassō stance, kesa cut, and "first strike" philosophy—accurate stylistic details—while the Piguaquan fighter embodies whipping circular strikes, evasive footwork, and a commoner's contempt for elite rigidity. The abandoned temple setting is vividly rendered (moonlight columns, headless statue, dais, cracked pillar) and the environment is actively used in the choreography rather than as mere backdrop. Physical coherence is the prompt's central demand, and the response largely delivers. Positions are tracked: the initial twelve paces, the slip left, the pillar interposition, the re-centering at four paces, the closing to inside sword range, the dais elevation change, the leap behind, and the final sweep-takedown. Each exchange is spatially legible. Minor quibbles: the "red and black armband" on both fighters is a confusing detail (deliberate mirror stated, but muddling), and a few transitions (Wei spinning clockwise, then reversing) require rereading, though they remain plausible. The prose is clean and muscular, with strong verbs and a controlled rhythm that mirrors the fight's tempo. Occasional flourishes ("coiled like a drawn bow," "arms hanging like ropes weighted with stone") are apt rather than purple. The crowd functions economically as stakes. The ending—mutual respect, a promised rematch—resolves slightly too warmly for a "blood debt" rivalry, a touch of incongruent positivity, and Takeshi's acceptance of the hand is a small unearned softening given his school's "contempt for outsiders." The closing line tries to have it both ways ("one grudging respect lighter") but earns it reasonably through the fight's mutual damage. Dialogue is minimal and serviceable; the final exchange is a bit quippy but fits young hot-headed fighters. The narrative is coherent, focused, never meandering, and emotionally engaging if not deeply complex—character interiority is thin, with pride and rivalry asserted more than explored. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation Count eight. Hit. Count eight. Hit. The mirrors run the length of the studio's north wall, floor to ceiling, and in them I can see all twelve of us arranged in three rows of four. I'm back row, far left—the corner where they hide the problem. Master Yoon stands center front, his back to the mirror, facing us. He doesn't dance anymore. He doesn't need to. He moves one finger and twelve bodies flinch. "Again. From the bridge." The speakers—one bolted into each corner of the room, four of them triangulating us in sound—kick the track back to the 3:12 mark. The volume sits just past comfortable, a deliberate pressure against the eardrums, so the bass isn't something you hear so much as something that colonizes your sternum. The bridge choreography: right foot steps out to second position on the *and* of one, arms snapping into a diagonal frame—left fist at the hip, right arm extended at exactly forty-five degrees, fingers bladed. Then a quarter pivot left on two, isolation roll through the chest on three-and-four, drop to a low lunge on five, and freeze. Hold the freeze through six, seven, eight. Twelve bodies becoming one machine. Back home, in the parking structure on Crenshaw where we battled under sodium lights, a freeze was a *flex*. You hit it when the music told you to, held it as long as the crowd's noise could carry you, broke it when your body found the next thing. Here, a freeze is a cage with a timer. We run the bridge. My step-out lands clean. My arm finds the diagonal. Then the chest isolation comes and my body—my traitor body—*rolls* it. Liquefies it. Lets the wave travel down through my hips the way a wave is supposed to travel, the way Pops taught me boogaloo in the kitchen, the way water moves because water doesn't know how to be a machine. In the mirror, eleven torsos tick through the isolation in three discrete, identical clicks. Mine pours. "Stop." The track dies mid-phrase. The silence the speakers leave behind has its own weight. Master Yoon crosses the floor toward me. He doesn't hurry. The other trainees hold position—actually hold it, lunged and frozen, quads trembling—because nobody told them to relax. I'm still standing, which is its own confession. "You." He stops two feet from me. He's shorter than I am, and it doesn't matter at all. "What was that?" "A body roll." "I know what it was. I asked what it was doing in my choreography." The trainee to my right—Jihoon, who's been here since he was fourteen, who eats the same portioned meals every day and bows to the vending machine—keeps his eyes locked forward. Sweat tracks down his temple. He doesn't blink. "Your isolation," Master Yoon says, "is three positions. Chest forward. Chest center. Chest contract. Three photographs. You are giving me a film. I did not ask for a film." *Where I'm from, the film is the point.* I don't say it. My scholarship says it for me, says it every month when it pays for the dorm bed and the cafeteria card and the flight I couldn't have afforded in three lifetimes of teaching kids to toprock at the rec center. "Again. Alone." The other eleven release the freeze on his hand signal and step backward to the wall, a synchronized retreat that opens the center of the floor. The mirrors hand me back to myself: one body, hardwood, four speakers aimed inward like an interrogation. The track restarts. 3:12. Step out. Frame. Pivot. And here it comes—the isolation, three-and-four—and I clench everything, I *robot* it, I think of my chest as a drawer sliding on a track: out, center, in. Click. Click. Click. It feels like lying. It feels like dancing with someone else's spine. The lunge drops me low on five and I hold the freeze and my left knee hovers an inch off the floor and the bass keeps pulsing through six-seven-eight and every cell in me is screaming to *answer it*, to let the hold breathe, to bounce. I don't bounce. "Better," Master Yoon says, which lands harder than any insult he's thrown all week. "Again. Then with the group." And in the gap before the track resets, I catch my own eyes in the mirror, and I see what he's building. I see the photograph I'm becoming. Three positions. Twelve identical bodies. A product with my face on it. Here's the thing nobody back home will understand if I quit: he's *right* about the precision. My freezes have always been mush at the edges. My lines collapse when I'm tired. The discipline is real and I'm hungry for it the way you're hungry for something that hurts going down. But here's the thing nobody *here* understands: the roll he killed was a conversation with the music, and the click he wants is a transcription of it. Track restarts. The group files back into formation around me—three rows of four, my corner waiting like a holding cell. I take my mark. The intro counts pulse from all four corners at once, too loud, surround-sound conformity. Step out on the *and*. Frame. Pivot. The isolation arrives. I give him his three positions—chest forward, click, center, click—and on the third click, the contraction, I let one thing live: a half-second melt at the very bottom of the movement, a single drop of water in the machine, small enough to be deniable, mine enough to be true. Then the lunge, the freeze, the hold. In the mirror, Master Yoon's eyes find mine across three rows of bodies. He saw it. Of course he saw it. He doesn't stop the music. Six. Seven. Eight. We move together into the chorus, twelve bodies, and somewhere inside the eleventh photograph, one frame of film keeps running.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding prompt. The spatial and kinetic tracking is excellent: the narrator's position (back row, far left), the mirror geometry, Master Yoon's position, the eleven trainees retreating to the wall, the choreography broken down count-by-count—all remain coherent throughout. The contrast between street fluidity and K-pop precision is rendered through concrete technical detail (chest isolation as "three photographs" vs. a "film," the boogaloo wave, the freeze as "a cage with a timer"). The internal monologue effectively carries class anxiety (the scholarship, the flight, the rec center) and the central tension of losing one's authentic voice. The decision point—smuggling a "half-second melt" into the third click—is a well-earned, small-scale act of rebellion rather than a melodramatic one, and Master Yoon's choice not to stop the music is a satisfying, understated resolution. The prose is controlled, with a few metaphors that flirt with overreach ("colonizes your sternum," "surround-sound conformity") but mostly land. Dialogue is minimal but sharp and characterful. Some elements are slightly familiar (the tough-but-seeing instructor archetype), and the ending's "one frame of film keeps running" is a touch neat, but it's earned by the piece's own metaphor system. Minor weaknesses: the trainees are thinly sketched (Jihoon is a single vivid detail), and the piece leans on its central metaphor heavily in the final third. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Court of the Dreaming: In Re: The Wildflower Field The hourglass dripped its shimmering sand, each grain a second of somebody's sleep, and the Lord of Dreams sat upon his throne of carved obsidian wishing, not for the first time, that his kingdom came with fewer lawyers. "Call the case," he said. The bailiff—a raven named Matthew who had not asked for this job either—cleared his throat. "Case number incalculable: *First Love versus Mora, Nightmare of the Slavic Tradition*, concerning the dreamscape designated 'Wildflower Field, Recurring, Property of One Max Pemberton, Aged Thirteen.'" First Love rose from the petitioner's bench. He was rosy-cheeked and held his hat in both hands, twisting it like a dishrag. "My lord. Thank you. I, um. Thank you." "You have said thank you," Dream observed. "Proceed." "Yes. Right." First Love produced a sheaf of notes that smelled faintly of cut grass. "The dream in question took me eleven months to construct. The light alone—my lord, do you know how difficult it is to get late-afternoon June light correct? The way it makes a girl's hair look like something the boy will compare every subsequent sunset against for the rest of his life?" "I have some familiarity with light," said Dream, whose eyes were two stars in a pool of night. "Of course. Of course you do. Apologies." More hat-twisting. "The dream proceeds thus: Max lies in the field. Sophie—the crush, my lord, a real girl, very nice, slightly gap-toothed, it's the gap that does it—lies beside him. They talk about nothing. There is an almost-kiss. The dream ends in confusion of the *pleasant* variety. The boy wakes up feeling like a held breath. It is *formative*, my lord. It is load-bearing. The man he becomes is built on this dream." "And the alleged subversion?" First Love's cheeks went from rosy to crimson. "She—the defendant—now, at the moment Sophie playfully, ah, *mounts* the boy—" "It was always a bit forward for a first-love dream," muttered Mora from the defendant's bench. "—Sophie *transforms*. Into *her*." He pointed. "She sits on his chest. She paralyzes him. She *feeds on his breath*, my lord. The boy wakes up terrified." "And?" said Dream. First Love hesitated. "And... confused. In a way I did not design." All eyes turned to Mora. She lounged rather than sat, a creature of shadow and long dark hair and a smile with too many implications in it. She had dressed for court, insofar as nightmares dress, in something that suggested funeral shrouds had a couture season. "Your defense," said Dream. Mora shrugged, a gesture that took a full three seconds and seemed to involve joints that ordinary anatomy did not provide. "A girl's gotta eat, my lord." The hourglass dripped. Somewhere in the gallery, a minor incubus snickered and was immediately turned into a moth by a glance from the throne. "That is your entire defense." "It's a *good* defense. Breath of the young, my lord—it's not like I can get it at a market. The boy is healthy, terrified, and produces excellent vintage. Besides—" she examined her nails, which were lengthy, "—I'd argue I've *improved* the dream. He used to wake up confused and happy. Now he wakes up confused, terrified, and—" the smile widened, "—*still somewhat interested*. That's emotional range. I'm an educator." "You are a parasite," said First Love. "Parasite, educator. Tomato, tomato." "Those are pronounced identically when written," Dream said wearily. He pinched the bridge of his nose, a gesture so rare that Matthew the raven made a note of the date. "Witnesses?" Dream asked. "I call the dream itself," said First Love. There was a smell of wildflowers. A patch of the courtroom floor became a field, June light and all, with a translucent memory of Max lying in the grass. The court watched the almost-kiss. Several jurors—assembled from the usual pool of fictions, dead poets, and one very confused man who was only dreaming he was on jury duty—sighed audibly. Then the gallery watched Sophie's gap-toothed smile melt into Mora's, watched the dream-boy's chest compress, watched his eyes go wide with terror and something terribly adjacent to terror. "He's *thirteen*," First Love said, anguished. "I had a schedule. Hand-holding by autumn. An actual kiss by the spring fair. Now he's going to spend his twenties writing poetry about women who frighten him." "Many great poets did exactly that," said Mora. "You're welcome, literature." Dream raised one pale hand. The field dissolved. The hourglass dripped. He considered. The court held its breath—except Mora, who held everyone else's on principle. The truth of it was, the case was beneath him. The truth of it *also* was that Dream had spent the morning adjudicating a dispute between two anxiety dreams over exclusive rights to "showing up to school without trousers," and the irritation had compounded into something almost playful. Almost. "Judgment," he said, and the room went still as held sleep. "First Love's claim of prior craftsmanship is upheld. Mora's claim of necessity is acknowledged—the Dreaming does not starve its monsters, however irritating she finds them." A pause. "*It* finds them." Mora winked. Dream did not acknowledge the wink. The wink was nonetheless entered into the record. "Therefore: the dream is restored to First Love's design. Mora is granted feeding rights—" First Love made a sound like a kettle, "—one night per month. *However.*" And here something flickered in the starlit eyes that, in a lesser being, might have been called mischief. "On those nights, Mora shall appear as herself from the *beginning*. No transformation. No theft of Sophie's face. The boy shall lie in the wildflowers with the nightmare herself, fully aware of what she is." Silence. "My lord," said Mora slowly, "he'll *talk* to me. About nothing. For *hours*. Before I can feed." "Yes," said Dream. "He'll ask if I like him." "Almost certainly." Mora looked, for the first time in several centuries, genuinely horrified. First Love, slowly understanding, began to beam. "Court is adjourned," said Dream, and allowed himself, in the privacy of eternity, the very smallest of smiles. The hourglass dripped on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of dark comic fantasy that hits nearly every brief requirement. The courtroom farce is grounded in familiar legal-drama beats (case numbers, petitions, witnesses, judgment) transposed into the Dreaming, and the humor is consistently understated and dry — Dream turning an incubus into a moth with a glance, Mora "holding everyone else's breath on principle," the jury of dead poets and a man dreaming he's on jury duty. The dialogue is the standout: Dream's clipped weariness, First Love's stammering hat-twisting, and Mora's louche, self-satisfied deflections all land. The "tomato, tomato" exchange and Dream's pedantic correction is a good deadpan beat. The resolution is the piece's cleverest move: Dream's "mischief" — sentencing Mora to endure hours of thirteen-year-old small talk before she can feed — is both a punishment and a genuinely Dream-like act of oblique justice, and it earns Mora's horror and First Love's dawning delight. It satisfies the prompt's requirement that Dream be "tempted to some mischief" without breaking character. Minor criticisms: the "confusingly attractive" element of the prompt is handled mostly through implication ("still somewhat interested," "terribly adjacent to terror") — appropriate, but slightly thin. A few jokes are near-misses ("The wink was nonetheless entered into the record" is a bit cute). The prose is economical as instructed, occasionally leaning on familiar constructions ("in the privacy of eternity"). The ending's small smile is well-earned rather than saccharine. Nothing meanders; the ~1000-word target is respected in spirit.
