+ Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Three: Vega, Neat I'm polishing a glass that doesn't need polishing when she walks in. You learn to read entrances in this job. Miners shuffle. Merchants stride. Smugglers slide in sideways like they're hoping the doorframe will forget them. This one—tentacled dreads frizzed out like she's been running her hands through them for three days straight, jacket buttoned wrong—she doesn't walk in so much as wash ashore. She plops onto the stool at the far end of the bar, away from the dart game and Old Marsten's nightly argument with the jukebox. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." "Rough cycle?" I pour. The whisky catches the low light, amber and honest. "Rough decade." She wraps both hands around the glass like it might float away. One of her dreads twitches—Ophiuchan, then, and stressed enough that her tells are showing. "You want food with that? Kitchen does a decent algae melt. 'Decent' is doing some heavy lifting in that sentence, but it's hot." That gets a flicker of a smile. "Just the whisky. And maybe... quiet?" "Quiet I can do." I drift down the bar, top off Marsten's ale, pretend to inventory the bitters. The thing about quiet, though, is that nobody who asks for it actually wants it. They want a witness. So when she clears her throat four minutes later, I'm not surprised. "This place. The Last Outpost. Cute name." "Owner thought so. It's technically the second-to-last outpost, but 'The Penultimate Outpost' didn't fit on the sign." She laughs—a startled, rusty sound, like she forgot she could. "You get a lot of traffic through here?" "Miners, mostly. Ore haulers. The occasional pilgrim who took a wrong turn at the Veil Nebula." I lean against the back counter, casual as anything, watching her dreads twitch in sequence now. "Why? Looking for someone?" Her glass stops halfway to her mouth. "Avoiding someone," she says quietly. "Ah." I nod like I haven't lived that exact sentence. "Well. We're good at avoiding here. It's our primary export, after iron and bad decisions." "You don't understand." She leans forward, voice dropping. "I worked for the Calloway Combine. Logistics. Boring stuff—manifests, cargo weights, routing. Except three weeks ago I noticed the weights didn't match. Containers listed as ore that massed like... like something else." My polishing rag goes still. The Combine runs half the shipping lanes in this sector. They also, rumor holds, run things that don't appear on any manifest. "You should maybe not be telling the bartender this," I say. "Bartenders are like priests. Confidential." "Bartenders are like bartenders. We gossip professionally." "Then I'm trusting you to be bad at your job." She knocks back half the double. "I copied the manifests. I don't even know why. Insurance, maybe. Stupidity, probably. And then I ran. And now there's a Combine enforcement vessel two systems back, and it's been two systems back for six days, and I am running out of systems." Somewhere behind me, a glass shatters—Dex at table four, knocking his tumbler off with one of his four elbows again. The stranger nearly comes out of her skin, half off the stool, hand diving into her jacket. "Easy," I say, raising both palms. "That's just Dex. He's got too many elbows and not enough coordination. Happens twice a week, minimum." "Sorry, Nets!" Dex calls cheerfully, already collecting shards. She settles back, breathing hard. Her hand comes out of the jacket empty, but I clocked the shape of what's in there. So she's armed. Wonderful. "Nets?" she asks, voice still shaky. "Nettle. Nets to friends. You're trending toward friend, mostly because you've made my evening interesting, which I will probably regret." "Sayuri." She extends a hand. Her grip is clammy. "And I'll be gone by morning. I just need somewhere to sit until the fuel depot opens. Then I'm dust." I should say *fine, sit, drink, go.* That's the smart play. I came to this rock specifically to stop collecting other people's trouble, having generated a lifetime supply of my own. Instead I hear myself say: "The depot's closed till oh-six-hundred. And Vance, who runs it, reports every fueling to the Combine commerce office. Standard kickback arrangement." Sayuri goes pale in a way that does interesting things to Ophiuchan skin tone, sort of a gray-green tide. "Then I'm dead." "You're not dead. You're complicated. There's a difference, though admittedly the difference is mostly me." I pour her another finger of Vega, on the house. "There's an old ore tug in dock seven. Belongs to nobody since Hettie passed. It still flies, and nobody reports anything about dock seven because officially dock seven doesn't exist." She stares at me. "Why would you help me? You don't know me. I could be lying about all of it." "Could be." I shrug. "But your dreads twitch when you're scared, not when you talk about the manifests. Whatever's in your jacket pocket, you've never drawn it in anger—you grabbed for it backwards. And you button your jacket wrong, which means you dressed running, in the dark, probably while crying." I slide the glass to her. "Liars are tidier." "You read people like that often?" "Used to do it for a living. Now I do it for tips." Sayuri's eyes narrow, and for the first time tonight she looks at *me* properly. "What did you do? Before this?" "That," I say, picking my rag back up, "is a story that costs more than a double Vega." The door chimes. Two figures step in—matte gray uniforms, Combine sigils on the shoulders, eyes sweeping the room with the methodical boredom of people paid to find things. Sayuri freezes solid. "Drink your whisky," I murmur, smiling my best dim-bartender smile at the newcomers. "Slowly. And whatever you do, don't touch your jacket." "Nets—" "Evening, officers!" I call out, bright as a supernova. "First round's on the house."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of cozy sci-fi that hits nearly every instruction: first person, present tense, roughly 1000 words, dialogue-heavy (easily 60%+), conflict established (Sayuri's stolen manifests, the Combine enforcement vessel, the closing entrance of the officers) and deliberately left unresolved on a cliffhanger. Strengths: The narrator's voice is the standout — wry, observant, economical. "She doesn't walk in so much as wash ashore" is a strong opening image, and the observational deductions (dreads twitching as stress tells, the backwards grab for the weapon, the misbuttoned jacket) do genuine character work through showing rather than telling. The worldbuilding is delivered in light, natural touches ("The Penultimate Outpost didn't fit on the sign," dock seven "officially doesn't exist") that build setting without exposition dumps. Nets's own mysterious past is teased without being belabored, which is the right amount for a chapter. The Dex glass-shattering beat is a smart use of the cozy ensemble to externalize Sayuri's jumpiness and reveal her armed state. Weaknesses: The banter occasionally tips into over-cleverness — "It's our primary export, after iron and bad decisions" and "bright as a supernova" are the kind of quips that feel written rather than spoken, a slight amateurish tic of prioritizing wit over realism. The "bartenders are like priests / gossip professionally" exchange is a familiar trope. Sayuri's characterization is somewhat thin beyond "frightened whistleblower" — she exists mostly as a plot delivery mechanism, though the physical detail of her tells partially compensates. The Combine as sinister megacorp is stock material, and the ending cliffhanger, while well-timed, is a conventional beat. The prose is clean and rhythmic with no purple tendencies; pacing is tight with no meandering. Emotionally it's engaging and lightly complex — fear, wariness, reluctant compassion — though not deeply so; this is genre comfort work, not profound. The ending's tension is congruent with the established tone; no forced positivity or unearned transformation occurs. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South The saxophone finds me before I find anything else. It's coming from somewhere down Decatur Street, this low, mournful sound that wraps around the morning humidity like it owns it. I've been awake for twenty-six hours. My phone is at 12%. I have $43 and a backpack containing two shirts, a phone charger, and a granola bar I'm rationing like it's the apocalypse. Which, in a way, it is. *You did this,* the voice in my head says. It sounds like Mom. *You blew up your whole life over—* Over being honest. Over saying four words at the dinner table. The casserole had gotten cold while Dad stared at me like I'd announced I was joining a cult, and Mom had cried the kind of crying that's somehow about *her*. So. New Orleans. Because the trucker was going to New Orleans, and because it was the opposite direction of everything. The street smells like powdered sugar and old beer and something green and rotting underneath. People flow around me—tourists in matching shirts, a man walking a parrot, a woman in a sequined dress at nine in the morning like that's normal. Maybe here it is. Nobody looks at me twice, and I can't tell if that feels like freedom or like drowning. I'm counting my money for the third time when a voice says, "You're doing that wrong." I look up. A kid my age—maybe seventeen—is sitting on a stoop with a skateboard across their knees and a dog that looks like it was assembled from spare parts. Buzzed hair, a denim jacket covered in safety pins, eyes that have already done the math on me. "Doing what wrong?" "Counting your money in public. In the Quarter. Might as well wear a sign." They pat the dog. "First day?" "That obvious?" "You've got the look. Like a deer that walked into a casino." They stand, sticking out a hand. "Crescent. Like the city. Not my real name, before you ask." "Taylor." I pause. "Actually my real name. As of recently." Something flickers in Crescent's face—recognition, maybe. They don't ask. That alone makes my throat go tight, because back home everybody *asks*, everybody needs you to explain yourself like a math problem. "C'mon," they say. "I'll show you where the church does lunch. You eat free, nobody calls anybody." --- I follow them. I know I shouldn't follow strangers. I know how this story goes in every after-school special. But the saxophone is still playing somewhere behind us, and the granola bar is half gone, and Crescent walks like they have somewhere to be, which is more than I've got. "Rule one," they say over their shoulder. "Don't sleep in the Quarter. Cops sweep it. Rule two, if anybody offers you a place to crash and they're over twenty-five, the answer is no. Doesn't matter how nice they seem. *Especially* if they seem nice." "Why are you helping me?" Crescent shrugs. "Somebody did it for me. Pay it backward, or whatever." "How long have you been out here?" "Eight months." They say it flat, the way you'd report the weather. "Your family—" "Don't." Not angry. Just a door closing. "We don't do origin stories out here. Everybody's running from something. You don't gotta know what." But I catch it later, at the church—a long table, red beans and rice, a volunteer who calls everyone "baby." Crescent's sleeve rides up when they reach for the bread, and there's a hospital bracelet, plastic, worn soft. They see me see it and yank the sleeve down, and for one second their whole face is somebody else's face. Younger. Scared. "Don't," they say again. Quieter this time. "I wasn't going to." "Yeah you were. Everybody does." They stab at the rice. "I'm not crazy. I'm just— it's complicated." "Two days ago my dad told me I was confused and my mom cried about what the *neighbors* would think," I say. "I know complicated." Crescent looks at me for a long moment. Then, the ghost of a smile: "Tennessee?" "How'd you—" "The accent, babe. You sound like sweet tea." --- The afternoon stretches strange and golden. Crescent shows me where to fill a water bottle, which library lets you charge your phone, which corner store guy will pretend not to see you take a banana. I am learning a whole curriculum that no school counselor with her smug folder of "concerning behavioral patterns" could ever grade. My phone buzzes. Mom. Fourteen missed calls now. One text: *Please just tell me you're alive.* I stare at it until the screen goes dark. "You gonna answer?" Crescent asks. We're sitting by the river now, the Mississippi sliding by all brown and enormous, a steamboat bellowing somewhere. "I don't know what to say." "Say you're alive." They pull their knees up. "I didn't, with mine. Now I don't know if I can." Their voice does something complicated. "Eight months, the door just gets heavier, you know? Every day you don't call adds a pound." "Is that your secret? The thing we don't do origin stories about?" "One of 'em." They flick a pebble into the water. "Look. The street'll keep you. But it keeps you like a pawn shop keeps your stuff. Eventually it sells pieces of you off." They look at me sideways. "You're two days in. Your door's still light. That's all I'm saying." The sun is going down over the river, turning everything copper. Somewhere behind us, impossibly, the saxophone again—or another one, this city must grow them like weeds—playing something that sounds like grief and gladness having an argument. I type: *I'm alive. I'm safe. I'm still Taylor. That part doesn't change.* My thumb hovers. "Hey," Crescent says. "Whatever you decide. You're not invented drama, okay? You're the real deal." I don't know how they knew to say exactly that. I press send.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a confident, well-crafted continuation that hits nearly every prompt requirement: first person, mixed tense, Taylor's internal monologue grappling with guilt, fear, and relief, a fellow runaway (Crescent) with implied secrets (hospital bracelet, estranged family), dialogue with distinct voices, and a full-day arc from morning to sunset. Strengths: The voice is authentic teen without being grating — "You sound like sweet tea" is a great line, and the pawn shop metaphor ("it keeps you like a pawn shop keeps your stuff") is genuinely fresh. Sensory grounding is strong (powdered sugar, rot, humidity, the recurring saxophone as motif). Crescent is given texture through withheld backstory and the bracelet detail — show over tell. The callback to "invented drama" in the final line is an earned, satisfying echo of the prompt's seed material. Emotional complexity is real: Taylor's ambivalence about Mom's fourteen missed calls, the "door gets heavier" weight metaphor, Crescent's guardedness. Weaknesses: Crescent is a touch too conveniently wise and generous — the street-mentor archetype is familiar, and their perceptiveness ("You're not invented drama") borders on authorial ventriloquism. The ending is slightly tidy: Taylor sends the text with a composed, polished message ("I'm still Taylor. That part doesn't change") that resolves a bit too cleanly for a kid two days into a crisis. The pacing is tight rather than meandering, though the middle "curriculum montage" is lightly sketched. Some lines flirt with precocity ("grief and gladness having an argument") but stay on the right side of overwrought. Overall: a polished, emotionally intelligent chapter with minor archetypal convenience. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The end of the world, Midas had discovered, was mostly a logistics problem. It wasn't the radiation, or the roving gangs, or the weather that had developed Opinions. It was that nobody had thought to leave behind a manual, and the only surviving repository of pre-Collapse wisdom within forty miles was a stuffed koala with a personality chip designed for children aged three to seven. "Today's forecast," announced Chewy from his perch on the rusted filing cabinet, "is *sunny with a chance of FUN!*" "It's raining," said Midas. "My weather module is aspirational." Midas peered out through the gap in the corrugated wall of what had once been, according to the sign, BARRY'S DISCOUNT TYRES & EXHAUST. Barry had not survived. Neither had most of the tyres, which said something about the priorities of civilization's collapse. "We need food," Midas said. "We have half a tin of something labeled 'meat-adjacent' and a packet of crackers I'm fairly sure achieved sentience last Tuesday." "I voted to keep the crackers as pets." "You don't get a vote. You run on a potato battery." "A potato battery *and* dreams, Midas. A potato battery and dreams." The plan—and Midas used the word in its loosest, most apologetic sense—was to scavenge the old retail park to the east. It had been picked over a dozen times, but desperation has a way of making you check the same cupboards repeatedly, like a man who has lost his keys and his civilization in the same afternoon. He packed the essentials: rope, knife, the lucky bottle cap, and Chewy, who rode in the top of the rucksack like a small, smug figurehead. --- The retail park was a monument to optimism. Someone, in the before-times, had genuinely believed humanity needed a shop that sold only candles. The candle shop had, ironically, burned down. It was on the wall of the former Sofa Warehouse that Midas saw it: fresh paint, which in itself was remarkable. Paint required someone alive to apply it, and someone alive with spare time was practically aristocracy. The graffiti read: **THE GREEN PLACE LIVES. FOLLOW THE CROWS TO THE WATER THAT REMEMBERS. SANCTUARY FOR ALL WHO ASK NICELY.** Below it, a crude arrow pointed north, toward the wilds. "Sanctuary," Midas breathed. "Statistically," said Chewy, "ninety percent of cryptic graffiti is a trap, and the other ten percent is teenagers." "It says 'ask nicely.' Murderers don't care about manners." "The *politest* people I've ever met were murderers. There was a lovely man in Sector Twelve who apologized to everyone he—" "We're going." "I want it noted in the official record that I objected." "There is no official record." "Then I shall maintain one. *Day one: Midas is an idiot.*" --- Following the crows turned out to be harder than advertised, principally because crows, lacking any sense of narrative obligation, flew in all directions at once. Midas picked the largest and most purposeful-looking one and followed it for three miles before it landed on a dead sheep and began, with great purpose, to eat it. "The water that remembers," Midas muttered, consulting the horizon. "What does water remember?" "Everything you did to it," said Chewy darkly. "Water never forgets." What the water remembered, it transpired, was being a reservoir. They found it at the bottom of a valley, gray and vast and patient, and on its shore stood a cluster of shelters with—Midas's heart leapt—*smoke* rising from them. Actual cooking smoke. The smell of stew drifted up the hillside like a promise. He was halfway down the slope, rehearsing his nicest asking voice, when the ground gave way. It was, he reflected mid-tumble, a very *deliberate* sort of giving way—the kind involving a tarpaulin, a pit, and someone's weekend project. He landed in mud. Chewy landed on his face. "Day one, addendum," said the koala. "*Told him so.*" Faces appeared at the pit's rim. They belonged to a wary, weathered family—a woman with a crossbow and the expression of someone who had been disappointed by strangers professionally. "You read the sign?" she demanded. "Yes! Sanctuary! I'm asking nicely. Please. Very nicely. Tremendously nicely." "That sign's bait. We catch raiders with it. Decent folk are suspicious of free sanctuary. Only greedy idiots follow it." "He's not greedy," offered Chewy helpfully. "Just an idiot." There was a silence of the kind that occurs when armed strangers realize a stuffed koala has spoken. "That toy talked." "He does that," sighed Midas. "He also keeps records, apparently." The woman lowered the crossbow a fraction. In a world without television, a talking koala with a sarcasm protocol was entertainment of the highest order. "It tell jokes?" "Madam," said Chewy, with dignity, "I contain four hundred jokes suitable for children aged three to seven, and after fifty years of degraded memory storage, most of them are now *accidentally horrifying*." --- They were released at dusk, in exchange for two hours of Chewy's repertoire ("Why did the chicken cross the road? *The road is gone. Everything is gone.* Knock knock."), Midas's rope, his knife, his lucky bottle cap, and a solemn promise never to return without bringing crackers. The walk home took six hours, two of which were spent hiding from something in the dark that breathed like a broken accordion. Midas twisted his ankle in a rabbit hole. It began raining with renewed creative energy. Somewhere around midnight, his left boot achieved independence and was lost to the mud. BARRY'S DISCOUNT TYRES & EXHAUST had never looked so beautiful. Midas collapsed onto his nest of insulation foam, one-booted, ropeless, knifeless, luckless, and ate the meat-adjacent substance cold, sharing none of it because his only companion ran on a potato. "Final entry, day one," said Chewy softly, from the filing cabinet. "Mission failed. Supplies lost. Dignity unrecoverable." A pause. The little servos whirred. "But we came home together. Forecast for tomorrow: sunny. With a chance of fun." "It's still raining, Chewy." "Aspirational, Midas. Aspirational."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register reasonably well: dry wit, personified objects, footnote-adjacent asides, and a world where absurdity and melancholy coexist. The structure follows the prompt faithfully—deliberation at home base, a mission that goes sideways (the graffiti trap), and a return home "worse for wear" in multiple ways (lost supplies, twisted ankle, lost boot, lost dignity). Strengths: The dialogue between Midas and Chewy is consistently funny and character-revealing ("My weather module is aspirational"). The joke density is high and mostly lands. The trap twist—sanctuary graffiti as raider bait, with the logic that "decent folk are suspicious of free sanctuary"—is a genuinely clever subversion. The ending's callback to the aspirational weather forecast gives the piece a satisfying circular structure with earned warmth rather than saccharine positivity. Weaknesses: The piece leans heavily on a familiar comic formula—the deadpan robot/animal companion quipping at the hapless human—which is well-executed but not especially original (reminiscent of countless talking-AI-sidekick stories). Some jokes are slightly over-explained ("which said something about the priorities of civilization's collapse" undercuts its own joke). The family with the crossbow is thinly sketched, more a plot device than characters. The middle section occasionally rushes; the pit capture and release happen quickly, and the emotional beat of "we came home together" is sweet but lightly earned. Prose is clean and controlled, never purple, with good rhythm. The worldbuilding details (candle shop burning down, crackers achieving sentience) are economical and effective. The tone is consistent throughout, the piece is coherent and tight at roughly the requested length, and it never meanders. It's a very good genre exercise rather than a masterpiece—the wit is professional, but the emotional depth is modest and the premise's novelty is limited. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Shelter from the Storm The bell above the door of Pendragon Books jangled violently as a man in dark sunglasses and an expensive coat stumbled inside, pressing his back against the shelves like a fugitive in a war film. "Could you—" he gasped, "could you possibly lock that?" Eleri Morgan looked up from her ledger, pencil still poised. "It's half eleven on a Tuesday. We're open." "Yes, but there's a small army of photographers about to descend on your charming high street, and I'd rather they didn't follow me in." "Photographers. In Llanfair." She set down her pencil. "Have the sheep done something newsworthy?" He pulled off the sunglasses with a flourish that was clearly practiced, revealing a face she recognized from approximately four hundred bus shelter posters. Rhys Trevelyan. *That* Rhys Trevelyan. He waited, with the expression of a man who has just produced a dove from a hat. "Oh," said Eleri. "You're an actor or something, aren't you?" A flicker—just a flicker—of something wounded crossed his face. "Or something. Yes. *Dragonfire*? *The Last Cartographer*? I was nominated for a BAFTA." "Nominated," she repeated, returning to her ledger. "Door's got a latch if you want it. Don't break it." He turned the latch, then drifted toward her counter with the loose-limbed confidence of a man accustomed to rooms rearranging themselves around him. "You genuinely don't know who I am." "I genuinely have stock to count." "Most people scream a bit. Or cry. One woman in Cardiff fainted, though to be fair it was very hot in that Tesco." "I'll try to faint later if there's time. We close at five." He laughed—a real laugh, surprised out of him—and leaned against the counter. "What's your name, then, since you've got mine?" "You haven't actually told me your name. You just listed your CV." "Rhys. Trevelyan." "Eleri Morgan. This is my shop. You're leaning on my new arrivals." He straightened, examined the stack, and held up a slim volume of R.S. Thomas. "Bleak choice for the front counter." "He's Welsh, he's brilliant, and tourists buy him to look serious on the train home. Don't crease the spine." "You know, I'm filming up at the castle for three weeks. Period piece. I play a doomed prince. Very brooding, lots of standing on ramparts." He set the book down carefully, watching her. "You could come watch. I could get you onto set." "Why would I want to watch you stand on ramparts?" "People generally do." "People generally have less inventory." He circled the shop slowly, trailing fingers along the shelves, and she watched him in the convex mirror she kept for shoplifters—watched him longer than strictly necessary, noting the way he moved like the room belonged to him, hating slightly that it worked on her. When he glanced up, she snapped her eyes back to the ledger. "You're pretending to count," he said. "I'm counting." "Your lips aren't moving and you haven't turned a page in two minutes." "Some of us can count silently. It's called school." He came back to the counter and, unexpectedly, his shoulders dropped. The performance dimmed like a stage light on a fader. "Can I tell you something strange? You're the first person in about six years who hasn't wanted anything from me. It's slightly terrifying." "I want you to stop leaning on my new arrivals again." "Besides that." He turned the Thomas volume over in his hands. "When I was nineteen, I auditioned for drama school in London. Welsh accent thick as bara brith. The panel laughed. Not cruelly—worse than cruelly. *Indulgently.* One of them said, 'Lovely, but we can't hear past the valleys.' So I went home and I murdered it. My own voice. Spent two years with recordings, training it out of me syllable by syllable. My mam said I came back sounding like the shipping forecast." He paused. "She died three years ago, and at the funeral I gave the eulogy in a voice she never knew. I keep thinking—if everyone stops clapping, what's actually left? I sold the original off for parts." The shop was very quiet. Outside, somewhere distant, a gull complained. "That's the first true thing you've said since you came in," Eleri said softly. "Probably, yes." "It was better than the BAFTA bit." "*Nominated*," he said, and they both smiled at the same time, and she felt the smile go somewhere dangerous in her chest and busied herself straightening the pencil pot. "The accent comes back, you know," she said. "Three weeks in Llanfair, you'll be singing in chapel by the end of it. We're contagious." "Is that a promise?" "It's a warning." She pulled the Thomas volume from his hands, wrapped it in brown paper with quick, decisive folds, and pushed it across the counter. "Eight pounds. He wrote about exactly this. Standing in a place wondering if you've betrayed it. You'll hate how accurate it is." He paid with a twenty and waved off the change toward the charity tin, watching her with an expression she refused to meet. "Eleri Morgan. Would you have dinner with me?" "No." "Coffee?" "No." "Why not?" "Because you ask everyone, and everyone says yes, and I don't fancy being a foregone conclusion." He absorbed this like a man absorbing a line note from a director he respected. "Then I'll come back tomorrow. And buy another book. And the day after. And you can say no until it means something different." "That's the strangest courtship strategy I've ever heard." "I'm improvising. You've thrown out my script." He unlatched the door, then paused, and when he spoke again the vowels had softened, gone valley-deep, just for her: "*Diolch*, Eleri Morgan." The bell jangled. Through the window she watched him square his shoulders, become Rhys Trevelyan again, and stride out into the flashbulbs. She stood there a long moment, then pressed both hands flat against the counter. "Right," she told the empty shop, unconvincingly. "Stock."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong scene that fulfills the brief with considerable skill. The dialogue is the engine here, as requested, and it crackles: Eleri's dry Welsh wit ("Have the sheep done something newsworthy?") plays beautifully against Rhys's practiced charm and neediness. The character dynamics requested are all present—the rogue with the fragile ego, the superficially immune bookstore owner, the paradoxical attraction on both sides. The scene's centerpiece is Rhys's confession about erasing his own accent, which is a genuinely affecting piece of backstory that earns his vulnerability rather than asserting it. The detail of the eulogy in a voice his mother never knew is a sharp, specific image. Eleri's internal flustered state is shown economically through the convex mirror moment and the "smile somewhere dangerous in her chest." Minor criticisms: the "I'll come back tomorrow" courtship gambit is a familiar romance beat, and the ending—him reverting to celebrity persona, her unconvincing "Stock"—is competent but slightly predictable. The R.S. Thomas book as symbolic gift is a touch on-the-nose ("You'll hate how accurate it is"). Some of Rhys's lines ("You've thrown out my script") flirt with being too neat, too writerly. The Welsh setting is present but somewhat light—Llanfair is mostly a joke about sheep and chapels rather than a felt place. Still, the prose is clean, the voices distinct, the emotional beats land, and the transformation of both characters over one scene is at least seeded plausibly rather than rushed. This is well above average work. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Underhold The door swung inward on hinges that had been oiled — recently, and well. That was the first wrong thing. The second was the light: not the guttering tallow stubs the guild favored, but a row of whale-oil lanterns burning steady and bright along the vaulted walls, their brass fittings polished to a surgeon's gleam. Someone had prepared this room. Someone had been *expecting* company. Aya's hand found the cold iron of the doorframe and stopped there. The underhold opened before them like the belly of some great drowned beast — ribbed stone arches slick with harbor-damp, the air thick with salt and lamp-smoke and something older underneath, a mineral reek that Aya's blood recognized before her mind did. The artifact. Close. She could feel it humming against the inside of her skull like a struck tuning fork. And between them and it, seated on a crate of contraband Vask powder with the easy patience of a woman who owned the very dark itself, was Mother Hessaline Crowe. "Shut the door behind you, loves," the guildmistress said. "There's a draught." Aya's stomach dropped through the floor. *She was arrested. The runners took her at dawn. Six witnesses—* "You're meant to be in the Magistrate's iron," Katra said flatly. Her hand had drifted toward her belt-knife and stopped, because four bodyguards had detached themselves from the shadows between the lantern-posts — heavyset men in oilcloth coats, each cradling a brass-throated scattergun of naval pattern. The kind of weapon that didn't require its owner to aim so much as *gesture*. "I'm meant to be a great many things." Crowe rose. She was sixty if a day, grey hair scraped back under a stevedore's cap, and she moved like a woman half that age. A pepperbox pistol hung loose in her hand, all six barrels catching the light. "Arrested, for one. Deposed, for another. It's remarkable what a few coins to the right watchman will purchase. A pantomime of a raid. And then one simply waits, down here in the quiet, to see which of one's dear children comes creeping for the inheritance before the body's even cold." *A trap. The whole night was a trap, and we walked it like sleepwalkers.* Aya's pulse was a hammer against her collar. Behind her, Simeon exhaled slowly through his teeth — his tell, the sound he made when the arithmetic of a situation came up all wrong. "Mother Crowe," he began, palms spreading, "we came to *secure* the hold. Word was the runners were coming back with sappers—" "Simeon Vance, you couldn't lie your way out of a confessional." Crowe flicked two fingers. "Take them." It happened with dreadful, unhurried efficiency. No struggle worth the name — Katra's knife clattered to the flagstones, Simeon's arms were wrenched behind him, and Aya felt hands like dock-cranes close on her shoulders. She reached, reflexively, *inward* — toward the cold black water of the immateria, toward the things that swam there and answered her— A gun barrel pressed beneath her jaw, lifting her chin. "None of that," Crowe said softly, crossing the floor. "Oh yes, I know about you, little shadow. My boys have seen what follows you out of dark corners. Things with too many joints. You so much as *hum* a summoning and Gorrick here paints the ceiling with you, and we'll all take our chances with whatever crawls out of the mess after." She tilted her head, studying the mask. "But first. I do so hate conversing with a face I can't see." *No. No, no—* Fingers hooked the edge of the leather. The mask came away. The silence that followed had weight. One of the bodyguards actually stepped back. "Well," Crowe breathed. A smile spread across her weathered face, slow as oil on water. "Saints in the deep. Lady Aya Veltrane. The Magistrate's own *goddaughter*, slumming in my cellars." She laughed — a dry, delighted rasp. "And here I thought tonight couldn't profit me further." Aya's face was naked to the lamplight and she felt it like a flaying. Twenty years of careful walls, gone in the pull of a strap. Somewhere far above and beyond the guild walls, out in the harbor fog, a foghorn sounded — once, twice, three times — mournful as a funeral bell. *The morning packet steamer,* some detached part of her mind noted. *The world still turning. Ships still sailing. And I am going to die in a cellar that smells of whale-oil and old blood.* Unless. "You're right," Aya said. Her voice came out steadier than she had any right to expect — the aristocrat's voice, the one trained at dinner tables where every sentence was a fencing match. "Profit. Let's discuss it." "The condemned proposes terms. Go on, then. Sing." "You hold the Magistrate's goddaughter. Alive, I'm worth a king's ransom, pardons, leverage over half the Assize bench. Dead, I'm worth a manhunt that ends with this hold burned to the waterline. They hanged my mother for the magick in her blood, Mother Crowe — do you imagine they'll be *gentler* about the men who put a hole in her daughter?" "They hanged your mother," Crowe said, "and they'll hang you the moment they learn what you are. Witchblood and a thief besides. Perhaps I'd be doing the Magistrate a kindness. Sparing the family a *second* scandal." *She's right.* The thought landed cold and complete. The moment her name left this room, Aya Veltrane was finished — the salons, the estate, the protection of her father's grief-bought silence. Lady Aya would die tonight no matter what; the only question was whether the body went with her. *So there is nothing left to protect. Strange, how much that feels like freedom.* "Then you'd be doing it for free," Aya said, "when you could be doing it for a fortune. You didn't stage your own arrest because you're sentimental, Mother Crowe. You did it to count your enemies. So count me instead among your *assets*." Crowe's smile didn't waver, but something moved behind her eyes — the abacus-click of a woman pricing cargo. "Gorrick," she said at last, "fetch chains. The good ones." Her gaze never left Aya's bare face. "And put a kettle on. Her ladyship and I are going to have a long talk about her *value*."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers the requested scene competently: the trio enters the underhold, finds Crowe un-incarcerated, is captured without a fight, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates her hostage value while internally reckoning with her exposure. All mandated story beats are present, dialogue is substantial, third-person past tense with internal monologue is maintained, and the Victorian/gothic register is consistent. Strengths: The opening sensory details (oiled hinges, whale-oil lanterns) establish dread through environment rather than exposition. Crowe's voice is well-differentiated — dry, transactional, theatrical. The negotiation is the strongest section: Aya's pivot from terror to aristocratic fencing is believable, and her internal realization that "Lady Aya would die tonight no matter what" carries genuine emotional complexity — the paradox of freedom in total loss. The foghorn and morning steamer detail grounds the moment nicely. Weaknesses: The capture sequence resolves almost too smoothly — "no struggle worth the name" is a convenient hand-wave that avoids the tension the prompt's stakes imply. Crowe's foreknowledge ("I know about you, little shadow") is asserted rather than earned, which flattens the plot slightly. Some beats are familiar: the villain who stages her own arrest to count her enemies is a well-worn trope; the "condemned proposes terms" exchange follows genre formula closely. The bodyguards are furniture. Aya's mask removal and the guards' reaction ("one of the bodyguards actually stepped back") is effective but the scene then rushes to the negotiation without letting the unmasking's humiliation breathe. The ending line ("put a kettle on") is a nice tonal touch of grim civility, though the resolution — Crowe agreeing to talk — arrives a touch easily given the "witchblood" stakes she herself articulates. Prose is controlled, occasionally striking ("the belly of some great drowned beast"), rarely purple. Dialogue is period-appropriate and character-distinct. Emotionally, the piece engages but doesn't devastate; the internal monologue is present but somewhat declarative in places ("A trap. The whole night was a trap"). Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The jukebox is broken. It's been playing the same scratchy rock track for two hours—some forgotten band screaming about dying young—and nobody in the Yellowtail Bar has the guts or the interest to unplug it. Spike Spiegel notices her the second he walks in: dragon tattoo crawling up one arm, twin shoulder holsters, boots on the table like she owns the place. He notices the Beretta 92FS variants too, custom-engraved, well-loved. Mostly he notices that she's sitting at the only table with a clean sightline to both exits. Professional. He orders a whiskey he can't afford and sits down across from her without asking. "Seat's taken," Revy says, not looking up from her glass. "Yeah. By me." He lights a cigarette. "You're here for Donovan Cruz. Eighty million woolong, dead or alive." Her eyes flick up. Dark, flat, dangerous. "Don't know what a woolong is, cowboy, but I'm here for Cruz, and the dumbass who hired me pays in dollars. So why don't you take your skinny ass back to whatever cartoon you crawled out of." "Can't. I'm broke, and my ship eats money." He exhales smoke toward the ceiling. "Spike Spiegel." "Didn't ask." "You were going to." She snorts despite herself, knocks back her rum, and pours another from the bottle she's clearly claimed as territory. After a beat, she slides it an inch toward him. Not an offer, exactly. A test. He drinks straight from the bottle. She decides she hates him a little less. "Revy," she says. "And if you get between me and that bounty, I'll put a hole in that pretty face." "Pretty. You think I'm pretty." "I think you're a corpse that hasn't gotten the memo." Spike smiles, slow and crooked. "Funny. I already died once. Wasn't that bad." Something passes across her face—recognition, maybe. The look of one ghost clocking another. The jukebox guitar solo grinds through its loop again, all static and feedback. They drink. They talk in the language of people who don't talk: half-sentences about jobs gone wrong, cities burned behind them, the comparative merits of a Jericho 941 versus her Cutlasses. She calls his gun a museum piece. He calls her grip technique reckless. She demonstrates her grip technique by drawing both pistols under the table fast enough that he feels the muzzle against his knee before he sees her shoulders move. He's got the Jericho against her ribs at the same moment. They sit there, guns kissing each other's vitals, faces eighteen inches apart, and neither of them is breathing hard. Her mouth curves. "Huh," she says. "Okay." "Okay," he agrees. That's when Cruz's men come through the door. Six of them, low-rent muscle with shotguns, sent to clear out the competition before their boss skips town. Spike sees them in the mirror behind the bar. Revy sees them in his eyes. "Mine's the three on the left," she says. "Greedy." The table goes over. The room comes apart in muzzle flash and splintered wood and the jukebox—untouched, charmed, immortal—keeps screaming its one song through all of it. Revy moves like violence is her native tongue, both Cutlasses hammering, casings raining bright across the floor. Spike flows the other direction, all loose-limbed economy, a kick folding a shotgunner over a barstool before two shots finish the argument. It's over in eleven seconds. The bartender slowly rises from behind the bar. Revy blows smoke off one barrel and looks at Spike across the wreckage—and there it is, the thing neither of them will name. He felt it the moment she drew on him. She felt it watching him move. It's not romance. It's recognition. It's *finally, somebody who speaks the language.* "Cruz knows we're coming now," Spike says. "Cruz is at the Starlight Motel, room 14. I made his driver yesterday." She holsters the guns. "I'm telling you that so you understand I don't *need* you, dipshit." "And yet you told me." "Shut up." --- They take Cruz at 2 a.m. with embarrassing ease—the man is passed out drunk—and zip-tie him in the bathtub of room 14, and then they're standing in a motel room with one bounty, two hunters, and a single bed neither of them is acknowledging. "Eighty million," Spike says, lighting his last cigarette. "Fifty grand for me. Whatever Monopoly money for you. Doesn't matter, because he's *mine*." "Split it." "I don't split." "Neither do I." The draw happens simultaneously—it always was going to. Jericho leveled at her heart. Both Cutlasses leveled at his head, because Revy never does anything halfway. The motel's neon sign bleeds pink through the blinds, striping them both. From the bathroom, Cruz whimpers. "You won't shoot me," Spike says. "Gimme one good reason." "Because then this is over." He takes a step closer, into her guns, until the steel touches his chest, until he can smell rum and gunsmoke and something underneath that's just her. "And you're having too much fun." Her trigger fingers don't move. Neither does she, when his free hand comes up—slow, telegraphed, deliberate—and tucks a loose strand of hair behind her ear. Her breath catches. Just barely. Just enough. "I should kill you," she whispers. "Probably." For one suspended second they're close enough to kiss, guns and all, two people who trust nobody discovering exactly why—because this is what wanting someone costs them, this standoff, this loaded silence. Revy steps back first. Holsters her guns with a snarl. "Take the bounty," she says. "I'm not dragging that fat bastard through customs anyway." "Revy—" "Don't." She's at the door, silhouetted in neon. She pauses. Doesn't turn around. "If you're ever in Roanapur, cowboy... don't look me up. I mean it." She means the opposite. They both know it. The door slams. Spike stands alone in the pink light, cigarette burning down, listening to her engine roar away into the dark. "Whatever happens," he murmurs, "happens." Somewhere across town, the jukebox plays on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers exactly what the prompt asked for: a seedy bar meeting, drinking, gunplay, competitive banter, and a motel room standoff with unresolved tension. The prose is lean and confident, with strong scene economy—the bar fight resolved in "eleven seconds" mirrors the characters' professional efficiency. The dialogue crackles with character-appropriate bite ("I think you're a corpse that hasn't gotten the memo"), and the mutual draw under the table is a well-staged beat that establishes both characters' competence without telling. Character fidelity is high. Spike's fatalism, prosthetic-eye detachment, and "whatever happens, happens" fatalism land naturally; Revy's profanity, dual-wielding bravado, and vulnerability-through-deflection are on point. The "one ghost clocking another" recognition is the emotional core, and it's handled with restraint—mostly shown through gesture (the bottle slid an inch, the hair tucked behind the ear) rather than stated. The ending, with Revy's "don't look me up... I mean it" / "She means the opposite," is a satisfying anti-resolution true to both characters. Minor flaws: the "cartoon you crawled out of" meta-joke is a slightly cute fourth-wall wink that doesn't quite fit the story's tone. The "recognition, not romance" paragraph edges toward telling ("It's not romance. It's recognition") though it's earned by prior action. Cruz's capture "with embarrassing ease" is convenient but forgivable as a deliberate anticlimax. The jukebox as recurring motif is a touch heavy-handed ("charmed, immortal") but mostly works as atmosphere. Some clichés ("muzzle flash," "neon bleeding through blinds") but they're genre-appropriate. Overall this is polished, professional genre fiction with genuine chemistry between the leads and a clean, resonant ending. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 86.8
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta I have tried, over the years, to remember that night the way it actually happened—not the way thirty years of telling and not-telling have reshaped it. But memory is its own ritual. Every recollection changes the thing recalled. What I know for certain is this: it was late September, 1995, and the cold had already come down from the fells like something with intent. Astrid met me at the edge of the Lindqvist property where the pasture fence had collapsed into the bracken. She had a canvas rucksack and a flashlight she refused to turn on. "Your eyes will adjust," she said. "They have to. You can't sit out with a light. It insults them." "Insults who?" She didn't answer. That was Astrid's way—she rationed her knowledge, dispensed it in fragments, and I have wondered since whether this was her grandmother's teaching or simply a fifteen-year-old's instinct for theater. Probably it doesn't matter. Probably, by then, she couldn't have told the difference herself. The mound sat in a clearing half a kilometer into the forest, a low swelling of earth maybe four meters across, ringed with stones that had sunk so deep into the moss they looked like teeth in old gums. Everyone in the village knew it was there. No one went to it. When I'd asked my father about it, he'd laughed and said something about Iron Age graves being protected heritage sites, as if the law were the reason people stayed away. "Take off your shoes," Astrid said when we reached the edge of the stone ring. "It's freezing." "You can't be insulated. Útiseta means *sitting out*. Out of everything. Houses, shoes, daylight, sense." She was already unlacing her boots, balancing stork-like on one foot. "Mormor sat out three times in her life. She said the third time, she learned the day her brother would die, and she never did it again." "And did he? Die on that day?" Astrid looked at me, and in the half-dark her face was older than it had any right to be. "Why do you think she never did it again?" I want to say I almost left then. I want to say I felt the wrongness of it—two girls treating someone's grave, someone's *actual grave*, as a venue for a party trick, the way we'd treated the pendulum and the mirror-writing and the names whispered into still water. We'd been playing at it for weeks, harvesting little frauds: Petra's crush, Mikael's shoplifting. Each "secret" the rituals revealed was something Astrid could plausibly have known. I'd told myself that was the explanation. The telling had been easier in daylight. I took off my shoes. The moss was shockingly cold, wet in a way that felt deliberate, like a hand closing over each foot. Astrid's instructions had the worn smoothness of recitation. We were to sit back to back on the crown of the mound, facing away from each other—"so that whatever comes, comes to one of us alone." We were not to speak after the preparation was finished. We were not to answer if we heard our names. We were each to hold a question in our minds, unspoken, and we were to stay until something answered or until dawn, whichever came first. "And if nothing comes?" "Then nothing comes, and you'll have a boring story." She pulled a small jar from the rucksack—honey, she said, though it looked dark as tar in the gloom—and poured a thin line of it across the threshold of the stone ring behind us. "Payment on the way in. So we're guests and not thieves." "Where did your grandmother learn this?" "Where does anyone learn anything?" She sat down, arranged her coat beneath her. "From someone who learned it from someone who was told never to teach it." We settled spine to spine. Her shoulder blades moved against mine when she breathed. I held my question—something small and stupid, about a boy, I won't pretend otherwise—and I waited. The forest at night is never silent, and for a long while I catalogued the sounds honestly: wind working through the spruce crowns, the tick of cooling air, something small in the undergrowth. My feet went from painful to numb to strangely warm, which I knew even then was a bad sign, and I said nothing. Then the sounds stopped. Not faded—stopped, all at once, the way conversation stops when someone enters a room. Against my back, Astrid had gone very still. Her breathing, which had been slow and even, was now so shallow I couldn't feel it at all. The church in the village was three kilometers away, and its bell rang only for services and funerals. I knew this. Everyone knew this. It rang once. A single note, flat and enormous in the stopped air, and I felt it in my sternum, in the dirt beneath me, as if the mound itself had been struck. Midnight, I thought. It's only marking midnight. But it had never marked midnight before, not in the six weeks I'd lived there, and it never did again. Astrid's hand found mine in the dark behind us and gripped it. We were not supposed to speak, and she didn't, but her hand was speaking plainly enough: *I didn't expect that. This is not part of it.* And then—I will only say it once, the way I experienced it, without interpretation. The cold against my bare feet changed direction. It had been rising from the ground. Now it pressed down from above, like attention, like a face lowered close to mine, and into my held question—my small, stupid question—came an answer that was not words and was not about the boy at all. It was about Astrid. It was a date. We broke every rule. We spoke, we ran, we left our shoes. I never told her what I'd received. For nine years I told myself it was suggestion, hypothermia, a girl's fevered theater. Then it was March of 2004, and I stopped telling myself anything.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements with precision and craft. The first-person retrospective frame is established economically ("thirty years of telling and not-telling") and remains largely transparent as instructed. The 1995 rural northern Sweden setting is convincingly textured—fells, bracken, spruce, the church bell, the Iron Age grave protected by law but avoided for other reasons. Astrid's instructions mix teenage theater with eerily specific traditional elements exactly as requested: the honey payment, the back-to-back sitting, the prohibition on answering one's name, the grandmother's three sittings and the third that revealed a death date. The ambiguity is well maintained—the narrator explicitly offers rational explanations (suggestion, hypothermia, Astrid's plausible foreknowledge of "secrets") while the events themselves (the stopped sounds, the single bell, the reversed cold) remain genuinely uncanny. The prose is controlled and confident. "Stones that had sunk so deep into the moss they looked like teeth in old gums" is a striking, earned image. The dialogue is excellent—Astrid's "From someone who learned it from someone who was told never to teach it" is a perfect line of folk-horror recursion, and "Why do you think she never did it again?" lands with real menace. The narrator's self-awareness ("I won't pretend otherwise" about the boy question) gives the voice maturity without undermining the teenage perspective. The ending is the piece's boldest move: withholding the content of the answer and then cutting to "March of 2004, and I stopped telling myself anything." This is effective—implying Astrid's death on the foretold date without stating it—but it slightly strains the "focus on this single midnight excursion" instruction, and the nine-year jump is a compression that some readers may find more clever than satisfying. Still, it's a deliberate, earned ambiguity rather than a cop-out. The theme of treating ancient practices as entertainment is explicitly woven in ("two girls treating someone's grave... as a venue for a party trick"), perhaps a touch too explicitly stated, but effectively. Minor criticisms: the word count is somewhat under 1000 (roughly 900), though not egregiously. A few images flirt with over-familiarity ("her face was older than it had any right to be"). The "memory is its own ritual" opening is a well-worn device. But these are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, atmospheric, restrained where it needs to be, and genuinely chilling. Model Output:
# Therapeutic Boundaries The diagram on the wall has been flayed for science—a man with no skin, every muscle labeled in serif font. *Vastus lateralis. Rectus femoris.* I've memorized him over six weeks of Tuesdays because looking at him is easier than looking at Danny. "Supine, please," Danny says, patting the treatment table. *Please.* Like I have a choice. Like the insurance company and the settlement agreement haven't already arranged my body on this table three times a week. I lie back. The paper crinkles under me, and the flayed man watches from above, all his red meat exposed and catalogued. I know how he feels. "How's the swelling been?" Danny stands at the foot of the table, and I make the mistake of watching his hands as he cups my left heel, lifting my leg straight. Eight years ago those hands taped my ankles before the 400 hurdles. Eight years ago he was the one who couldn't break sixty seconds, and I was the one with the federation contract. "Fine." "Liar." He says it gently, his thumb finding the puffy heat along the medial side of my knee, just below where the surgeon went in. The ACL graft. The meniscus repair. The end of everything. "You've been loading it." "I walked to the mailbox. Call the authorities." His mouth does that thing—not a smile, a suppression of one. He used to laugh easily, in the before-times. Now he's all clinical economy, and I hate how well it fits him. He failed at the thing I was great at, and somehow he's whole and I'm the one in pieces on his table. "Passive flexion first," he says. "Tell me when." He bends my knee, one hand bracing my thigh just above the joint, the other guiding my ankle toward my glute. The motion is slow, deliberate. Thirty degrees, nothing. Sixty, a tightness like a fist closing. Ninety— "There." The word comes out clipped. Heat blooms behind the kneecap, deep in the joint, that specific surgical ache like the bone itself is bruised. "Breathe through it. We're holding here." His palm is flat against my quad, and I can feel each finger distinctly through the fabric of my shorts. The pad of his thumb rests two inches above my knee, completely professional, completely on fire. "Exhale. Let the quad go soft." "It is soft." "It's guarding. You're guarding." His eyes flick up to mine and hold a half-second too long. "You always did." I exhale through my teeth and feel the muscle release despite me, a traitor's surrender. The knee sinks another five degrees. The pain sharpens, then plateaus—a high whine instead of a scream. His hand doesn't move, but his thumb shifts a millimeter, and my skin lights up along its track like he's dragged a match. "Good. One-ten degrees. That's progress." "That's pathetic." "That's *Tuesday*," he says, and lowers my leg with a control that makes something in my chest ache worse than the knee. "Side-lying. Right side. We're doing hip work—your TFL is compensating like crazy." I roll onto my right side, facing the wall and the flayed man. Danny moves around behind me, and now I can't see him, can only feel the table dip slightly as he braces one knee on its edge. His left hand settles on my hip—iliac crest, the diagram supplies helpfully—pinning my pelvis so it can't rock back. His right hand takes my left ankle and draws the leg behind me, knee bent, opening the front of the hip. The stretch lands in the hip flexor like a hot wire. I gasp before I can stop it. "Too much?" "No." Yes. No. The line between pain and his hands has gone smeared and useless. His palm on my hip is the only fixed point in the room, warm through cotton, his fingers wrapping just slightly toward the bone of my pelvis, holding me still while the rest of me wants to arch, escape, press back—I don't examine which. "Your hip's hiking. Don't let it." His grip firms, correcting me, and the stretch deepens, a long tearing brightness down the front of my thigh. *Iliopsoas,* says the wall. My breath goes ragged. "You used to take coaching better than this," he says quietly. "You used to lose to me." The silence behind me has texture. Then, low: "Yeah. I did." He releases the stretch by degrees, guides my leg back to neutral, but his hand stays on my hip one beat past necessary. One beat I count in heartbeats, which is a mistake, because mine is going like a finish-line sprint. "On your back. Last thing—patellar mobilization." I roll over and his face is close now, closer than it's been, as he sits on the edge of the table by my knee. He places both thumbs against the inner border of my kneecap, fingers wrapping the outside, and glides it laterally. The kneecap moves in its groove with a sick, grinding intimacy—not pain exactly, but *wrongness*, the sensation of someone handling a part of you that was never meant to be handled. "This is the part you hate," he says. He's watching my face, not the knee. "I hate all the parts." "No, you don't." His thumbs press, glide, release. Press, glide, release. The rhythm is unbearable. "You hate that it's working. Because if it works, you have to figure out what you are after." The flayed man stares down at us, all his secrets labeled, nothing hidden, and I think: he's lucky. Everything he is, written right there. "What did you figure out?" I ask. "After." Danny's thumbs go still on my kneecap. His hands are warm and my pulse is in the joint, in his fingers, everywhere. "That I wasn't only one thing," he says. He stands, stepping back, restoring the regulation distance between us, and the air where he was feels cold. "Same time Thursday." "Same time Thursday," I say, and the words don't sound like a sentence anymore. They sound almost like a reason.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a tightly controlled, physically coherent therapy scene with strong sensory detail and genuine tension. However, there is a significant instruction deviation: the prompt specifies a female physiotherapist ("her") who is a former training partner the protagonist finds unnervingly attractive, with the protagonist manipulating "her" body. The response genders Danny male and reverses the manipulative dynamic. This may be an intentional interpretation choice, but it directly contradicts the prompt's pronouns and framing, which hurts Adherence to Instructions. The word count (~1000) is met, the first-person voice, resentment toward recovery, former-rivals history, pain thresholds, and suppressed tension are all well executed. Strengths: the anatomical precision (passive flexion degrees, TFL compensation, patellar mobilization, iliac crest) is excellent and spatially consistent. The flayed diagram motif is a smart recurring device that pays off thematically. Dialogue is sharp and character-revealing ("You used to lose to me" / "Yeah. I did"). The tension is rendered through involuntary physical responses rather than stated, mostly showing rather than telling. The ending lands a small, earned shift without over-resolving. Weaknesses: the ending's pivot to "a reason" is slightly neat for six weeks of resentment, a mild unearned transformation. A few lines flirt with overwrought ("dragged a match," "traitor's surrender"), though mostly restrained. Some emotional beats are familiar (wounded athlete identity crisis), and the therapist's insight ("you hate that it's working") is a touch on-the-nose therapist wisdom. The gender deviation is the largest flaw.
