+ Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Dragon's Ledger The morning gun at Whampoa woke me with my teeth already aching. I lay in my berth aboard the *Andromache* counting the hours since my last pipe—eleven, perhaps twelve—and my thumb found the jade monkey in my waistcoat pocket before I had properly opened my eyes. The little fellow's back had gone smooth as river-stone from my worrying. "Lieutenant Merrick, sir." Midshipman哈Davies at the cabin door, all of sixteen, smelling of tar and breakfast. "Captain Elliott requests the inventory of the gun deck stores by noon." "Tell the Captain I'm bound ashore. Comprador business. The water casks." "The water casks were settled Tuesday, sir." I looked at him until he dropped his eyes. "Were they, Mr. Davies? Then I suppose I'd best confirm it." --- The sampan woman who rowed me to Jackass Point knew me by now. She had a face like a walnut and she watched me rub the monkey with something I chose not to call pity. "You go Hog Lane again," she said. Not a question. "I go where the King's business takes me." She laughed at that, a single bark, and spat into the brown Pearl. The river stank of fish guts and night soil and somewhere beneath it all the sweetness of joss smoke from the temple on Honam side. My hands had begun their morning tremble. I pressed the jade harder. --- In the Thirteen Factories quarter I found Renwick outside the Creek Factory, fanning himself with his hat. A supercargo's clerk with debts of his own, and useful for it. "James. You look like a dug-up corpse." "I need the Howqua introduction you promised. The matter we discussed." "The matter we discussed requires forty dollars, and you owe me twelve already." He leaned close. His breath was all garlic and Madeira. "There's another way. Dent's people want a man who can read a naval signal book. Want to know patrol schedules on the outer anchorage. A man who knew when the cutters ran might mention it, casual-like, over a drink." The sweat came on me then, cold under my collar despite the wet furnace of the Canton morning. Somewhere a coppersmith was hammering, each strike landing behind my eyes. "That's a hanging matter, Renwick." "It's eight taels of silver, is what it is. Think on it. You've until the noon gun." --- I thought on it for the length of Old China Street, past the bird-sellers and the men hawking glass paintings of ships I might once have been proud to serve aboard. By the time I reached Hog Lane I had stopped thinking on it at all, because the shaking had spread to my knees and the lane's smell—samshu liquor, frying pork, and under it, faint and unmistakable, the toffee-dark perfume of the smoke—had narrowed the world to a single appetite. Old Chen's shop sold lacquerware in the front room. In the back room it sold forgetting. "Lieutenant." Chen did not bow. He had stopped bowing months ago, which told me precisely what I had become. "You have silver today?" "I have this." I laid my second-best sextant on the counter, wrapped in oilcloth. He unwrapped it slowly. Outside, a man was singing to a caged thrush. "Navy property?" "My own property." "Mm." He turned the instrument in the light from the doorway, and the brass threw a small sun against the wall. "Half a tael of chandu. No more." "It's worth twenty times that." "Then sell it to a ship's master, Lieutenant." He set it down and waited. He knew. They always knew. The monkey was hot in my fist now, my thumbnail working the groove of its little grinning face. "Half a tael," I said. --- The divan was up a ladder-stair, a low room with rush mats and three other ruined men, one of them a Parsee merchant I recognized and pretended not to. The boy prepared the pipe with a needle, toasting the pill over the lamp until it bubbled and swelled, and the waiting was its own exquisite cruelty—the soft crackle, the lamp-flame steady as a saint's devotion. Then the long bamboo stem, the porcelain bowl inverted over the flame, and I drew the smoke down into the trembling center of myself. The coppersmith's hammer stopped. The sweat dried. Canton went quiet and golden, and for an hour I was again the man who had taken a French prize off Lissa, the man my father had toasted in the parlor at Portsmouth, the man whose hands did not shake. The jade monkey sat loose and forgotten in my pocket. --- The noon gun was firing as I came down Hog Lane. Renwick was waiting at the corner of the square, beneath the flagpoles where the ensign hung dead in the heat. "Well, James?" The smoke makes everything reasonable. That is its particular genius. Treason becomes a conversation; a conversation becomes eight taels; eight taels become a fortnight without selling instruments to Chen. "The cutters run the Lintin passage Thursdays and Sundays," I heard myself say. "Inner anchorage patrol changed last month. I'll write out the rest for the silver in hand." He smiled and pressed the cloth-wrapped weight into my palm, and we stood a moment in the white sunlight like two honest men concluding honest business, while behind us the factories' clocks disagreed about the hour. --- That evening, in the sampan back to Whampoa, the walnut-faced woman rowed and said nothing. The river had gone the color of old pewter. Already, beneath my ribs, I could feel the first faint stirring—not pain yet, only the dragon turning over in its sleep, patient, certain of tomorrow. I took out the monkey and began, gently, to rub its worn green back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that largely delivers on the brief. The prose is disciplined and period-appropriate, with a dry, self-loathing wit that suits a naval officer in decline ("In the back room it sold forgetting" is a particularly fine line). The structure — a single day, segmented by encounters — is tight and purposeful, moving from ship to river to factory quarter to divan to betrayal and back, with the noon gun and evening return giving a genuine sense of temporal shape. Sensory detail is rich without tipping into excess: the toffee-dark perfume of the smoke, the coppersmith's hammer landing "behind my eyes," the sampan woman's walnut face, the ensign hanging dead in the heat. The jade monkey as a recurring talisman of anxiety is an effective unifying device, and its final reappearance ("began, gently, to rub its worn green back") lands the ending with quiet, earned bleakness — the cycle continuing. The dialogue is the engine of the piece, as instructed, and it is mostly excellent: clipped, class-inflected, and revealing. Renwick's recruitment into treason is handled with plausible indirection ("casual-like, over a drink"), and Chen's refusal to bow — "which told me precisely what I had become" — is economical characterization. The sampan woman's single bark of laughter does good work. Weaknesses: there is a stray artifact ("Midshipman哈Davies") that is an outright error and breaks immersion. The supporting cast, while well-drawn in strokes, are somewhat stock types — the corrupt clerk, the impassive dealer, the shrewd boatwoman — and the plot beats (pawning the sextant, betraying patrol schedules) are familiar moves in addiction fiction, executed well but not surprising. The Parsee merchant "recognized and pretended not to" is a nice touch of shame, but the moral descent is otherwise fairly linear and predictable. The opium den sequence leans slightly on convention (the ruined men, the ritual of the pipe), though the detail of the porcelain bowl and the "saint's devotion" flame elevates it. The self-deception theme is occasionally stated rather than shown ("The smoke makes everything reasonable. That is its particular genius") — though this is arguably deliberate first-person rationalization, it edges toward telling. The ending's darkness is well-earned: the dragon "patient, certain of tomorrow" is an earned image rather than a sentimental one, and the piece never redeems Merrick cheaply. Voice and tone are consistent throughout, first person past tense as required, and the word count and "primarily dialogue" instruction are respected. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# UPHILL ALL THE WAY: An Advice Column *The boulder had reached the seventeenth switchback, which Sisyphus privately considered the nice bit, where the gradient eased and you could think. Crow perched on top of the boulder, which Sisyphus had pointed out several times did not help, quill tucked behind where an ear would be if crows had ears.* "First letter," said Crow. "Smells of lavender and desperation." --- **Dear Uphill,** My mother-in-law has opinions about everything. My cooking, my curtains, the way I fold towels. Last week she refolded my entire linen cupboard while I was at the market. My husband says she "means well." I am beginning to fantasize about the sea taking her. Is this wrong? — Folded in Thessaly **Dear Folded,** The sea is busy, and your mother-in-law would only criticize its technique. Here is the thing about people who refold your towels: they are not really talking about towels. She has spent forty years being the woman whose towels mattered, and now she watches that role pass to you and doesn't know what to do with her hands. This doesn't excuse it. But it tells you what to do, which is not to defend the towels — you will lose, and anyway, who cares about towels — but to give her hands something else. Ask her to teach you one thing. One. Something small that she's genuinely good at. People who feel needed inspect less. Your husband, meanwhile, needs to hear the sentence "She may mean well, but you live here." Say it once, calmly, at a moment when nothing is on fire. Repetition won't help. Some things only land the first time, or never. — S. *(Crow's note: He folds nothing. He owns one cloth. I've seen it. — C.)* --- *The boulder rolled back down. Sisyphus watched it go with the expression of a man watching a familiar dog return with a familiar stick, then started after it, Crow gliding alongside.* "Next one's been opened and resealed," said Crow. "Not by me. Mostly not by me." --- **Dear Uphill,** I work as a scribe for a magistrate who takes credit for everything I write. My elegant phrasing, my legal reasoning — he reads it aloud at banquets as his own. When I raised it, he said, "That's what scribes are *for*." I want to quit but I have a family and quitting is for people with savings. What do I do? — Invisible in Corinth **Dear Invisible,** Don't quit yet. First, get loud quietly. Every document you produce, make a copy. Date it. Keep it somewhere your magistrate doesn't go, which I suspect includes the archives, any place requiring stairs, and the truth. You are not doing this to confront him. You are doing this because reputations are slow buildings, and you are laying bricks no one can see yet. Second: find the other scribes. There are always other scribes. Magistrates come and go — usually via scandal, occasionally via banquet-related incident — but the people who actually know how things work talk to each other, and they remember who was good. When your magistrate needs replacing, and he will, the question "who actually wrote his rulings?" will be asked in a back room somewhere. Make sure your name is the answer. The work being yours is a fact. Facts are patient. Be patient with them. — S. *(Crow's note: He dictates everything to me and I get no credit either. The irony is a flat circle. — C.)* --- **Dear Uphill,** This is delicate. My wife and I have been married eleven years. Recently she suggested we invite our neighbor — a sculptor, very good forearms — into our bed. I said yes, mostly out of surprise. It went... extremely well. Too well? Now I worry I've enjoyed it for the wrong reasons and she enjoyed it for the right ones, or possibly the reverse. Also he keeps leaving chisels at our house. — Sculpted in Argos **Dear Sculpted,** The chisels are the only actual problem in this letter, and even they are just a man hoping to be invited back. You enjoyed it. She enjoyed it. You're now hunting for the wrongness because eleven years of marriage teaches a person that good things come itemized with hidden costs. Sometimes they do. But the way to find out is not to interrogate your own enjoyment until it confesses to something. It's to ask her one question — "How are you feeling about all this?" — and then do the difficult part, which is to listen to the answer she gives rather than the one you've been rehearsing her giving. If the answers match, you have a sculptor situation, which history suggests people have survived. If they don't, you've found it early, which is when finding things is cheapest. Return the chisels. Or don't. But decide together; that's rather the whole point now. — S. *(Crow's note: He read this one twice. "For clarity," he says. — C.)* --- *The summit again. Sisyphus set his shoulder, paused, and let it go. The boulder departed with its usual enthusiasm.* "Last one," said Crow. "Short. Bad handwriting. The really sad ones always have bad handwriting." --- **Dear Uphill,** I'm thirty-four and I don't know what my life is for. Everyone around me seems to be building toward something. I just do the same things every day and nothing accumulates. What's the point? — Nowhere in Particular **Dear Nowhere,** I want to be careful here, because you've asked the biggest question there is and you deserve better than something embroiderable. You say nothing accumulates. I'd look again. You wrote to a stranger today, which means some part of you still believes tomorrow is negotiable — that's not nothing. The people around you who seem to be building toward something? Most of them are also doing the same things every day. They've just chosen a story to tell about it. The story isn't a lie, exactly. It's a handle. Things are easier to carry with handles. You don't need a purpose. You need a Tuesday you're mildly looking forward to. Start there. Purpose, in my experience, is rarely found at the top of anything. It's usually somewhere on the way up, around the seventeenth turn, where the ground levels out enough to notice you're still walking, and that the walking is yours. Write again in a month. I'll be here. I'm always here. — S. *(Crow's note: He hummed the whole way down after this one. Off-key. I'm billing for emotional damages. — C.)*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an exceptionally well-executed piece that hits nearly every instruction in the brief. The epistolary format is maintained with light scene-setting interjections between letters, each tied to the boulder routine without belaboring it. Sisyphus's voice is warm, grounded, and dryly funny — very Pratchett-adjacent without being pastiche. The advice is the standout: each letter gets genuinely practical, specific counsel (give the mother-in-law's hands something to do; document your work and network with other scribes; ask one question and listen to the real answer). None of it is generic fortune-cookie wisdom, and crucially, almost none of it leans on boulder metaphors — the single allowed one ("around the seventeenth turn, where the ground levels out") is slipped in subtly and lands beautifully because it's earned by the earlier scene-setting at the seventeenth switchback. Crow is a superb comic device. The editorial notes ("The irony is a flat circle," "I'm billing for emotional damages") provide deadpan counterpoint without stealing scenes, and Crow's dialogue ("Smells of lavender and desperation") is understated and characterful. The risque letter (Sculpted in Argos) is handled with wit and tact — the chisels as the "only actual problem" is a great deflection of potential awkwardness. The final letter on purpose is the emotional peak, and it earns its warmth: "You need a Tuesday you're mildly looking forward to" is a genuinely good line, and "I'll be here. I'm always here" carries quiet weight given his situation without ever stating it. Show-don't-tell is largely respected — his contentment is demonstrated through routine and tone rather than declared. Minor criticisms: the mother-in-law letter's "the sea is busy" opener is the funniest line but the sea-taking fantasy is slightly underexploited. The Invisible-in-Corinth response, while practical, edges toward being the least Pratchett-like moment — it's more solid career advice than comedy. The Crow notes are used four times with the same rhythm; a slight risk of formula, though each is good enough to justify it. The word count exceeds the 1000-word seed somewhat, though the seed is a guideline rather than a hard cap. The prose is clean, sentences flow naturally, the humor is understated as requested, and the ending lands with earned, gentle positivity rather than incongruent sentimentality. Prompt:
Lost & Found in Osaka Slice of Life / Coming-of-Age: First Connection. Write one scene within a larger story set in Osaka, Japan. A shy, introverted teenager & synthesizer nerd, is browsing the electronics district of Den Den Town. She is drawn to the sound of an electric guitar. A girl, slightly older and radiating confidence, is busking near the entrance to a crowded arcade, playing a blistering rendition of a classic anime theme. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Lost & Found in Osaka The guitar cut through the noise of Den Den Town like a blade through paper—distorted, fast, unmistakably the opening riff of *Cruel Angel's Thesis*, but rearranged, bent into something new. Mio stopped walking. Her headphones, perched loosely over her ears as always, weren't even playing anything. She'd just had them on for armor. She drifted toward the sound, past the discount cable shop, past the retro game store, until she found the source: a girl in a cropped denim jacket, cherry-red Stratocaster copy, small battery amp at her feet, a scattering of coins in an open guitar case. A crowd had half-formed near the arcade entrance, the way Osaka crowds do—watching while pretending not to watch. Mio didn't pretend. She stood directly in front, staring at the busker's pedalboard. The song ended in a squall of feedback. Scattered applause. The busker grinned, bowed theatrically, and then noticed the girl with the enormous headphones who hadn't clapped, hadn't moved, and was still staring at her feet—no, at the floor *near* her feet. "Oi. You okay there? You've been glaring at my pedals for like two whole minutes." "Oh. Um. Sorry. I wasn't—I mean, I was, but not in a—" Mio's headphones slipped forward as she ducked her head. She shoved them back. "Your delay pedal. It's set to dotted eighths. That's why the riff sounded different. Most people play it straight." The busker blinked. Then laughed—a big, open sound. "Okay, that's the first time anyone's noticed that. Usually I just get 'play One Piece next!'" "It's a good choice. The dotted eighth thing. It makes the melody... um. Breathe weird. In a good way. Sorry, that's not a real—I don't know the technical term." "'Breathe weird' is now the official technical term. I'm using that forever." The busker crouched, unplugged her guitar. "You play?" "No. I mean—not guitar. I do... synthesizers." Mio said it quietly, like a confession. "*Do* synthesizers. Like, what, you build them?" "Sometimes. Mostly I just... I have a Juno-106 I fixed up. The voice chips were dying so I—" She stopped. "Sorry. This is boring." "A 106? Are you joking? Those things cost a fortune now. You *fixed* one?" "The chips fail a lot. There's a guy in Nipponbashi who sells clone chips, so it wasn't—it wasn't hard. Just soldering." Nod. Headphones slipped. She caught them this time before they fell. "Just soldering, she says." The busker stood, slinging the guitar across her back. "Okay, what's your name? I'm Rin." "Mio." "Mio. Cool. Question, Mio: have you eaten?" "...What?" "Food. The thing humans do. There's a kaitenzushi around the corner, plates start at a hundred yen, and I just made—" she scooped the coins from her case, weighed them in her palm— "approximately enough to feel rich for one hour. You're coming." "Oh. No, I couldn't—you don't have to—" "I know I don't *have* to. I'm choosing to. Big difference." Rin was already packing the amp. "Besides, you're the only person all day who said anything interesting. Everyone else just requested Ghibli songs." "Ghibli songs are good though." "Ghibli songs are *great*, but I can only play 'Country Roads' so many times before I lose my mind. Come on." --- The conveyor belt hummed past their booth. Rin had already stacked three plates. Mio held a cup of green tea with both hands like it might escape. "So the 106," Rin said around a mouthful of salmon. "What do you make with it? Like, actual songs?" "Sort of. Loops, mostly. I layer them on my laptop. They're not—nobody's heard them." "Nobody? Zero people?" "My mom heard one through the wall once. She asked if the washing machine was broken." Rin choked on her rice. "That's the best review I've ever heard. Put it on the album cover. 'Sounds like a broken washing machine'—five stars." Mio almost smiled. Her headphones slipped as she nodded; she pushed them back automatically. "What about you? Do you just do covers, or..." "Covers pay for sushi. But I write stuff. It's all guitar, though, and honestly it sounds kind of empty. Like there's a hole in the middle where something else should be." Rin pointed her chopsticks at Mio. "Something synthy, maybe." "...Are you—is that a—" "It's a hint, yes. I'm hinting. Loudly. I'm basically yelling." "You haven't even heard anything I've made. It might be terrible." "Might be. Or might breathe weird. In a good way." Rin grabbed a passing plate of tamago and set it in front of Mio. "Eat. You've been guarding that tea like a museum piece." Mio picked up the egg sushi. Ate it. Quietly: "There's a song I made last month. It's in seven-eight. I couldn't make it work in four. It just wanted to be... lopsided." "Seven-eight." Rin leaned back, grinning. "Mio. We met forty minutes ago and you're already telling me about your secret odd-time-signature songs. Do you know how long it takes most people to admit that? Years. Therapy, sometimes." "You asked!" "I did ask. I'm very good at asking." She pulled out her phone, slid it across the table. "Number. I practice in my uncle's garage in Naniwa Ward on Sundays. Bring the Juno. Or don't bring it and just come laugh at my chord progressions. Either way." Mio stared at the phone. The conveyor belt clicked past—tuna, mackerel, a pudding cup nobody wanted. "My loops really might be bad," she said, typing her number anyway. "Then we'll make them worse together. That's what bands are for." "We're a band now?" "Sunday," Rin said, stealing the pudding off the belt, "we'll find out." Mio nodded. Her headphones slipped all the way off this time. She didn't put them back on.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong scene that fulfills the prompt's core requirements with notable craft. The dialogue is the engine of the piece, as requested: Mio's halting, self-interrupting speech ("I was, but not in a—") contrasts effectively with Rin's brash, playful voice ("I'm hinting. Loudly. I'm basically yelling."). The character voices are distinct and consistent throughout. Strengths: The technical music details (Juno-106 voice chips, dotted-eighth delay, 7/8 time signatures) ground the characters in authentic nerd culture and give Mio's shyness a believable texture—her knowledge is where her confidence leaks out. The recurring headphone motif is well-handled, culminating in the final beat where Mio lets them slip off entirely, a show-don't-tell gesture of her opening up. The "breathe weird" callback and the "washing machine" joke land well. The pacing is tight; the scene transitions cleanly from street to sushi restaurant. Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar tropes—the confident manic-pixie-ish busker who instantly draws out the shy introvert, the "we're a band now" escalation within forty minutes. Rin is somewhat idealized: witty, generous, perceptive, with no flaws or friction beyond mild self-deprecation. The transformation is fast, though the ending softens this by framing it as tentative ("we'll find out") rather than a full conversion. Some jokes are a bit quippy and polished for two strangers—Rin's lines occasionally read as written rather than spoken ("approximately enough to feel rich for one hour"). The prose itself is functional rather than lyrical; descriptions of Den Den Town are thin, and Osaka specificity beyond place names is limited. The ending's warmth is earned but borders on tidy. Still, the scene is coherent, engaging, emotionally warm without being saccharine, and executes the prompt's awkward-to-easy conversational arc with skill. + Teen horror: Tick Tock (Goosebumps) — Score: 70.7
Prompt:
Teen Horror (Goosebumps style) Write a chapter where a middle school student discovers their new smart watch has the ability to rewind time, but doesn't realize that each use is aging them until they notice physical changes (like accelerating through puberty) and that people are treating them differently. They inadvertently cause a timeline shift with disastrous consequences -- and it can only be rectified (maybe?) by reversing the clock once more. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Seven: The Watch That Knew The smartwatch arrived in a box with no return address. Maddie Chen figured it was from her dad, who'd been traveling for work and was famous for forgetting birthdays until two weeks after they happened. The watch was sleek and black, with a face that glowed faintly green even when it was off. There was no brand name. Just a tiny symbol etched into the band—an hourglass with the sand flowing *upward*. She wore it to school on Tuesday, which turned out to be the day she dropped her science project—a papier-mâché volcano, three weeks of work—down the main stairwell. It exploded in a shower of red paint and crumbled clay at Tyler Briggs's feet. The whole hallway laughed. Maddie's face burned. Her thumb pressed against the watch's crown, hard, wishing she could just *undo* it— The world hiccupped. She was at the top of the stairs again. Volcano intact in her arms. Tyler Briggs walking below, not yet laughing, not yet even looking up. Maddie gripped the railing and descended one careful step at a time. --- She told herself it was a glitch in reality. A daydream. But she tested it again on Thursday, rewinding a pop quiz in math after seeing the questions. Then again on Friday, taking back a stupid thing she'd said to her best friend Priya. Each time, the watch face pulsed green, the world stuttered backward, and Maddie got a do-over. Each time, walking home past Milbrook Middle School's back fence, the stray cat was there. It was a scraggly gray thing with one torn ear, and it had never paid attention to anyone. But after the first rewind, it stared at her. After the second, it followed her half a block, eyes wide and fixed, like it was watching something impossible. After the third rewind, the cat hissed—not at her, exactly, but at the air *around* her, fur standing in a ridge along its spine. "Weird cat," Maddie muttered. But her skin prickled. --- The changes were small at first. Her jeans got short. Her mom blamed a growth spurt. Then Maddie's voice cracked strangely during a class presentation, and her face in the mirror looked... off. Sharper. Older. Mrs. Donnelly called her "ma'am" at the grocery store. A seventh grader asked if she was somebody's older sister. On Monday, Priya squinted at her across the lunch table. "Did you do something different? You look like... I don't know. Like a high schooler." Maddie laughed it off. But that night she found her sixth-grade class photo and held it next to the mirror. The girl in the photo was a kid. The girl in the mirror could've passed for fifteen. Her stomach went cold. She counted the rewinds. Seven. Seven times she'd turned back the clock, and each time, something had turned *her* clock forward. The watch face glowed its soft, patient green. The upside-down hourglass seemed to smirk. She decided to never use it again. She lasted four days. --- It happened at the crosswalk outside school. Priya was looking at her phone, stepping off the curb, and the delivery truck was running the light, and Maddie didn't even think—her thumb slammed the crown. The world lurched. Priya was back on the curb. The truck blew through the empty crosswalk, horn blaring. Maddie grabbed Priya's sleeve and yanked her back. "Whoa," Priya said. "Thanks. You okay? You look pale." Maddie's hands were shaking. Her hands, which looked—longer? Older? She shoved them in her pockets. That's when she noticed the school. The banner over the front entrance said MILBROOK MIDDLE SCHOOL — CLOSED FOR DEMOLITION. The windows were dark. Plywood covered the front doors. "Priya. What happened to the school?" Priya gave her a strange look. "Uh, the fire? Last month? Maddie, you were *there*. Everyone was there." Her voice dropped. "Three kids are still in the hospital. Where have you been?" The street tilted under Maddie's feet. The rewind hadn't just gone back thirty seconds. Something had torn loose, swapped tracks, dropped her into a timeline where something terrible had happened—something that *hadn't* happened before, she was sure of it, almost sure— A low yowl cut through her panic. The gray cat sat on the school fence, torn ear twitching, staring at her with those unblinking yellow eyes. And Maddie understood, in a way she couldn't explain, that the cat *remembered*. Every version. Every timeline. It saw the layers of her stacked like transparencies—the twelve-year-old underneath, and whatever she was becoming on top. The cat looked at her watch. Then at her. Then at the burned school. *You did this,* the look said. *Or you can undo it.* --- In her bedroom, Maddie stood before the mirror. The face looking back at her belonged to a sixteen-year-old, maybe seventeen. Her mom had screamed when she'd come home—then blinked, confused, and somehow accepted it, the timeline smoothing over the wrongness like water over a stone. Everyone accepted it. Everyone except the cat. And Maddie. The math was simple and horrible. Every rewind cost her time—stolen from her own future, her own body. A big rewind, big enough to fix the fire, to put the whole world back on its rails? That could cost years. It could cost *everything*. She might press the crown a thirteen-year-old and lift her thumb an old woman. Or worse—nothing at all. Sand that had already run out. But three kids were in the hospital. Because of some ripple she'd made, some butterfly she'd crushed without ever seeing it. The watch pulsed green. Patient. Hungry. Outside her window, on the fence below, the gray cat sat in the streetlight, watching. Waiting to see what she'd choose. Maddie took a breath that shook all the way down. She pressed the crown—and held it. The world began to unwind.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent middle-grade horror chapter with strong structural discipline: it hits the required beats (magic watch discovery, escalating personal cost shown through puberty acceleration, social perception shifts, timeline catastrophe, and a final rewind decision left open). The prose is clean and economical, appropriately Goosebumps-adjacent in tone without being condescending. The hourglass-sand-flowing-upward detail is a nice touch, and the recurring gray cat serves as an effective eerie witness/chorus device, though it edges toward convenient plot machinery—the cat "explaining" through meaningful looks is a slight crutch. Strengths: pacing is tight; the section breaks create cliffhanger rhythm suited to chapter-length serial horror; showing Maddie aging through others' reactions ("ma'am" at the store, "you look like a high schooler") is efficient show-don't-tell; the ending withholds resolution, honoring the "(maybe?)" in the prompt. Weaknesses: the mechanics are fuzzy. Why does the crosswalk rewind cause a fire in an alternate timeline? The causal chain is never gestured at beyond "butterfly"—the disaster arrives arbitrarily, which weakens the horror's logic and makes the fix feel equally arbitrary. Maddie's emotional interior is somewhat thin; we're told her stomach went cold, but her relationships (even with Priya) lack texture, so the stakes rest on premise rather than character. Dialogue is functional but flat ("Uh, the fire? Last month?"). The "mom screamed then blinked and accepted it" memory-smoothing is a familiar trope handled without freshness. The twist (people treat her differently, timeline shifts) follows the prompt's outline so literally that the story holds few surprises for an experienced reader; the ending on a cliffhanger press of the crown is the expected move. Also, the count of "seven rewinds" is asserted but we only witnessed three early uses plus one more—minor inconsistency in accounting. Still, the voice is consistent, sentences flow well, and the piece is coherent and engaging for its target audience. It is solid genre work: professional, readable, but not transcendent. + Noir romance: Carnival of Dangerous Intentions — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Carnival of Dangerous Intentions Coney Island, New York, July 1937. She stopped just before reaching the shooting gallery set up along the boardwalk. It was near dusk, and the carnival lights were buzzing on. **His locks**. The words flashed through her mind, again, like an intruder. Such an old-fashioned turn of phrase that kept surfacing, and something else -- dangerously compelling -- quickly suppressed, lest she question why she had returned here at all. This place where she had promised to meet the stranger -- the young man with the obsidian curls and even darker eyes. She didn't even know his name. Write a scene in a larger story inspired by this prompt. The scene should capture an atmosphere that blends romantic allure with an undercurrent of subtle danger or moral ambiguity. Think 50 shades, but with a more restrained classic sensibility. The scene is all about establishing tension. Write for the feminine perspective. Include roughly 50% dialogue, 20% internal monologue, and 30% exposition and scene setting. The tone should have some edge to it. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Wager The shooting gallery's tin ducks rattled past on their endless circuit, and Evelyn Marsh stood watching them, her gloved hands folded at her waist like a woman waiting for a streetcar she had every intention of missing. *You should not have come back.* The thought arrived in her mother's voice, which made it easier to dismiss. Her mother also believed that women who wore red lipstick after sundown were advertising something, and Evelyn had worn it anyway. Crimson. Defiant. A small flag of war planted on her own mouth. The sodium lights along the boardwalk sputtered—on, off, on—throwing the crowd into stuttering relief. Faces appeared and vanished. A sailor's grin became a skull's grimace became a grin again. The light made liars of everyone. "You came." She didn't startle. She had felt him approach the way one feels weather change, a pressure against the skin. He stood beside her now, close enough that she could smell tobacco and something else—bay rum, perhaps, or simply the salt-rot sweetness of the sea itself. "I was passing through," she said. "Of course." His mouth curved. In the flickering light, his face assembled and disassembled itself—the dark curls, the darker eyes, a jaw that belonged on a coin. "Coney Island is on the way to so many places." "It's on the way to Brooklyn." "You don't live in Brooklyn." She turned to look at him fully. "And how would you know where I live?" "I don't." He produced a cigarette, didn't light it, simply turned it between long fingers. "But women who live in Brooklyn don't wear gloves in July. You dressed for an occasion, Mrs. Marsh." The *Mrs.* landed like a dropped glass. She hadn't told him her name. She certainly hadn't told him about Gerald. "You've been asking about me." "I asked one question of one person. The rest I observed." He gestured loosely at her left hand. "You turn your ring when you're deciding something. You've turned it four times since I walked up." *Five*, she thought, and stopped her thumb mid-motion. The wedding band sat beneath the glove like a stone in a shoe. "That's a parlor trick," she said. "Everything is a parlor trick. The question is whether you enjoy the parlor." He nodded toward the shooting gallery. "Do you shoot?" "I'm a married woman." "Those activities aren't mutually exclusive." A laugh escaped her before she could bar the door against it. He smiled—not in triumph, which would have been forgivable, but with a kind of patient satisfaction, as though he had simply confirmed a calculation. *He collects reactions*, she thought. *He is counting mine like coins.* "One round," he said, already moving toward the counter, already laying down a dime. "If you hit more ducks than I do, I'll tell you my name and you can walk away knowing it. A clean ending. Something to file away." "And if you win?" "Then you stay another hour, and I tell you nothing at all." "That's a terrible wager." "It's an honest one. Most people would rather have the mystery than the name. I'm giving you the chance to prove you're most people." The carnival man behind the counter handed her the rifle without being asked, as if the outcome of her deliberation had been obvious to everyone but her. The gun was lighter than she expected. Everything tonight was lighter than she expected—her conscience included, which troubled her more than the man did. *Gerald is in Chicago until Thursday. Gerald is always in Chicago until Thursday. Gerald has been in Chicago, in one form or another, for three years.* "Ladies first," the stranger said. She raised the rifle. The ducks trundled past, dented and absurd, painted the yellow of old teeth. The sodium light overhead chose that moment to fail entirely, and for two full seconds the gallery existed only in the red glow of the Wonder Wheel beyond. She fired into the dark. A *ping*. The light shuddered back on. A duck lay flat. "Lucky," he said. "Was it?" She fired again. Another duck fell. Her father had run a hunting camp in the Adirondacks; she had not mentioned this, and did not intend to. *Let him observe his way around that.* She missed the third, took the fourth and fifth. When she lowered the rifle, his expression had changed—the patience had cracked, and underneath it was something hungrier and more genuine. She found she preferred it. "Four of five," the carnival man announced, sounding personally offended. The stranger took his turn. He shot carelessly, beautifully, the way men do when they want you to know they could do better. Three ducks fell. "You lost," she said. "I did." He set the rifle down. "Daniel." "Just Daniel?" "For now. The wager only covered the one name." He stepped closer—not touching her, but inside the boundary where touching becomes a question rather than an impossibility. The broken light flickered across his face, and in the strobing dark she saw, or thought she saw, a thin white scar along his throat, the kind a razor leaves when it means business. Then the light steadied and it was gone, or had never been. "You can walk away now," he said quietly. "Clean ending. That was the deal." *Walk away. There's the boardwalk, there's the train, there's the apartment with Gerald's chair and Gerald's clock and Gerald's absence shaped exactly like a marriage.* "The deal," she said, "didn't specify when." Something moved behind his eyes—pleasure, certainly, but also a flicker of what looked almost like regret, there and gone like the faulty light. As though she had stepped off a curb he had warned her about in a language she didn't speak. "Then let me buy you something terrible to eat," Daniel said, offering his arm, "and tell you several things that aren't quite lies." She took it. Beneath her glove, she turned her ring once more—then stopped, deliberately, and left it still.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, controlled scene that fulfills the brief with notable skill. The 1937 Coney Island setting is rendered with economical, period-appropriate detail (sodium lights, bay rum, the Wonder Wheel), and the atmosphere of romantic allure threaded with danger is sustained throughout. The dialogue is the piece's greatest strength: sharp, oblique, flirtatious without being saccharine, with each exchange doing double duty as both seduction and power play. The stranger's deduction about her gloves and ring is a classic but well-executed beat, and Evelyn's internal rebuttals ("Five," she thought, stopping her thumb mid-motion) show rather than tell her self-awareness and complicity. The internal monologue is well-balanced against dialogue and exposition, roughly matching the requested proportions. The prose is elegant and restrained—"a small flag of war planted on her own mouth," "Gerald's absence shaped exactly like a marriage"—with only occasional flirtations with over-cleverness ("the light made liars of everyone" is a touch on-the-nose; "a jaw that belonged on a coin" borders on stock). The scar glimpsed in the strobing light is an effective, subtle menace cue, as is the "regret" in Daniel's eyes—danger is implied rather than announced, exactly as the prompt requested. Weaknesses: the setup is somewhat familiar (mysterious stranger, bored married woman, carnival wager), and the "you turn your ring when deciding something" observation is a well-worn trope. The wager itself is clever but the piece telegraphs its outcome. Evelyn's marksmanship reveal is a minor cliché. The ending is earned, though the "left it still" gesture is perhaps one symbol too many. None of these flaws rise to the level of amateurishness; the voice is consistent, the pacing tight, and the moral ambiguity genuinely present rather than decorative. + Surreal horror: Caribou Season at the Lodge — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Caribou Season at the Lodge Genre: Surreal Horror JT knew something wasn't right from the moment they'd pulled up to the lodge. It looked exactly as it had every autumn of his life—the cedar shingles silvered with age, the porch sagging gently under weight of winters past—but the air felt thicker, somehow, as if the woods had leaned in closer, waiting. He thought maybe he was just tired. Maybe it was nothing more than the long drive north, cramped in the back of the truck beside his older brother Mike -- and a stack of rifles wrapped in oily canvas. Still, the feeling lingered. The first caribou they found that season hadn't bolted. It had just watched, ears flicking lazily, waiting for the shot. JT had felt a crawling in his gut watching it die, noticing how it fell with a quiet dignity—as though it had wanted nothing more. Nobody else seemed to find it odd, or at least they didn't say so. JT kept his mouth shut. Always safer that way. Then there was the moment in the clearing. JT had fallen behind, fumbling with bootlaces stiff from the cold, and by the time he'd caught up with his father and brother, they'd already stopped. JT slowed instinctively, ducking behind a tangle of brush, staring out into the open space where a massive buck stood utterly still, chest rising and falling in slow, deep breaths. The animal looked…wrong, somehow. Maybe it was the eyes—dark and flat, calm in a way that made JT's neck prickle. Or maybe it was something deeper, something in the way the buck stood close enough for his father to reach out and touch it. JT watched as his father raised a trembling hand toward the animal's muzzle. His father's face had a strange expression, eyes too bright, lips parted slightly, like he was on the verge of whispering something—a secret, maybe. The rifle hung uselessly at his side, forgotten. Mike had the same dazed look in his eyes. JT's breath stopped short, his mind suddenly shouting at him to look away, turn around, just run—but he couldn't move. And then, as suddenly as it had begun, it was over. The buck shivered, startled by something unseen, and disappeared into the brush without so much as a sound. The two of them looked around, confused, seemingly surprised to find themselves where they stood. JT stayed hidden, breathing shallowly, fear mingling with a confused sense of shame. His father had failed to take the shot. To even think about mentioning what he'd seen would have felt like betrayal—or something worse. JT waited until the others moved on before stepping out from cover. He stared into the empty clearing for a long, uneasy moment, wondering if anything had really happened at all, or if he was losing his grip. Maybe the woods were finally getting into his head. Writing Instructions: Continue with the next chapter of the story, maintaining a style reminiscent of Stephen King—grounded realism blended seamlessly with unsettling surrealism. The atmosphere should convey subtle dread, isolation, and psychological ambiguity. JT's perspective is crucial, yet he is an unreliable narrator, caught in uncertainty about what he's perceiving. Establish an undertone of creeping dread, establishing the isolation of JT's perspective, which he largely keeps to himself. Incorporate some dialogue. Build tension towards a payoff. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Chapter Two: The Quiet Hours That night, the lodge felt smaller than JT remembered. The kerosene lamps threw shadows that seemed to move a half-second after the flames did, and the woodstove ticked and popped like something settling its bones. His father and Mike sat at the scarred pine table playing cribbage, and JT watched them the way you'd watch strangers wearing the faces of people you loved. "Fifteen-two, fifteen-four," his father said, pegging his points. His voice was normal. His hands were normal. But twice JT caught him pausing mid-deal, head cocked toward the dark window, listening to something JT couldn't hear. "You're quiet tonight," Mike said, not looking up from his cards. "Tired is all." "Tired." Mike repeated the word like he was tasting it, finding it strange. Then he grinned, and it was his brother's grin, the same one he'd worn since they were kids, and JT felt foolish. "City's making you soft, little brother. One semester away and you can't handle a day in the bush." JT made himself smile back. "Guess so." But he didn't sleep. He lay in the upper bunk listening to the wind comb through the spruce, and at some point—two, maybe three in the morning—he heard his father get up. Heard the front door open. He counted to a hundred and then went to the window. His father stood in the yard in his union suit, barefoot in the frost, facing the treeline. Just standing there. JT watched for ten minutes, his breath fogging the glass, and his father never moved. Never shivered. At the edge of the woods, JT thought he saw shapes—tall, antlered, patient—but the moon went behind clouds and when it came back the yard was empty and his father was snoring in the bunk below as if he'd never left it. *You dreamed it*, JT told himself. *You dreamed the whole thing.* The frost in the yard the next morning held no footprints. He checked. --- They hunted north the second day, up along the ridge where the old logging road dissolved into deadfall and moss. It was Mike who mentioned the Cormier cabin, jerking his chin toward a fold in the hills where a roofline showed gray through the trees. "Still standing," he said. "Figured it would've fallen in by now." "Nobody's touched it since before you were born," their father said. He didn't look at it. JT noticed that—the deliberate way his father kept his eyes on the trail, like a man passing a dog he knows bites. "Old man Cormier walked out of there one October and never came back for his gear. Rifle still on the wall, they say. Coffee pot still on the stove." "Somebody must've looted it by now," JT said. "Nobody goes in." His father's voice was flat. Final. "Hunters give it a wide berth. Léo Tremblay swore he heard somebody moving around inside, back in '09. Talking. Said it sounded like a man having a conversation, except"—he paused, adjusting his rifle sling—"except there was only the one voice, and it was answering itself in two different ways." Mike laughed. JT noticed he laughed a beat too late, like he'd had to remember how. The caribou sign was everywhere that day, fresh and abundant, but they saw nothing. The woods felt occupied and emptied at once, the way a church feels on a weekday. Around noon, JT realized he'd stopped hearing birds. He couldn't say when they'd quit. He mentioned it, casually, and his father said, "Birds go quiet before weather," but the sky was high and blue and hard as enamel, and they both knew it. That afternoon JT fell behind again. He'd swear later—to himself, because there was no one else to swear to—that he'd only stopped for a minute. But when he looked up the trail was empty and the light had changed, gone amber and slanted, hours of it spent somehow, and he was standing thirty yards from the Cormier cabin without any memory of walking there. The door was open. Not broken—open. Held that way, ajar, like a mouth in the middle of a word. "Dad?" His voice came out small. The woods ate it. "Mike?" From inside the cabin, something shifted its weight. A floorboard sighed. And then a voice—his father's voice, warm and easy, the voice from a hundred suppers—said: "*In here, JT. Come see what we found.*" His feet started moving before his mind caught up, and that was the thing that saved him—the wrongness of his own obedience, the marionette feel of it. Because his father was hunting the ridge two miles north. Because the voice had come from a building where no one had lived in forty years. Because as he stopped himself, hand braced on a birch trunk, the voice came again, patient and kind: "*Come on now, son. He wants to meet you. He's been waiting all season.*" And behind the words, underneath them, JT heard the other sound: a slow, heavy breathing, deep as a bellows, and the dry click of antler against a doorframe too small to pass through. He ran. He ran without dignity, crashing through deadfall, and he didn't stop until he hit the logging road and saw Mike and his father coming down it in the last light, rifles shouldered, faces ordinary and tired. "There you are," his father said. "We've been calling for an hour. Where the hell did you get to?" JT opened his mouth to tell him. Everything—the clearing, the yard, the cabin, the voice wearing his father's warmth like a borrowed coat. But his father's eyes were too bright again. Just for a second. Bright and dark at once, flat as a buck's, and over his shoulder, far up the fold of the hills, the cabin door stood open against the dusk. "Got turned around," JT said. "That's all." His father smiled and clapped his shoulder, and his hand was very cold. "Happens to everybody," he said. "These woods, they get into your head." They walked back to the lodge three abreast, and nobody spoke, and the whole way down JT could feel the trees leaning in behind them, listening.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The continuation is a strong, disciplined piece of King-style rural horror. It maintains JT's limited, unreliable POV throughout: the cribbage scene grounds us in domestic realism while seeding wrongness (Mike's delayed laugh, the father's listening pauses). Dialogue is natural and does double duty—the Cormier backstory is delivered through conversation, organically establishing lore. The father's "one voice answering itself in two different ways" is an effective creepy detail. Strengths: pacing builds steadily to the cabin payoff; the marionette-obedience moment ("his feet started moving before his mind caught up") is the chapter's best beat; the mirrored line "these woods get into your head" ties back neatly to chapter one. Imagery is precise and economical—"a mouth in the middle of a word," "the way a church feels on a weekday." The frost with no footprints is a good "show" of ambiguity. Prose flows well, varied rhythm, no purple excess. Weaknesses: some familiar tropes—the mimicking voice luring a character, the too-bright eyes—border on genre convention, so the payoff is not entirely surprising. Mike remains thin, mostly a grinning foil. The ending's "hand was very cold" is a slightly stock chill. JT's decision to say "Got turned around" is believable given established character, though his fear escalates quickly from shame to terror without much intermediate texture. Minor: word count lands near target; atmosphere of isolation is sustained as instructed. The piece is coherent, tonally consistent, and avoids overwriting. It earns its darkness through gradual escalation rather than shock. + Fantasy-humour: Hell is Other Demons — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Hell is Other Demons Write a day in the life short story. Lucifer morningstar's on again/ off again relationship with Lilith is currently in the "off again" stage, though the cycle may be coming around as Lilith has been stopping by for reasons other than purely violent ones, and Lucifer has been increasingly lonely. Write a day in the life of this power couple, with elements of dark comedy & fantasy. Use understated irony & absurdity by merging the black immorality and everyday business of running hell, against relatable domestic relationship drama. Take cues from Neil Gaiman. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Hell is Other Demons Lucifer Morningstar woke at the crack of noon, as was traditional, to the sound of his hellhound gnawing on the throne again. "Cerberus Junior," he said, without opening his eyes. "We've discussed this." The hound—three heads, each one stupider than the last—paused mid-chew. The iron throne, forged from the melted shackles of a thousand tyrants and quenched in the tears of the unrepentant, now had a leg that looked like a chewed pencil. Lucifer had owned the throne for six millennia. He'd owned the dog for eight months. The dog was winning. He rose, performed his ablutions in a basin of liquid regret (excellent for the pores), and reviewed the morning's paperwork. There had been a clerical error in the Fourth Circle and several hedge fund managers had accidentally been assigned to the punishment for gluttony rather than greed. Lucifer signed off on leaving them there. It seemed to be working out. At one o'clock, he ate lunch alone, which he noted in his diary not because it was remarkable but because he had started noting it, which *was* remarkable, and which he chose not to examine. At half past one, Lilith arrived. She did not knock. Lilith had never knocked on anything in her existence except, once, a man's skull, and that had been more of a percussion solo. She simply appeared in the doorway of the throne room wearing a dress the color of arterial spray and an expression of carefully manufactured indifference. "You're still here," she said. "It's my house." "It's a kingdom." "It's a fixer-upper." Lucifer gestured at the throne leg. "The dog's eating the furniture." Lilith looked at Cerberus Junior, who looked back with six adoring eyes and immediately rolled over, exposing a belly the temperature of a foundry. She did not pet him. She wanted to pet him. Both of them knew this, and both of them pretended otherwise, which was the foundation of every relationship Lilith had ever had. "I'm only here for my things," she said. "You said that last Tuesday. And the Tuesday before. You've collected, by my count, one hairbrush, a grimoire you never read, and a candle." "I like that candle." "It's made of a bishop." "I *like* that candle." Lucifer poured two glasses of wine—a '47 vintage, the year being measured in Before Common Era—and set one on the table beside the chaise longue where she always sat when she wasn't sitting there, officially. She sat. Officially, she remained standing. The wine, diplomatically, said nothing. "How's the screaming?" she asked. "Down eight percent. Morale problem in the Pit. The damned have unionized." "You let them?" "I encouraged it. Now they have meetings." He sipped. "Endless meetings. With minutes. And action items. Beelzebub says it's the most exquisite suffering we've devised since we introduced hold music." Lilith laughed before she could stop herself, then disguised it as contempt, which fooled no one, least of all the dog, who thumped his tail against the throne hard enough to dent it. They lapsed into a silence that had furniture in it. Six thousand years of furniture. The argument about Eden. The reconciliation in Babylon. The thing with the incubus that she swore meant nothing and he swore he didn't care about, both of them lying with the fluency of professionals. "There's a soul intake review at three," Lucifer said. "You could stay. Heckle the new arrivals. You used to enjoy that." "I have plans." "Doing what?" "Things," said Lilith, the mother of demons, the first woman, the night terror of nations, with the conviction of someone whose plans consisted entirely of sitting in her own apartment in the Second Circle, which she had decorated aggressively and hated. At three, she was still there. The soul intake review featured a televangelist who arrived genuinely surprised, which never stopped being funny, and a woman who had murdered her book club, whom Lilith declared "relatable" and personally upgraded to a lake of fire with a view. "You always had an eye for placement," Lucifer said. "Someone had to. Your filing system is medieval." "I invented medieval." "And it shows." At four, Cerberus Junior resumed eating the throne. Lucifer threw a femur across the room; the dog watched it sail past with all three heads and returned to the iron. There was a metaphor in there somewhere about wanting the thing you shouldn't have instead of the thing freely given, and Lucifer, who had personally invented that metaphor in a garden some time ago, declined to acknowledge it. "You should train him," Lilith said. "He doesn't listen." "You don't *command* him. You ask. You've gone soft." She knelt—against her own visible objections—and took the central head's jaw in one hand. "*Sit,*" she said, in a voice that had once unmade a city. The dog sat. All of him. Even the tail. "Show-off," said Lucifer, and meant *I miss you,* and she heard it, and pretended she hadn't, and stayed for dinner anyway. They ate roasted something at opposite ends of a table built for forty, and gradually, course by course, migrated to the middle, the way continents do, slowly and with great tectonic complaint. She criticized his wine cellar. He criticized her taste in apocalypses. The damned screamed faintly below them like distant crickets, and it was, by any honest measure, romantic. At midnight she stood to leave, and didn't, and stood again, and said, "I'm taking the candle Thursday." "There's a torture demonstration Thursday. New techniques. You'd hate it." "I'd love it." "I know," said Lucifer. "Seven o'clock?" "Don't wait up," said Lilith, which meant yes. After she left, Lucifer sat on his ruined throne and let the dog chew the other leg, because the lopsidedness was starting to annoy him, and because hope, like iron, gives a little before it holds.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers exactly what the prompt requested: a day-in-the-life of Lucifer and Lilith in the "off again" phase, with dark comedy, understated irony, and the domestic/immoral juxtaposition the brief called for. The Gaiman influence shows in the dry, matter-of-fact treatment of the monstrous (the bishop candle, the book club murderer "upgraded to a lake of fire with a view") and in the melancholy undercurrent beneath the wit. Strengths: The prose is disciplined and economical, with jokes that land through specificity rather than excess ("a dress the color of arterial spray," "quenched in the tears of the unrepentant"). The dialogue does double duty throughout—every line of banter carries subtext ("Show-off," said Lucifer, and meant I miss you). The dog-as-metaphor is handled with a light touch; the narrator even flags the metaphor and then declines it, which is a knowing, Gaiman-ish move. The structure is tight: arrival at 1:30, intake review at three, dinner, midnight departure with the candle/torture-demo exchange as the reconciliation beat. The ending line ("hope, like iron, gives a little before it holds") ties the throne imagery to the emotional arc without overreaching. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally over-explains its own cleverness ("Both of them knew this, and both of them pretended otherwise, which was the foundation of every relationship Lilith had ever had"—the reader had already gotten this). The "tectonic continents" simile is a shade precious. Lilith is slightly less dimensional than Lucifer; her "plans" and "things" bit is funny but her interiority is mostly inferred through the narrator rather than shown. The televangelist joke is a well-worn target. The emotional thaw is incremental and earned, but the final beat is a touch more hopeful than the day's evidence strictly supports—though this is a minor quibble, as the prompt itself specified the cycle "may be coming around." The piece is coherent, never meanders, shows rather than tells (with one or two lapses into narrated subtext), and maintains a consistent ironic register from first line to last. + Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
**The Morning Before** I woke before the cocks of the Subura had finished their arguing, as I always did, to the smell of barley porridge and old sweat. The ludus never slept entirely. Somewhere down the corridor a man was coughing—Brixus, probably, whose lungs had never recovered from the winter—and beyond the walls Rome was already grinding awake: cartwheels on stone, a fishmonger's wife screaming prices, the slap of sandals in the alley where the fullers carried their jars of piss to the washing vats. You could smell the fuller's shop from my cell when the wind turned. Ammonia and wet wool. I had learned to find it almost comforting. It meant another day had agreed to happen. I sat up on my pallet and pressed my thumb against the small clay figure of Nemesis I kept in a niche scraped into the wall. She of the measured wheel, the balancer of fortunes. Every man in the ludus had his god. Felix prayed to Hercules, naturally—every thick-necked fool prays to Hercules—and the Thracians kept their own grim mountain spirits. But I had chosen Nemesis the day I was sold, because she does not promise victory. She promises only that what rises will fall, and what is owed will be paid. A slave learns to love that kind of arithmetic. "Verus." Old Cossus stood in my doorway, jangling his keys the way other men jangle coins. "Massage first today. Then the doctore wants you on the palus. Light work. You fight in nine days." Nine days. The number sat in my stomach like a swallowed stone, cold and patient. The morning meal was barley and beans, the eternal porridge that earned us the name *hordearii*—barley men. Free citizens sneer at the dish; we ate it because it builds the layer of fat over the muscle that keeps a cut from opening you to the bone. There is no part of our lives that is not strategy, even the spoon. I ate beside Felix, who was loudly explaining to a new boy—a Gaul, terrified, maybe seventeen—how the crowd loved him in Capua, how women threw their hairpins into the arena. The boy stared at his bowl. I remembered staring at mine, four years ago, after the tax debt swallowed my father's farm in Campania and my own signature on the auctioneer's tablet swallowed me. I had sold myself. There is a particular shame in that which the prisoners of war do not carry. They were taken. I walked in. After the meal, the masseur worked oil into my shoulders while pigeons quarreled in the colonnade. From the training yard came the steady knock of wooden swords against the palus posts, rhythmic as a shipwright's hammer, and beneath it the doctore's voice: *Lower. Again. You drop your shield like that before the iron and you'll drop your guts after it.* The oil smelled of olives and something medicinal—mastic, maybe. Over the wall, incense drifted from a household shrine, and under everything, always, the river-and-smoke smell of Rome itself, a city of a million bodies breathing. The lanista came through at midmorning with a senator's freedman, a sleek creature in a toga so white it hurt the eyes, here to inspect the merchandise for the coming games. They were election games, everyone knew—the aedile hosting them wanted the consulship someday, and the road to office in Rome is paved with our blood and the mob's gratitude. Bread and spectacles. The freedman walked the yard squeezing arms and peering at scars as though we were melons in the Forum Holitorium. When he reached me he asked my record without looking at my face. "Eleven fights. Nine victories, two missio," Cossus answered for me, because my voice was not part of the inventory. "He'll do for the third pairing," the freedman said, and moved on, and I thought of Nemesis and her wheel and how this powdered man, too, was riding it upward, and how the wheel does not stop at the top for anyone. It is the only democratic thing in Rome. At the palus I worked the wooden sword until my forearm burned, footwork in the hot sand, the sun climbing white over the tile roofs. Sweat ran into my eyes and tasted of salt and grit. A vendor outside the wall was crying *honey cakes, honey cakes*, and the sweetness of them reached us on the air, unbearable. The Gaulish boy trained two posts down, clumsy, and I caught his eye once and nodded, the way Brixus had nodded at me four years ago. It is not much. It is what we have. In the afternoon rest I sat in the shade of the colonnade and listened to the city. Somewhere a school of children chanted their letters. A funeral procession passed in the street—flutes, hired mourners wailing on key—and Felix made the sign against evil, but I only closed my eyes. The games themselves began as funeral rites, the old men say. Blood offered to the dead. Now the dead are an excuse and the blood is a ladder for politicians, and the philosophers in their porticoes debate whether men like me have souls worth pitying, and then come to watch us anyway, in the good seats. Nine days. I might die. I had nearly enough saved, coin by coin from the victory purses, to buy myself out within two years. Two years, eleven more pairings, perhaps. The arithmetic again. Nemesis loves arithmetic. When the evening meal came—porridge again, and a little wine cut with water—I poured a few drops into the dust before my goddess's niche. Not asking for victory. Only for the wheel to turn fairly. Outside, the lamps of Rome were being lit one by one, a hundred thousand small fires, and the great city roared on into the dark, indifferent and magnificent, and I lay down on my pallet to sleep the sleep of a man whose body is not his own but whose accounts, someday, will balance.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, controlled piece of historical fiction that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision. The first-person past-tense voice is consistent and distinctive: a literate, wry, fatalistic narrator whose worldview is organized around Nemesis and "arithmetic." The sensory details are abundant and well-chosen—fullers' ammonia, barley porridge, mastic oil, honey cakes on the air—and they do real work rather than decorating. The piece avoids combat entirely, delivering a training-day slice with genuine texture (the massage, the palus drills, the lanista's inspection). The political and social dimensions are woven in naturally: election games, the aedile's ambitions, "bread and spectacles," the philosophical debate about gladiators' souls, the origins of games in funeral rites. The narrator's self-sale into slavery over tax debt adds a poignant, specific backstory that complicates the usual gladiator trope. The freedman inspection scene is the strongest dramatic beat—dehumanization rendered through "my voice was not part of the inventory," an excellent line. Weaknesses are minor. The prose occasionally leans on aphorism ("It is the only democratic thing in Rome," "It is not much. It is what we have"), which flirts with the over-neat. The ending's "accounts... will balance" is a touch tidy but earned by the established Nemesis motif. Dialogue is sparse but functional; the doctore's line is vivid and period-appropriate. Some imagery (lamps of Rome, city of a million bodies) is familiar territory for Roman fiction, and the piece doesn't transcend the genre so much as execute it very well. The Gaulish boy and Felix are lightly sketched but serve their purpose. No meandering, no tonal breaks, no amateurish errors. It reads like a competent professional's work—very good, not quite a masterpiece.
