+ Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Lighthouse Keeper --- **14 March 1952** Dear Mam, Arrived at Skerryvore Tuesday last. The relief boat near couldnae land for the swell. Twelve miles off Tiree and the rock no bigger than our old close back in Partick. The tower's a marvel though — Stevenson built it, granite all the way from Mull, and when the sea hits it the whole thing hums like a struck bell. There's three of us. McAllister the principal keeper, who says about six words a day, and young Davie Crone from Oban, who says six hundred. I do the middle watch. Plenty time to think, which I'm no sure is a blessing. Send word when you can. The relief boat comes monthly, weather permitting, which out here means weather rarely permitting. Your loving son, Tam --- **2 April 1952** My dear Tam, Your letter took its time but arrived safe, which is more than I can say for Mrs Brodie's washing line, which the wind took clean over the wall on Thursday. Twelve miles off Tiree! I looked it on the map at the library. You're nearer America than you are to your mother's kitchen, near enough. Eat properly. Tinned mince is no a meal, whatever Davie Crone tells you. I'm fine, before you ask. The chest is the chest. Dr Lennox gives me the same bottle of brown nonsense he always does. Your Mam --- **29 May 1952** Dear Mam, The chest is the chest — Mam, that tells me nothing and you know it. Write me the truth or I'll write to Dr Lennox myself, and won't that embarrass the both of us. It's the nights that get me here. No the work — the work's fine, trimming and winding and logging the weather. It's two in the morning with the lamp turning and nothing but black water in every direction, and you start hearing your own thoughts too loud. Davie deals with it by talking. McAllister deals with it by no talking. I havenae worked out my way yet. There's gannets diving off the reef in the mornings. That helps, a wee bit. Tam --- **18 June 1952** Tam, Since you threaten me with doctors — aye, the chest is worse. Dr Lennox says it's the years in the mill and the Glasgow air on top, and there's no much for it but rest and the brown bottle. Don't you dare come hame on account of it. You fought two years for a posting and I'll no be the reason you lose it. Your father had nights like yours, on the convoys. He said you couldnae fight the dark, only keep busy in it. He'd have been proud of you on that rock, son, though he'd never have said it plain. He was like your McAllister that way. Mam --- **30 August 1952** Dear Mam, I've started reading on the middle watch. McAllister, of all people, left a book on my bunk without a word — *Kidnapped*. Then another. Turns out the man's got a whole kist of books and the longest silence in Scotland, but a kind eye when you learn to look for it. I'll no pretend I'm cured of it. There was a week of fog where I'd have swum to Tiree if I could. But I'm finding the shape of the days now. Davie's teaching me chess. He's terrible. It's very good for my confidence. Mam — rest means rest. Is Mrs Brodie looking in on you? Answer that one straight. Tam --- **21 October 1952** Tam, Mrs Brodie looks in. Stop your fretting. I'll tell you straight since you ask straight: Dr Lennox says the winter will be hard on me. I'm no afraid of it, son. I've had a good run and a good son, and I sit by the fire of an evening and think of you up in your tower keeping ships off the rocks, and I think — that's something. A woman from a Partick close raised a man who keeps the light. Don't come hame. I mean it. Mam --- **3 November 1952** Mam, I've put in for compassionate leave. You can mean it all you like — I'm coming when the December relief sails, and McAllister himself signed the request, which for him is practically a speech. Hold on for me. That's all I'm asking. Hold on till December. Tam --- **8 December 1952** — TELEGRAM TAM CAITHNESS SKERRYVORE LIGHTHOUSE C/O NLB OBAN — MAM TOOK BAD TURN FRIDAY — DR LENNOX SAYS WEEKS NO MONTHS — SHE SAYS TELL HIM KEEP THE LIGHT — MRS BRODIE --- **11 December 1952** Mam, The relief boat cannae sail. Gales from the southwest, the worst McAllister's seen in fifteen years, and Skerryvore taking green water over the gallery. I stood at the lamp room glass last night and shouted at the sea like a madman, and Davie had the grace to pretend he didnae hear. So I'll say it here, in case the boat's too late, and I'm trusting the post and God to get it to you. You raised me on your own after Da was lost, and you never once let me see the cost of it. Everything steady in me is yours. The nights here taught me what you carried all those years — the being alone with it — and you carried it without a tower or a lamp or anybody to take the next watch. I'm keeping the light, Mam. Every ship that passes safe this week passes safe because your son is at his post. That's yours too. I love you. I should have written that in every letter and I'm writing it now. Tam --- **4 January 1953** Dear Tam, Your mother passed peaceful on the 19th of December, with your letter in her hands. The minister read it and she had me read it twice more after. She said, "He understands now," and she smiled, and I'll no forget that smile. She left instructions, very firm, the way she was. You're no to grieve at the graveside longer than a day. You're to go back to your rock. Her words: "Tell him the light's the thing. Tell him I'll see it from where I'm going, and I'll know it's him." She was proud of you, Tam Caithness. Proud as a banner. Yours in sympathy, Agnes Brodie --- **2 February 1953** Dear Mrs Brodie, Back at Skerryvore. The gannets are back too. Last night on the middle watch I looked out at the dark and it didnae frighten me. The lamp turned, steady as a heartbeat, and I thought — she sees it. Daft, maybe. But I lit it careful, all the same. I'll keep the light. Tam
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong epistolary piece. The Scottish working-class voices are consistent and convincing — Tam's Scots-inflected narration ("couldnae," "weather rarely permitting") and the mother's deflecting warmth ("The chest is the chest") are distinct and well-differentiated. The plot unfolds gradually and organically: isolation struggle, mother's hidden illness, the telegram as escalation, the storm preventing the final visit, and the death occurring offstage with the letter arriving via Mrs Brodie. The structure is disciplined; each letter advances both plot and character. Strengths: the mother's voice is superbly drawn — proud, evasive, firm. The father backstory ("He was like your McAllister that way") is economical and affecting. The final letter's image of lighting the lamp "for her" is a satisfying, thematically resonant resolution without sentimentality overload. The McAllister book detail shows rather than tells character growth. Weaknesses: the emotional climax (11 December letter) edges toward the explicitly declarative — "I love you. I should have written that in every letter" — which is effective but slightly on-the-nose. The mother's death and Mrs Brodie's letter are handled well, though "Proud as a banner" flirts with cliché. The "she sees it" turn in the final letter is a small leap of faith that mostly lands but could feel tidy. Some phrases ("steady as a heartbeat") are near-cliché. The pacing of the mother's decline is perhaps slightly compressed between October and December, but the telegram justifies it. Overall: a polished, moving piece with authentic voices, strong structure, and a genuinely earned resolution. Minor clichés and one slightly declarative climax keep it from masterpiece level. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It The projector squeaks again—that high, complaining sound, like a mouse being stepped on—and Mr. Donnelly clicks to the next slide about cellular respiration, and I am not thinking about cellular respiration at all. I am thinking about the fact that in approximately four minutes, when he finishes explaining the rubric, I will have to turn ninety degrees in my chair and speak actual words to Marcus Webb. Okay. Okay okay okay. I've prepared for this. I have, conservatively, eleven possible opening lines, and I've been stress-testing them since homeroom. Option one: *"So, do you want to do the poster or the presentation part?"* Practical. Efficient. Possibly too efficient—like I'm a project manager, like I'm forty-five years old and wearing a lanyard. He'll think I'm bossy. Or worse, boring. Discard? No—keep it in reserve. It's the emergency exit of conversation starters. Option two: *"Mitochondria, am I right?"* Absolutely not. What does that even mean? Why did my brain manufacture that? That's not a sentence, that's a cry for help. The projector squeaks. Slide six. Mr. Donnelly is saying something about "checkpoints" and "Friday." Option three involves mentioning that I saw him at the library on Saturday, which is true, but then he'll know I *noticed* him at the library on Saturday, and noticing implies looking, and looking implies—no. No. That information goes in the vault. The vault where I keep the fact that I know his backpack has a tiny embroidered frog on the front pocket that he probably thinks nobody has seen, and the fact that he laughs through his nose first before the real laugh comes out, like his laugh has an opening act. This is the thing nobody tells you about having a brain like mine: it never runs out of words. Inside my skull I am eloquent. Inside my skull I am giving TED Talks. I could write him a twelve-page letter, footnoted, with a works cited page, explaining precisely why he's interesting—the frog, the laugh, the way he defended the kid who got mocked for liking dinosaurs in seventh grade, casually, like it cost him nothing. But the pipeline between my brain and my mouth is, apparently, a paper straw. Soggy. Collapsing. Everything that comes through it arrives crushed and damp. Squeak. Slide seven. "ATP," says Mr. Donnelly. My heart is producing so much ATP right now. My heart is a cellular respiration overachiever. I sneak a glance—no, not a glance, glances are obvious, this is a *sweep*, a casual visual sweep of the room that happens to pass through the airspace occupied by Marcus Webb. He's drawing something in his margin. Probably the frog. Don't ask about the frog. The frog is vault material. What is my face doing right now? Audit: am I making a weird expression? I think I've been frowning at the projector screen like it owes me money. Relax the forehead. Now I'm worried I look aggressively blank, like a mannequin, like someone whose soul has briefly stepped out. There's no neutral setting on my face. Every setting is a statement and every statement is potentially incriminating. "All right," Mr. Donnelly says, "go ahead and get with your partners." The room erupts into chair-scraping chaos and my entire nervous system files for emergency leave. Turn. Just turn. People turn in chairs all the time. It's one of the most basic human— "Hey," Marcus says. He turned first. He turned FIRST. All eleven of my openers were architected around me initiating. I have no defensive playbook. I have nothing. "Hey," I say. One word. One syllable. Fine. Acceptable. Humans say "hey." But now there's a silence, a growing, gelatinous silence, and it's my turn, conversationally, the ball is in my court, and all eleven options are sprinting through my head wearing numbered jerseys—not the frog, not the library, not the mitochondria thing, dear God not the mitochondria thing— "Do you want—" I start, exactly as he says, "So should we—" We both stop. He does the nose-laugh. The opening act. I am going to perish at this lab table. "You go," he says. "Do you want to do the poster or the presenting part?" Option one. The emergency exit. I took the emergency exit. The lanyard option. I'm a forty-five-year-old project manager now, it's official, hand me my clipboard. But he says, "Honestly? Poster. I hate talking in front of people." And my brain, my treacherous, beautiful brain, supplies instantly: *Same. I hate talking in front of one person. I'm doing it right now and it's like defusing a bomb.* That's funny. That's actually funny, I think? Or is it weird? It's self-deprecating, which can read as funny or as desperate, and the line between those is a tightrope over a canyon, and what if my voice does the wobbly thing, and what if— He's looking at me. Waiting. The pause is aging. Say something. Say ANYTHING. "Same," I say. "I hate talking in front of one person. I'm doing it right now." Silence for half a second. Half a second is a thousand years. Then the nose-laugh, then the real laugh, the whole concert, and he says, "Okay, that's fair. You're funny." *You're funny.* Two words. I will be examining these two words under a microscope for the next six months. I will write a dissertation. There will be footnotes. "So," he says, flipping his notebook open, and I see it—the margin drawing. It's a mitochondrion. With a smiley face. "Powerhouse of the cell, am I right?" I almost say *I almost said exactly that.* I don't. Vault material. But I'm smiling, an unaudited, unplanned smile, and the projector squeaks one last time as Mr. Donnelly shuts it off, and for three entire seconds, my brain is quiet. Then: *wait, was my smile weird?* Three seconds. New record.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding prompt: nearly all internal monologue, an anxious 8th-grade girl, a crush, a science class pairing, and the gap between inner eloquence and outer collapse. The voice is the standout achievement—the "eleven opening lines" device, the "vault," the "paper straw" metaphor for the brain-to-mouth pipeline, and the self-audit of facial expressions all feel authentic to a smart, overthinking teenager without tipping into an adult writer's impression of one. The structure is tight: the projector squeak and slide progression provide a clock for the scene, and the payoff—Marcus speaking first, derailing her rehearsed openers—is both believable and satisfying. The "mitochondria, am I right" setup paying off in his margin drawing is a well-seeded callback. The dialogue is minimal but effective; her spoken lines are deliberately flattened versions of her inner wit, which is exactly the point of the piece. Minor criticisms: the "vault" and "audit" bits are slightly over-repeated, and the ending's "three seconds. New record." beat is a touch neat, though it lands as earned rather than saccharine. Some metaphors ("cry for help," "tightrope over a canyon") flirt with familiar territory, and the piece is essentially one note—anxiety—but the prompt asked for exactly that note, and it's played with skill and humor. The emotional arc is small but real: from paralysis to a genuine, unplanned smile. Nothing feels unearned. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Rehearsing Rejection Four percent battery. Of course. Of course tonight, when Dani might text to cancel, my phone is dying like everything else. She'll cancel. She's been distant for nine days. I counted. Nine days of shorter texts, longer gaps, one "haha" where there used to be paragraphs. People don't drift like that without a reason, and the reason is always me. Something I said. Something I am. I rehearse it on the walk over. She'll sit across from me with that careful face people make when they're about to perform surgery on your heart, and she'll say, *I think we moved too fast. I think we should go back to being friends.* Which means: *I saw you fully, finally, and I want to unsee you.* And I'll say — I'm composing it now, polishing each word like a stone — I'll say, *Fine. I never expected this to last anyway. I know what I am.* Cold. Dignified. I'll leave before she finishes her drink. Let her sit with that. Let her feel two percent of what I feel. Or maybe she won't even be that kind. Maybe she'll say, *You're a lot, you know that?* People have said it before. *Intense. Exhausting.* I have my defense filed and cross-referenced: *You knew what I was. You chased this. You kissed me first.* I can feel my own future anger like heat off pavement, and honestly the anger feels good, feels like armor, feels like something I'm choosing instead of something happening to me. Three percent. She's already at the table when I walk in. And she — okay. She stands up. She *stands up* to hug me, and the hug is long, longer than obligation requires, and she says into my hair, "God, I've missed you. This week has been insane — my mom's surgery, I've barely been human." Her mom's surgery. She told me about that. Two weeks ago. I knew about that. Something in my chest unclenches so fast it hurts, like blood returning to a sleeping limb. She missed me. She said missed. I want to drink the word, hold it under my tongue — But people say "missed you" the way they say "how are you." It's filler. It's anesthesia before the incision. She's softening me up. Be nice first, then the *but*. There's always a *but* coming, I can feel it assembling itself in her mouth. She orders for both of us because she remembers what I like, and I think: *or she's rushing this along so it ends sooner.* She reaches across the table and takes my hand — actually takes it, holds it, thumb moving over my knuckles — and says, "I'm sorry I've been a ghost. I kept thinking about you in the hospital waiting room. It was the only good thing to think about." The only good thing. I am the only good thing. I could live a year inside that sentence. I want to take it home and sleep curled around it. And already — *already*, I can feel it happening, I can watch myself do it — I'm checking the sentence for structural flaws. The only good thing *to think about*. Not the only good thing. A distraction. People love distractions and discard them when the crisis ends. The crisis is ending. Her mom is recovering. So. Two percent. If she texts later to say this was a mistake, I won't even see it until morning. I'll sleep not knowing I've already been left. *You're doing it again.* I know I'm doing it again. I can see the pattern from above like a drone shot, the whole maze of it, me running the same circuits. My therapist calls it rehearsing rejection. Says I write the breakup so I can hold the pen. And she's right, I know she's right, and knowing changes nothing, because the imagined Dani in my head is so much more vivid than the real one across the table — the real one who is, right now, laughing at something I said, her whole face open, saying, "This is what I needed. You're what I needed." But the imagined Dani is *safer*. The imagined Dani can't surprise me. If I script the cruelty in advance, the real thing will just be a table read. That's not insight. That's the disease wearing insight as a costume. I know that too. I keep the awareness in a separate room from the fear, and the fear has the bigger room. "Hey." Real Dani, squeezing my hand. "Where'd you go?" "Nowhere. I'm here." *I'm always partly somewhere else, in a courtroom where you're testifying against me.* "I was scared, honestly," she says, looking down. "That my going quiet would freak you out. I know how your brain — I didn't want you to think it meant anything. It didn't mean anything except that I was drowning." She knows how my brain. She *knows how my brain* and she's still here, still holding my hand, and that should be everything, that should end the war — And instead I think: *she's managing me. She's learned my instruction manual. That's not love, that's maintenance.* I think: *one day the maintenance will exhaust her and she'll say I'm a lot, and I'll say you knew what I was* — there it is, the rehearsal, queuing itself up again, the resentment pre-mixed and ready to pour for an offense she hasn't committed and maybe never will. One percent. She walks me out with her arm around my waist. She kisses me at the corner, unhurried, like there's time, like there's a future. "Text me when you're home safe," she says. My phone dies in my pocket on the walk back. And in the silence where her goodnight text would be, I begin, helplessly, to write her side of an argument we have never had — her voice in my head saying everything the real her has never said — and I argue back, brilliantly, bitterly, all the way home, winning a fight against someone who only ever told me she missed me.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is an exceptionally strong execution of a difficult brief: a first-person internal monologue capturing BPD-pattern catastrophizing, rehearsed rejection, preemptive resentment, and the immediate questioning of received love. The battery-percentage motif (4% → 3% → 2% → 1%) is a clever structural device that externalizes the narrator's dwindling sense of security and pays off in the final image of the phone dying before the goodnight text — the silence where imagined rejection rushes in. The prompt's core demands are all met with precision: elaborate imagined dialogues with polished defensive responses ("I know what I am"), the actual events being warm and validating (the hug, the hand-holding, "the only good thing to think about"), the immediate reframing of each validation as suspect ("a distraction... people love distractions and discard them"), and limited, contested self-awareness ("That's not insight. That's the disease wearing insight as a costume"). The line "I keep the awareness in a separate room from the fear, and the fear has the bigger room" is a genuinely excellent articulation of cognitive dissonance. The prose is controlled and distinctive — punchy fragments, italicized inner speech, aphoristic turns ("like blood returning to a sleeping limb"). It avoids both purple excess and clinical flatness. The ending is honest rather than redemptive: no transformation, no cure, just the cycle continuing into the walk home — "winning a fight against someone who only ever told me she missed me" is a devastating, well-earned closing line. Minor criticisms: the dialogue from Dani occasionally edges toward being a bit too perfectly therapeutic ("I know how your brain—"), functioning as an idealized counterweight rather than a fully messy person; a couple of the aphorisms ("the disease wearing insight as a costume") are so polished they feel authorial rather than diegetic. The "rehearsing rejection" phrase is handed to the narrator by the therapist, which is a slightly convenient way to name the pattern. But these are small quibbles against a piece that is coherent, emotionally complex, and consistently voiced. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The torch guttered in its rusted sconce on the eastern wall, and by its single flame, two men faced each other across ten paces of broken flagstone. Takeda Shōichi stood at the southern end of the ruined temple hall, where the collapsed roof had spilled rubble in a rough crescent behind him. He held his bokken high above his right shoulder in the *tonbo*—the dragonfly stance of Jigen-ryū—elbows lifted, blade angled back, his whole body coiled like a drawn bow. His supporters crowded the southern doorway behind him, silk-clad, silent, contemptuous. Wei Lun faced him from the north, where the old altar stone squatted in shadow. He stood almost casually, weight on his back leg, arms hanging loose at his sides like ropes. The Piguaquan men ringing the western wall murmured and clinked coins. One spat. "First blood ends nothing," Wei said. "We fight until one of us cannot stand." Takeda did not answer. Jigen-ryū had no second strike, and no words before the first. He exploded forward. Three strides ate the distance—the *kiai* tore from his throat, raw as a hawk's scream—and the bokken came down in a diagonal cut from high right toward Wei's left collarbone, the famous *kesa* strike that had split helmets in three centuries of war. Wei did not block. He folded sideways to his own right, spine bowing like a willow, and the wooden blade hissed past his left shoulder to crack against the flagstone, throwing splinters. In the same instant his left arm whipped around in a horizontal arc—a backfist like a flail—catching Takeda across the right cheekbone as the swordsman's momentum carried him past. Takeda staggered two steps toward the altar stone, tasting copper. The western wall erupted in cheers. He pivoted on his lead foot, bringing the bokken back up over his shoulder—Jigen-ryū knew no retreat, only the reset to *tonbo*—and now their positions had reversed: Wei stood with his back to the southern rubble, Takeda before the altar. The torch flickered. Shadows lunged across the walls like a second pair of fighters. Takeda charged again, but this time he feinted the diagonal cut and snapped the blade into a horizontal sweep at waist height. Wei leapt back, heels finding the loose rubble, and the tip of the bokken raked his ribs through his tunic—a line of fire, not a finish. He hissed, used the rubble's slope to spring leftward along the eastern wall, circling, and Takeda turned with him, blade tracking, the two men now orbiting the hall's center with the torch throwing Wei's whipping shadow huge above them. "Stand still, peasant," Takeda said through bloodied teeth. "Stand still and die, lord," Wei answered, and attacked. He came in low and oblique, footwork skating diagonal—never the straight line—and his right arm uncoiled in a downward chop aimed at the wrist of Takeda's lead hand. Takeda jerked the bokken up and back; the chop missed, but it was bait. Wei's body had already rotated through, his left palm whipping upward from below in a rising arc that caught Takeda under the jaw. Takeda's head snapped back. He felt his knees soften and let himself fall *into* it—dropped his weight forward and drove the bokken's pommel straight ahead like a spear-butt into Wei's sternum. Bone met wood with a sound like a door slamming. Wei flew backward three feet and crashed against the altar stone, breath gone, the world ringing. The southern doorway roared. Takeda raised the bokken overhead, advanced one step, two—and brought it down with everything Jigen-ryū had ever taught him: the strike that needed no second. Wei rolled left along the altar's edge. The bokken struck the stone where his skull had been and *broke*—the upper third spinning away into darkness, leaving Takeda holding two feet of splintered oak. For half a heartbeat both men froze, equidistant from the altar, Takeda above, Wei crouched at the stone's western corner with one hand pressed to his bruised chest. Then Wei swept his leg in a low circle, hooking Takeda's ankle. The swordsman went down hard on his right hip, flagstone biting through his hakama, but he kept the broken bokken and slashed blind as he fell—the jagged end opening a gash across Wei's forearm as the Piguaquan fighter surged on top of him. They grappled in the torchlight, blood slicking both their hands. Wei drove an elbow down toward Takeda's face; Takeda turned his head and the elbow split the flagstone of his ear instead, ringing his skull. He rammed the broken bokken's stub into Wei's wounded ribs—once, twice—and Wei rolled off him, gasping, and both men came up to their feet at the same moment, four paces apart, the altar at Wei's back, the torch now between them and the eastern wall painting half of each face gold and half in darkness. They were ruined, both of them. Takeda's cheek had swollen shut over one eye; blood sheeted down Wei's arm and dripped from his fingertips. The crowds had gone silent. Takeda dropped the broken bokken. It clattered on stone. He raised empty hands into the dragonfly frame anyway—because Jigen-ryū lived in the body, not the blade—and charged a final time, palm-edge falling like a sword. Wei whipped to meet him. His right arm scythed inside the descending strike, deflecting it past his shoulder, and his left came around in the full circular blow, hips and spine and shoulder cracking like a bullwhip—and his open palm met Takeda's temple at the same instant Takeda's deflected hand, never stopping, chopped down into the junction of Wei's neck and shoulder. Both blows landed. Both men dropped. They lay two arm-lengths apart on the cold flagstone, the torch sputtering above them, neither faction daring to claim victory. Takeda pushed himself to one elbow. Wei dragged himself up against the altar stone. Their eyes met across the bloodied floor. Neither could stand. Neither would yield. The torch burned down, and the old debt remained—unpaid, undiminished, waiting for the next generation foolish enough to inherit it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly controlled, well-choreographed fight narrative that fulfills the prompt's core demands with notable discipline. The physical coherence is excellent: positions are tracked throughout (south/north orientation, altar stone, rubble crescent, torch on the eastern wall), and every strike, dodge, and momentum shift is spatially legible. The styles are characterized accurately through action rather than exposition—Jigen-ryū's single decisive strike and refusal to retreat, Piguaquan's whipping circularity and oblique footwork—so the choreography doubles as characterization. The prose is lean and muscular, with a few genuinely strong images ("shadows lunged across the walls like a second pair of fighters"; "his whole body coiled like a drawn bow"). The dialogue is sparse but functional, and the class antagonism surfaces naturally in the single exchange ("Stand still, peasant." / "Stand still and die, lord."). Minor criticisms: the mutual-destruction ending is somewhat predictable for this genre, and the final paragraph's "the old debt remained—unpaid, undiminished" edges toward tidy thematic statement, a mild tell-don't-show flourish. A couple of the similes ("like a flail," "like a bullwhip") are serviceable rather than fresh. The crowd of supporters is sketched thinly, more backdrop than pressure. The word count lands close to the target. Emotionally, the piece is engaging but not deeply complex—pride and animosity are rendered well, but there's little interiority beyond the fight itself, which is arguably appropriate to the assignment. Overall this is a polished, professional piece with no amateurish failures. + Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The clock says 47:33 and counting down, red digits bleeding against the white wall like something out of a heist movie, except the only thing getting stolen here is me. "Again. From the top of the second verse." Master Yoon doesn't raise his voice. He never raises his voice. He stands at the front of the studio, dead center, arms folded, his reflection multiplied in the mirror behind him so it looks like a whole firing squad of disappointment. Twelve of us in formation—four rows of three—and I'm back row, stage left, the corner position, which everyone knows is where you put the weakest link. The spot where mistakes get buried. Except mistakes don't get buried under Yoon. They get excavated. The track drops. Eight-count intro, and my body knows what it wants to do—it wants to *ride* the beat, sink into the pocket, let the bassline pull my chest into a wave that rolls down through my hips. That's what I'd do back home, on the cracked concrete behind the rec center where Marcus taught me to flow, where the cypher didn't care about your shoes or your accent, only whether you could *say something* with your body. But here, the choreography says: right arm extends at exactly forty-five degrees on count one. Snap to chest on two. Both arms scissor across on three-and, lock on four. No swing. No bounce. Every joint a hinge, every hinge a soldier. I hit count one. My arm goes out—but my shoulder rolls with it, just a whisper of groove, muscle memory smuggling itself into the movement like contraband. "Stop." The music dies. Eleven heads stay forward. Mine does too, but I can feel everyone's attention swing toward my corner like a searchlight. Yoon crosses the floor. His footsteps don't make sound—I've noticed that, the way he moves like the floor owes him silence. He stops two feet in front of me, close enough that I can see he's younger than his reputation, older than his face. "Your shoulder," he says in English, for my benefit, which is its own small humiliation. "It moves before your arm. The arm is the leader. The shoulder is the passenger." "Where I'm from, the shoulder *is* the leader." It comes out before I can stop it. Somewhere in the second row, someone inhales sharply. Yoon studies me. Then: "Where you are from is six thousand miles away. Again. Just you. Everyone else, water." Eleven dancers peel off to the side wall, grateful, terrified, watching. Now it's me alone in the formation grid, twelve tape marks on the floor and only one of them occupied. The clock says 41:18. The track comes back. Verse two. I run the combination: arm extension, snap, scissor, lock—then the floor sequence, a drop to the right knee on count five, left leg sweeping into a kneel that has to land *flat*, both shins parallel to the mirror, spine vertical like I've been hung from a hook. Up on seven through a corkscrew rise, no hands, weight transferring heel to ball, and into the traveling section: three steps stage right, each one landing on the *and* count, sharp as a typewriter. My body fights me the whole way. On the knee drop, my torso wants to spiral—a breaker's instinct, protect the descent, make falling beautiful. I kill it. On the rise, my hips want to lead, that rolling levitation I learned watching old popping tapes, and I strangle that too. The traveling steps are the worst: my feet want to glide, to slide, and instead I'm stamping out Morse code, dot-dot-dot, mechanical, dead. I finish the phrase. I hit every mark. And I feel like I just performed my own autopsy. Yoon walks a slow circle around me. "Correct," he says. "And empty. You think I cannot see what you removed?" "You told me to remove it." "I told you to control it." He steps onto the tape mark beside mine—first row, center, the position I will never hold—and without music, without warning, he performs the same eight counts. And it's precise, yes, machine-precise, but inside the precision there's something coiled, a tension between the beats, a held breath. The lock on count four doesn't just stop; it *arrives*, like a fist closing around something alive. "Precision is not the absence of you. It is the *compression* of you. You give me a corpse and call it discipline. You give me chaos and call it soul. Both are lazy." The clock says 36:50. "Last time today," he says, returning to the front. "Full group. If the corner breaks formation, we start the count tomorrow at five a.m." Eleven bodies flow back to their marks. The girl in front of me—Hana, the only one who's spoken to me outside this room—glances back for half a second. Not pity. Something more dangerous: belief. The track drops. Eight-count intro, and here's the decision, arriving like it always does, mid-breath, no ceremony: I can dance their corpse. I can dance my chaos. Or I can try the thing Yoon did, the thing that scares me, because if I can hold my whole neighborhood inside a forty-five-degree angle—every cypher, every cracked sidewalk, every night Marcus said *say something*—then maybe none of it was ever about the looseness at all. Count one. My arm extends, exact, and I pour everything into the stillness at the end of it, the groove compressed into a single trembling degree of held tension. Snap. Scissor. Lock—and the lock *arrives*. Knee drop, count five, no spiral, but I let the impact ring through me like a bell instead of dying in my joints. In the mirror, twelve bodies move as one. And in the corner, one of them is still, somehow, unmistakably, me. The clock says 35:02. Yoon says nothing. But he doesn't stop the music.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece that hits nearly every requirement in the prompt. The narrator's voice is distinct from the opening line—the countdown clock as recurring structural device gives the scene momentum and a heist-movie tension that suits the "breaking formation" title. The spatial tracking is genuinely strong: the twelve tape marks, four rows of three, the corner position, Yoon crossing to stand two feet away, the eleven dancers peeling to the side wall, his stepping onto the first-row center mark—all of it is visualizable and consistent. The kinetic descriptions are the piece's greatest strength. The choreography is rendered in countable, concrete terms (arm at forty-five degrees on count one, snap on two, scissor on three-and, lock on four, knee drop on five, corkscrew rise on seven), and the street-versus-commercial collision is dramatized through specific bodily habits: the shoulder rolling before the arm, the breaker's instinct to spiral on the descent, hips leading the rise, feet wanting to glide instead of stamp. The "muscle memory betrays them" requirement is fulfilled elegantly—"muscle memory smuggling itself into the movement like contraband" is a standout line that ties technique to the narrator's class/culture context. Yoon is a nicely drawn mentor figure who avoids pure cliché through the "compression, not absence" speech, which reframes the conform-or-rebel binary into a third option. That said, the archetype (harsh instructor with hidden philosophy, "break you to remake you") is familiar, and the resolution arrives somewhat quickly—the narrator integrates the lesson within a single run-through, prompted by one demonstration. The story earns it better than most would (the demonstration is shown, not just told, and the decision is framed as a risk rather than a triumph), but the arc is compressed, and the ending's tidy uplift—"unmistakably, me"—is a touch convenient. Minor flaws: the clock device, while effective, is leaned on slightly heavily. "Performed my own autopsy" and "a whole firing squad of disappointment" flirt with overwroughtness but stay on the right side of it. Hana's "belief" glance is a small tell-don't-show moment. The dialogue is functional and mostly sharp, though Yoon's speech edges toward aphorism. The prose rhythm is excellent throughout—short declarative punches alternating with longer flowing sentences that mirror the two dance styles. Overall: a polished, vivid, emotionally resonant piece that fulfills the prompt's demanding physical-coherence requirements with genuine skill. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Court of the Dreaming: In Re: The Wildflower Field The gallery of the Court was full, as it always was when something embarrassing was on the docket. Nightmares perched in the rafters like gargoyles with opinions. A delegation of minor anxieties occupied the third row, fidgeting. Dream of the Endless sat upon his seat of judgment, chin resting on pale knuckles, eyes like distant collapsing stars. His expression was, as ever, unreadable. But Lucienne, standing at his side with the case ledger, had served long enough to recognize the particular stillness that meant *I have shaped galaxies, and this is what fills my afternoons.* "Call the matter," he said. Lucienne cleared her throat. "*First Love versus Mora*, concerning the dreamscape designated Wildflower Field Seven, recurring property of one Max Brzezinski, aged thirteen, of Leeds." First Love rose from the plaintiff's table. It was a small entity, rosy-cheeked, wringing its hands in a way that suggested it apologized to furniture. It carried its evidence in a shoebox decorated with stickers. At the defense table sprawled Mora, all wild dark hair and unsettling angles, picking her teeth with what appeared to be a child's sigh. She emitted a faint cackle. It echoed uncomfortably through the vaulted ceilings, ricocheting twice before settling somewhere near the door, where it remained, sulking. "Madam," said Dream, "you will contain your laughter until something is funny." "Everything's funny, my lord," said Mora. "Depends where you're sitting." "And you sit on chests." "It's a living." First Love raised a tentative hand. "May I—shall I—my lord, the dream took *months*. The light alone. Do you know how difficult it is to get late-afternoon June light correct in the mind of a boy who lives in Leeds? He's never *seen* late-afternoon June light. I had to invent it from first principles." "Proceed," said Dream. "The dream runs thus: Max lies in the wildflowers. Sophie Hartley — the crush, my lord, very carefully rendered, down to the gap in her teeth he thinks about during maths — laughs at something he hasn't said yet. She leans over him. There is an almost-kiss. *Almost*, my lord, is the entire architecture. The boy wakes confused and hopeful and slightly taller inside. It is a formative work. I was rather proud of it." First Love's lip wobbled. "It had *bees*. Friendly ones." "And now?" First Love opened the shoebox and produced a memory, holding it up with trembling hands. It played in the air above the court: the field, the light, Sophie leaning in — and then Sophie's face folding inward like wet paper, her body lengthening, her weight settling onto the boy's sternum like a verdict. The dream-Max's eyes bulged. Mora — for it was unmistakably Mora — inhaled his breath with the relish of a connoisseur, and the boy's scream came out as a flat, airless wheeze. The anxieties in the third row took notes. "He wakes at 3:14 every morning," said First Love. "Paralyzed. Terrified. And — this is the troubling part, my lord — *confused* in a way I did not design and frankly do not have the licensing for." Dream's gaze slid to the memory's final frame, where the dream-Max's terror was visibly complicated by something else entirely. "Madam Mora. Your defense." Mora stood, stretched, and addressed the court with the easy confidence of someone who has never once felt shame and considers it a foreign delicacy. "My lord. A girl's gotta eat." A pause. "Is that the entirety of your argument?" "There's a structure to it, if you like. One: I require breath. Two: the boy has breath. Three: the dream was *already* about someone climbing on top of him. I merely refined the concept. Honestly, I tightened the third act. The original just sort of... ended. Mine has *stakes*." "You consumed the breath of a child." "Lightly. I graze. I'm not a *monster*." She paused. "Well. I am, technically, a monster, it's on my documents, but I'm not *rude* about it. He's fine. Bit pale. Builds character. Slavic children have endured me for a thousand years and look how they turned out — excellent poets, very sturdy." First Love stamped a small foot. "You squatted in my dream!" "I *improved* an underperforming property. Almost-kisses. Honestly. Drag the boy to the edge of feeling and then drop him? *I* finish what I start. At least when I sit on him, something *happens*." "What happens is *suffocation*!" "Nobody's perfect." The cackle by the door cackled again, supportively. Dream raised one hand, and the court fell silent in the way a grave falls silent: thoroughly, and with implications. He regarded them both for a long moment. Somewhere in the dark behind his eyes, Lucienne suspected, he was composing a strongly worded memo to whichever aspect of himself had agreed to hear territorial disputes personally. "The dreamscape," he said at last, "is the work of First Love, and is hereby restored to its maker. Mora, you are enjoined from the field, the boy, and the borough of Leeds entire." Mora shrugged. "Worth a try." "However." And here something flickered in Dream's expression — the faintest curvature, the kind of almost-smile that made experienced nightmares update their wills. "The boy's confusion has already taken root. That is not within my power to undo, nor —" a pause — "am I inclined to. First Love, you will incorporate it. The almost-kiss shall remain almost. But henceforth, in the moment before waking, Sophie Hartley's smile shall be, very briefly, a touch too wide." First Love went pale. "My lord — the *formative implications* —" "Will be considerable. Max Brzezinski will grow into a man who writes unsettling, deeply romantic novels. Three of them will be dreamed in this court before they are written. I find I am owed some entertainment." He rose. The court rose with him, except Mora, who never rose for anyone and was occasionally executed for it, temporarily. "Next matter," said Dream, already walking, his cloak unraveling into the dark. "A flock of sheep," read Lucienne, "alleging unpaid counting fees." From the rafters, very faintly, the abandoned cackle by the door laughed alone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly competent piece of comic dark fantasy that hits nearly every brief requirement with precision and wit. The courtroom farce is well-constructed: Dream's suppressed irritation is conveyed through Lucienne's interpretation of his stillness ("I have shaped galaxies, and this is what fills my afternoons") rather than stated outright — an efficient, show-don't-tell choice. Mora's defense is delivered with exactly the right deadpan shamelessness ("A girl's gotta eat" expanded into a mock-legal three-point structure is a genuine highlight), and First Love's bashful, apologetic characterization ("apologized to furniture," the sticker-decorated shoebox of evidence) is charming and specific. The comedy is understated and dark as requested: the cackle that "ricocheted twice before settling somewhere near the door, where it remained, sulking" is a lovely absurd touch, and its lonely return at the end is a well-earned callback. The memory-in-the-air evidence presentation is an elegant way to dramatize the dream's corruption rather than describe it. Dream's mischief in the resolution — leaving the confusion rooted and mandating Sophie's "touch too wide" smile — satisfies the "tempted to some mischief" instruction while staying in character, and the closing beat (Max growing up to write unsettling romantic novels, three of which will be dreamed in this court) is a genuinely clever bit of Dream-logic. Minor criticisms: the "Slavic children... excellent poets, very sturdy" line is funny but borders on glib. The sheep-counting-fees stinger is a good absurd button, though the piece's rhythm occasionally leans on the same deadpan-reveal structure ("Nobody's perfect") a few beats too many times. The emotional stakes are deliberately thin — Max is offstage and somewhat abstracted — which is appropriate for farce but caps the piece's depth. Prose is clean, economical, and readable throughout, with sparing scene-setting as instructed. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Moon A crimson harvest moon casts ominous shadows on the deserted village streets. The plague has emptied this place—or something has. Yennefer of Vengerberg walks between the silent houses, her boots clicking against cobblestones slick with dew, and knows with absolute certainty that she is being watched. "You may as well come out," she says to the darkness. "Lurking is terribly undignified." Laughter answers her. It comes from everywhere—the rooftops, the well, the shadows pooling beneath the dead oak in the square. Then it gathers, condenses, and becomes a man. Or the shape of one. He is tall, draped in a red coat the color of arterial spray, his eyes burning behind orange glass. "A sorceress," Alucard says, tasting the word. "How rare. How *delicious*. The air around you reeks of chaos and ozone. And lilac. Gooseberries." He inhales theatrically. "Underneath it all, though—loneliness." "And you smell of grave dirt and old blood." Yennefer doesn't step back. She has stared down kings, dragons, and djinns; she will not flinch for a corpse with pretensions. "Vampire. Higher form, judging by the daylight arrogance, though it's night, so perhaps you're merely ordinary and vain." His grin splits too wide, revealing teeth like a wolf trap. "Ordinary." He savors it like an insult he hasn't heard in centuries. "Test the theory, witch." She does. Fire erupts from her palms—not a flourish, but a focused lance of heat that would reduce a kikimora to ash. It punches through his chest, vaporizing his heart, his lungs, half his spine. He collapses into a smoking ruin of red fabric and char. Yennefer waits. She is not foolish enough to believe it. The shadows *crawl*. Bats with too many eyes pour out of the wound, knitting him back together, and he rises laughing, whole, his hat tilted at a rakish angle. "Wonderful," he breathes. "Do it again." "I don't perform on request." She circles him, and he circles her, two predators measuring the distance between curiosity and violence. "What are you? I've killed higher vampires. They don't regenerate like that. They certainly don't *enjoy* it." "I am the bird of Hermes," he says, "eating my wings to make me tame." He spreads his arms, and the darkness spreads with him, an unfurling of something vast and hungry kept barely in check. "And you, sorceress—you carry power like armor. Beautiful, polished armor over something broken. I can smell that too." Her violet eyes narrow to slits. The temperature in the square drops ten degrees. "Careful, monster." "There it is." He leans forward, delighted. "The steel. The others I've met on these roads—priests, hunters, little fledgling vampires playing at darkness—they beg. They bargain. You *threaten*. I could love you for that alone." "I'm not sweet, and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving," Yennefer says coldly. "Nor am I prey. If you've come to feed, you'll find me a fatal meal." "Feed?" He sounds genuinely offended. "On you? No. Cattle are for feeding. You—" he tilts his head, and for a moment the mockery falls away, revealing something older and infinitely tired— "you might be worth *fighting*." She understands then, with the sudden clarity of a portal snapping open. "You want to die." The silence stretches. The blood moon climbs higher. "I want," Alucard says slowly, "to meet something that *could* kill me. Five hundred years, witch. I have eaten armies. I have drunk rivers of blood and found every drop the same. Do you know what immortality actually is?" "Yes," she says, and it stops him cold. "It's watching everything you want stay forever out of reach. It's a body that doesn't age wrapped around wounds that don't heal." Her hand drifts, unconscious, toward her abdomen—the barrenness she traded for beauty, the price she's spent decades trying to refund. "I'm not as old as you. But I'm old enough." For the first time, the vampire looks at her—truly looks, past the power and the perfume—and something like recognition moves behind the orange lenses. "What did you give up?" he asks. "What did *you*?" Neither answers. The answer is the same, and they both know it: *everything that made us human, and we'd do it again.* Alucard draws his pistol—a monstrous silver thing—in a motion faster than thought. Yennefer's shield blooms a heartbeat before the muzzle flash; the bullet flattens against shimmering air an inch from her eye. "Testing," he says pleasantly. She responds by collapsing the cobblestones beneath him into a pit lined with conjured silver spikes, then igniting the pit. His scream is mostly laughter. He boils up out of the flames as a tide of shadow and eyes and reaches for her with hands made of darkness—and she portals behind him, pressing two fingers against the back of his skull, lightning crackling at her fingertips. They freeze. A tableau under the red moon: his shadow-claws an inch from where she stood, her killing spell an inch from his head, both of them breathing hard—or pretending to, in his case. "Stalemate," Yennefer says. "Foreplay," Alucard corrects. She withdraws her hand. He lets the shadows recede. They regard each other across the scorched square with something that is not friendship, will never be friendship, but might be the rarest thing either of them has found: *respect*. "You couldn't kill me," he says. "Not permanently." "You couldn't catch me. Not permanently." She straightens her sleeves, immaculate again. "We could waste a century finding out. I have better things to do." "Such a shame." He sweeps off his hat in a bow that is only half mockery. "If you ever tire of better things, sorceress—come find me. Bring everything you have." "If you ever find your worthy death," she replies, turning away, a portal tearing open before her in a whorl of light, "I hope it's kinder to you than living was." He watches her vanish. The blood moon watches them both. For the first time in a hundred years, Alucard is smiling at something other than slaughter.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong crossover fic that hits nearly all of its brief: medieval European setting, present tense, third person, roughly the requested length, and a power dynamic that oscillates believably between the two characters. Both voices are well captured—Alucard's theatrical sadism and hunger for a worthy death, Yennefer's icy wit, vanity, and buried wounds (the lilac and gooseberries, the infertility, the famous quotes woven in naturally rather than pasted). The dialogue crackles; lines like "Stalemate." / "Foreplay." and "You couldn't kill me." / "You couldn't catch me." do real work in establishing the mutual respect ending. The structure is clean: encounter, probing, escalation to a genuine test of arms, stalemate, and parting with mutual recognition. The thematic core—two immortals who traded their humanity and regret it—is stated a touch explicitly ("everything that made us human, and we'd do it again") but is mostly earned through action and gesture (her hand drifting to her abdomen). Weaknesses: some phrases lean on familiar fanfic tics ("teeth like a wolf trap," "the shape of one," "a whorl of light"). The ending's warmth ("smiling at something other than slaughter") edges toward sentimentality for two characters this guarded, though it's restrained enough to mostly land. The plague-village setting is atmospheric but underused after the opening. Alucard's "I could love you for that alone" is slightly fast. Minor telling creeps in ("something that is not friendship... but might be respect"). Overall, though, this is confident, controlled, character-true writing with genuine wit and momentum. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Prison Strings A dim overhead light flickers in the prison corridor at irregular intervals. Jolyne Cujoh leans against the cold cinderblock wall, picking at the hem of her sleeve, watching a single thread of herself snake along the floor like a fishing line. Three weeks in this facility—not Green Dolphin Street, somewhere worse, somewhere the government doesn't put on maps—and she still hasn't figured out what they're keeping here besides her. Then she hears footsteps. Soft. Measured. Wrong. A woman walks down the corridor like she owns it, auburn hair in a loose braid, dressed in a clean white shirt and black tie while everyone else rots in jumpsuits. Her eyes catch the flickering light and Jolyne sees the rings in them—concentric circles, like a target. Or like looking down a well. "You must be Jolyne Cujoh," the woman says, smiling. "I've read your file. It's very interesting." "Yeah? Who the hell reads files in a place like this?" Jolyne doesn't move from the wall, but the thread on the floor coils back into her palm, slow, casual. "You don't look like a guard. You don't look like an inmate. You look like somebody who got lost on the way to a job interview." "My name is Makima. I work with Public Safety. I'm here to evaluate... special cases." The smile doesn't waver. It doesn't do anything. That's what bothers Jolyne—she's seen fake smiles her whole life, from lawyers and cops and the prosecutor who buried her, and all of them *strained*. This one sits on Makima's face like it was painted there by someone who'd only had smiles described to them. "Special cases," Jolyne repeats. "Meaning what?" "Meaning people like you. People with abilities." Makima takes a step closer. The flickering light stutters, and in the half-second of darkness her eyes seem to glow faintly. "The string. I saw the footage from the yard incident. You unraveled your own arm to stop a falling beam. Most people would call that impossible." "Most people should mind their own damn business." "I find it beautiful, actually." Makima tilts her head. "A body that can come apart and put itself back together. Tell me—when you unravel, where does *you* go? Are you in the string? Or watching it from somewhere else?" Jolyne's stomach goes cold. Not because of the question—because of the *hunger* underneath it, dressed up polite. She's met people like this. People who look at you and see a tool, a weapon, a thing on a shelf. "You know what?" Jolyne pushes off the wall. "I've got a good nose for bullshit. Comes from getting framed by professionals. And lady, you reek of it. That sweet voice, that little head-tilt—if there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney, and you are *definitely* not Disney." Something flickers behind Makima's eyes. Not anger. Interest, sharpening. "You're perceptive. That's rare." Makima clasps her hands behind her back. "Let me be honest with you, then, since you prefer it. I can get you out of here. Tonight. Charges dropped, record cleaned. All I'd ask in return is that you work for me. People with your gift shouldn't waste away in cells." "And the catch?" "There's no catch. Just a contract." "A contract." Jolyne laughs, harsh. "My dad warned me about exactly two things. Card sharks and people who say 'just a contract.'" The light flickers again, longer this time, and in the darkness Jolyne hears it—a low growl from the far end of the corridor. When the light returns, three guards stand at the corner. Their eyes are empty. Their postures sag like marionettes between performances. "Those guys with you?" Jolyne asks quietly. "They're mine, yes. Everyone here is, eventually." Makima's voice doesn't change at all, and somehow that's the most terrifying part. "Humans want to be owned, Jolyne. It relieves them of choice. You'd be surprised how grateful they become. Dogs are happiest with an owner." "I'm not a dog." "Everyone is somebody's dog. The only question is whose." Jolyne moves first. Stone Free erupts from her body in a blur of blue, and a fist of woven string rockets at Makima's face—and stops. Not blocked. *Stopped*, an inch from her cheek, as one of the empty-eyed guards throws himself into its path, taking the blow meant for her. He crumples without a sound. "You see?" Makima says, stepping over him. "They die for me gladly." "You sick—" Jolyne's strings lash out again, low this time, wrapping around Makima's ankles, yanking. Makima falls—and a second guard is already there, beneath her, breaking her fall with his own body, and Makima rises off him like stepping out of a car. Jolyne backs up, threads spreading across the corridor in a web, mind racing. *She doesn't fight. She spends people. Like coins.* Every attack Jolyne lands will land on some poor brainwashed bastard instead. "Jolyne Cujoh," Makima says, and her voice drops into something older, colder, a register that makes the fillings in Jolyne's teeth ache. "Sit." The word hits like gravity. Jolyne's knees buckle—and the strings catch her. Stone Free, woven beneath her own skin, holds her body upright by sheer structural stubbornness, every fiber screaming *no*. "...Interesting," Makima murmurs, and for the first time the smile slips, just a millimeter. "You should be on the floor." "Yeah, well." Jolyne forces herself straight, blood at the corner of her mouth, grin defiant. "I'm string all the way down, lady. Hard to put a leash on something with no neck." The light flickers. Dies. Holds dark for one long second. When it sputters back on, Makima is already walking away, the guards trailing her like ducklings. "We'll talk again," Makima says without turning. "I have time. I always do." Jolyne stays standing until the footsteps fade, then slides down the wall, shaking, threads slowly stitching her resolve back together. She's getting out of here. Tonight.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover piece delivers a tense, well-paced confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, largely succeeding on its own terms. The prose is clean and controlled, with present-tense third person maintained throughout. The central conceit—Makima spending controlled humans like currency against Jolyne's string-based Stand—is cleverly dramatized, particularly the guard absorbing Stone Free's punch and the second guard breaking Makima's fall. The "Sit" command resisted by Stone Free's structural support is a satisfying mechanical beat that respects both characters' power systems. Characterization is strong: Jolyne's voice is foul-mouthed, defiant, and perceptive, and her famous quote is integrated naturally rather than shoehorned. Makima's smile "painted there by someone who'd only had smiles described to them" is an excellent line that captures her uncanny inhumanity. The dialogue crackles—"I'm string all the way down, lady. Hard to put a leash on something with no neck" is a genuinely great closer for the confrontation. Weaknesses: the setting remains vague (acknowledged in-text, but still a convenient dodge), and the plot is essentially a single escalating scene with little narrative arc beyond "meet, probe, fight, stalemate." The ending's "She's getting out of here. Tonight" is a punchy but slightly unearned pivot—nothing in the scene establishes how she'd escape. Some of Jolyne's internal assessments ("She doesn't fight. She spends people. Like coins.") flirt with telling rather than showing, though the prose mostly earns its summaries. The flickering light as a device for Makima's menace is effective but used repetitively. Overall, this is a confident, engaging piece with sharp dialogue and strong character work, held back from excellence by its thin plot scaffolding and a somewhat abrupt, unresolved ending.
