+ Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 79.1
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7734: "Yesterday's Tomorrow" ## Personal Log Compilation — Dr. Miriam Okafor, Site-43 **Note from RAISA:** The following document combines Dr. Okafor's personal logs with recovered anomalous notes (designated SCP-7734-1 through -23). Classification pending. --- I found the first note on March 3rd, tucked under my coffee mug in my locked office. I recognized the handwriting immediately, because it was mine. > **SCP-7734-1:** *Miriam. The breach happens on April 19th. SCP-6510 gets out through the eastern drainage conduit. Don't trust the readings on the humidity sensors. They've been compromised for weeks. —M* I reported it within the hour, as protocol demands. Dr. Vance from Temporal Anomalies took the note, photographed it, ran graphological analysis. The handwriting was mine—not similar to mine, but *mine*, down to the pressure variance I developed after breaking my wrist in 2019. The paper was standard Foundation memo stock, batch-traceable to Site-43's own supply room. "Either you wrote this and don't remember," Vance said, "or something wants you to believe you did." I appreciated her bluntness then. I miss it now. --- The second note appeared on March 11th, inside my badge wallet. I had not opened the wallet since the previous evening, when I'd locked it in my desk drawer. > **SCP-7734-4:** *They put me on observation. Don't let them. You need access to the eastern wing. The conduit, Miriam. Check the conduit BEFORE the 19th. Vance doesn't believe you because Vance isn't Vance anymore.* I want to be clear: I did not believe the note. Dr. Vance passed her quarterly cognitohazard screening on March 9th. I checked. Then I checked again, and I noted with some discomfort that I had checked, because checking twice is how it starts. Site Command's working theory split two ways. Temporal Anomalies argued for retrocausal information transfer—possibly linked to SCP-6510, a Keter-class entity in the eastern wing whose containment relies on environmental regulation. The Psychology Division argued the notes were a manipulation vector: SCP-6510 has documented memetic influence over its handlers, and I had logged eleven hours in its observation gallery in February. The problem with both theories was the paper. I began locking blank memo stock in a sealed evidence container in my quarters. The notes kept appearing on that exact paper. When I switched to keeping no paper at all, the notes appeared anyway—on memo stock with serial watermarks from a batch the supply office confirmed *had not yet been printed*. Temporal Anomalies got very excited about that. I did not. --- > **SCP-7734-9 (March 24th):** *The drainage maps are wrong. There is no eastern conduit. There never was. I checked after the breach and the walls were solid and 6510 came through anyway, it came through the SOLID WALL where the conduit should have been, where it WAS, Miriam, I remember the conduit, I walked past it every day for six years—* I pulled the architectural schematics. There is no eastern drainage conduit at Site-43. There has never been one. But I remembered it. I remembered the grated cover, the smell of standing water, the maintenance ticket I'd filed in 2021 about corrosion. There is no ticket in the system. There is no conduit. Forty-one staff members were surveyed; thirty-eight have no memory of any conduit. Three do. All three of us had logged observation hours with SCP-6510. The Psychology Division considered this conclusive. The entity was seeding false memories and false documents—a slow campaign to make me doubt the site's actual layout, perhaps to engineer the very breach the notes "warned" about. Have the panicking researcher demand emergency access to the eastern wing. Have her open something that should stay closed. It was a good theory. It was clean. I wanted it to be true, because the alternative was that reality had been edited and I was holding the only errata sheet. --- > **SCP-7734-15 (April 2nd):** *I don't know what day it is here. There are two of everything. Two Vances. The clocks disagree with each other and both of them are right. Don't go to the eastern wing. GO to the eastern wing. I wrote one of those sentences and something else wrote the other and I can't tell which anymore. The handwriting is mine. It's all mine. That's the trick, Miri. Everything that happens to you is in your own handwriting.* I stopped sleeping well after that one. Dr. Reyes prescribed monitored rest and pulled my eastern wing clearance—exactly as note -4 had predicted, which the Psychology Division noted was exactly what a manipulating entity would *want* predicted. Every data point fed both theories equally. The anomaly was perfectly ambiguous, and I began to suspect the ambiguity was the point. On April 14th, I was placed under voluntary observation in a sealed humanoid containment suite. No paper. No writing implements. Continuous video. On April 16th, a note appeared under my pillow, on camera. The footage shows nothing: one frame the pillow is flat, the next frame it is not. Memo stock. My handwriting. > **SCP-7734-22:** *It was never about the breach. The breach already happened. You're inside it. Look at the date stamps on your own logs.* I looked. This log, the one you're reading, contains entries I do not remember writing. The entry for March 11th references events from March 24th. The graphological analysis says all of it is mine. --- **Addendum 7734-A:** On April 19th, no containment breach occurred. SCP-6510 remained inert. Dr. Okafor was released from observation on April 30th. On May 1st, a final note was recovered from Dr. Okafor's quarters: > **SCP-7734-23:** *Good. You made it. I'm sorry for the fear—it was the only material I had to work with. The breach was never 6510's. It was mine. I needed an anchor on your side, someone who would keep checking, keep doubting, keep* watching*. Doubt is containment, Miri. Don't ever stop. —M* Dr. Okafor remains on active duty. She reports no further notes. She checks anyway. Twice.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a tightly constructed SCP piece that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt: first-person researcher perspective, past tense, escalating desperation in the notes, contradictory information (the conduit that never existed), the Foundation's dual theories (temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation by SCP-6510), and the researcher's collapsing trust in her own perception. The format—personal log interspersed with designated anomalous notes—matches the requested structure, and the length lands near the 1000-word target. Strengths: The prose is disciplined and clinical in the Foundation register, with the notes fracturing convincingly into desperation ("There are two of everything. Two Vances."). The central ambiguity is well-engineered: every data point (the unprinted paper batch, the camera footage, the conduit memories shared by three staff) feeds both theories equally, and the narrator explicitly names this ambiguity, which is a smart meta-move. The false-memory survey (41 staff, 38 vs. 3) is a genuinely chilling detail. The ending is clever—the predicted breach doesn't occur, and the final note reframes the entire campaign as an act of containment-by-doubt, with the closing "She checks anyway. Twice." echoing the earlier "checking twice is how it starts" to suggest the anchor took hold. That's an earned, ambiguous resolution rather than a tidy one. Weaknesses: The twist ending risks being too neat—the final note explains too much, converting productive ambiguity into a semi-answer, which slightly deflates the horror. The "it was never about the breach / you're inside it" beat is a familiar SCP-adjacent trope. Dr. Vance and Reyes are functional sketches rather than characters; dialogue is minimal and serviceable. The "two of everything" note flirts with incoherence-by-design but occasionally reads as incoherence-by-convenience. Some emotional interiority is stated rather than felt ("I stopped sleeping well after that one" tells rather than shows). The piece is more intellectually engaging than viscerally affecting—there's admiration here more than dread. Overall: a polished, professional, conceptually satisfying piece with minor losses in character depth and a slightly over-explained ending. + Scp: Unmarked Doors Archive — Score: 83.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP entry about a series of identical unmarked doors appearing in abandoned buildings worldwide that lead to a massive, architecturally impossible archive. Documents within reference a previous global civilization destroyed by an unspecified containment failure. Foundation researchers discover references to their own organization under a different name, including personnel files for current staff dated centuries ago. Include exploration logs revealing sections of the archive actively being removed by entities resembling hazmat teams who flee when approached, and evidence that O5 Council members have visited the archive without authorization. Third person (exploration team perspective) with recovered document excerpts. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# SCP-7741 **Object Class:** Keter **Special Containment Procedures:** All confirmed instances of SCP-7741 are to be secured under fabricated structural condemnation orders. Entry is restricted to Level 4 personnel with O5 approval. Mobile Task Force Sigma-12 ("Card Catalogue") conducts exploration operations on a rotating 72-hour schedule. As of Incident 7741-19, no member of the O5 Council may enter SCP-7741-A without unanimous Council vote and Ethics Committee observation. **Description:** SCP-7741 designates a series of identical unmarked wooden doors (currently 214 confirmed instances) manifesting in abandoned structures worldwide. Instances appear exclusively in buildings unoccupied for ten or more years. All doors are physically identical: oak construction, brass doorknob, no manufacturer markings. Every instance displays an identical pattern of fine scratches surrounding the doorknob—seventeen parallel grooves consistent with repeated, hurried key insertion attempts. Forensic analysis confirms the scratch patterns are identical to a tolerance of 0.02mm across all instances, including instances that manifested simultaneously. All doors open into SCP-7741-A: a single contiguous archive space of architecturally impossible dimensions. Interior mapping has confirmed at least 340 km² of floor space across multiple intersecting levels that violate Euclidean geometry; corridors have been observed to pass through one another without intersection. SCP-7741-A contains an estimated 4 billion documents, the majority concerning a global human civilization with no historical correlate, apparently destroyed by an event referred to only as "the Failure." Approximately 7% of recovered documents reference an organization designated the **Custodial Initiative**, whose structure, nomenclature, and operational procedures closely parallel the Foundation's. See Addendum 7741-3. --- **Addendum 7741-1: Recovered Document Excerpts** > **Document 7741-A-0331** (administrative memorandum, undated) > > ...the Directorate has voted 9–4 to proceed with the transfer despite the Stewards' objection. We are assured the Archive will persist regardless of what happens above. I confess I no longer find this comforting. If the Archive is built to outlast us, then someone has already calculated that we will not last. > **Document 7741-A-0904** (final bulletin fragment) > > CUSTODIAL INITIATIVE EMERGENCY BROADCAST — SITE-PRIMUS BREACH IS NOT, REPEAT NOT, CONTAINED. ALL REGIONAL DIRECTORS EXECUTE PROTOCOL LETHE. THE ARCHIVE WILL REMEMBER WHAT WE CANNOT. THE DOORS WILL FIND THE NEXT ONES. TELL THEM WE TRIED. TELL THEM NOT TO— > > [DOCUMENT ENDS] > **Document 7741-A-1146** (personnel file, partial) > > NAME: [Matches current Site-19 Director Tilda Moose] > CLEARANCE: Steward, Level 4 > DATE OF HIRE: [Date corresponds to 1741 CE under recovered calendar conversion] > NOTES: Subject has requested reassignment away from Archive duty three times. Requests denied. Subject does not remember making them. To date, 61 personnel files matching current Foundation staff have been recovered, all dated between 200 and 600 years prior to those individuals' births. Photographic attachments match current appearance. --- **Addendum 7741-2: Exploration Log 7741-12 (Excerpt)** **Team:** MTF Sigma-12, four members. Entry via Instance #88 (Gary, Indiana). The team proceeded through the Eastern Stacks toward an unmapped wing. At the 2.1 km mark, Sgt. Okafor reported empty shelving—the first observed anywhere in SCP-7741-A. Dust patterns indicated documents had been removed within the previous 48 hours. At 2.4 km, the team observed light and movement. Cpl. Reyes's helmet camera recorded six humanoid entities (designated SCP-7741-B) in white full-body suits resembling hazmat gear, loading document boxes onto wheeled carts. The suits bore an insignia: three arrows pointing inward toward a circle—an inversion of the Foundation crest. Team leader Cpt. Vance hailed the entities. All six ceased movement simultaneously. The following is transcribed from audio: > **Vance:** Foundation personnel. Identify yourselves. > > *(Four seconds of silence. One entity slowly raised a gloved hand—gesture ambiguous: warning or farewell.)* > > **Unidentified entity (voice muffled, distorted):** Not yet. You're not supposed to read it yet. All six entities then fled at high speed, abandoning two carts. Pursuit was attempted; the entities turned down a corridor that, upon the team's arrival four seconds later, terminated in a wall of filled shelving with undisturbed dust. The abandoned carts contained 412 documents, all concerning the Custodial Initiative's final 30 days of operation. An estimated 90,000 documents had already been removed from the wing. Subsequent explorations confirm SCP-7741-B activity is ongoing and accelerating. Approximately 0.3% of the archive's total contents are now removed per month. Targeted sections exclusively concern the Failure itself and the Initiative's Directorate—the Custodial Initiative's apparent O5 equivalent. --- **Addendum 7741-3: Incident 7741-19** During Exploration 7741-15, Sigma-12 recovered a guest ledger near Instance #88's interior threshold. The ledger, of recent manufacture inconsistent with archive materials, contained handwritten entries. Handwriting analysis matched samples on file for O5-3, O5-7, and O5-11 with >99% confidence. Entries were dated across the previous fourteen months. No authorization for these visits exists in any Foundation record. The final ledger entry, in handwriting matched to O5-7: > Third visit. Confirmed it. My file is here too. We did this before. We are doing it again. The doors aren't an anomaly—they're a *deadline*. The scratches on every knob are the same because they're not damage. They're a tally. > > Seventeen marks. Seventeen cycles. > > The cleanup teams aren't hiding the Failure from the world. They're hiding it from *us*. From the Council. Because the last Directorate read these files, and reading them is what The entry is unfinished. When formally questioned, O5-3, O5-7, and O5-11 denied entering SCP-7741-A. All three subsequently submitted to voluntary memetic screening; results indicated targeted amnestic exposure of unknown origin within the previous 60 days. A formal inquiry is ongoing. As of this revision, 22 additional empty shelving sections have been documented, and Instance #215 has manifested—in the abandoned east wing of decommissioned Foundation Site-13. Its doorknob bears eighteen scratches.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-executed SCP entry that hits every required element: identical doors in abandoned buildings, impossible archive, prior civilization destroyed by unspecified containment failure, Custodial Initiative as Foundation parallel with centuries-old personnel files, hazmat entities removing documents who flee when approached, and unauthorized O5 visits. The format is authentic to SCP conventions—object class, containment procedures, addenda, exploration logs, recovered document excerpts. The piece's greatest strength is its escalation structure. Each addendum deepens the mystery while adding concrete, chilling details: the 0.02mm scratch tolerance, the seventeen marks as a tally of cycles, the inverted Foundation crest on the hazmat suits, the unfinished ledger entry cutting off mid-sentence. The ending—eighteen scratches on a door in decommissioned Site-13—is an excellent earned dark note that implies the cycle has already begun again. The prose is clinical where it should be (SCP register) and lets the horror emerge from implication rather than declaration. The entity's single line, "Not yet. You're not supposed to read it yet," is efficient and unsettling. The recovered documents are convincingly fragmentary and dated. Weaknesses are minor. The dialogue is sparse and functional; Vance's hail is flat, though appropriate to the format. Some twists (personnel files matching current staff) are prompt-mandated rather than invented, so creativity credit is partly in execution. The "amnestic exposure" resolution of the O5 questioning slightly deflates tension, though the unfinished ledger entry compensates. The piece occasionally leans on familiar SCP tropes (Site-13, memetic screening, MTF nicknames), and the "deadline" revelation is spelled out a bit too explicitly in O5-7's entry—slightly tell-don't-show, though the format permits documentary exposition. Classic sci-fi: Offworlder (Author style: Le Guin) Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. Upon returning to their quarters, the envoy is reprimanded by Command, and is tasked with approaching the stationed Minister of Science (a political posting rather than scientific). A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder. Length: 1000 words.

# Offworlder ## Chapter Three: The Walking The briefings had said: *The Tessel are a servile caste, bred low and broad for the mines, content in their station.* The briefings had said: *The Aulit ruling lineage maintains harmony through hereditary wisdom.* The briefings, Enwe Salas had begun to suspect by the second day, had been written by someone who had never left the Residence. So on the third evening, between the reception for the Trade Cartels and the dinner she was meant to attend with the Minister of Waters, Enwe put on a gray traveler's cloak bought from a Residence laundress, and went out through the kitchen gate into the city of Sennorath. The streets were stone, and the stone was carved. That much the briefings had mentioned, though they had not conveyed it: every lintel, every cistern-mouth, every stair bore glyphs in the old colonial syllabary, and the glyphs told stories that Enwe, walking slowly with her hood back, found she half-knew. Here a woman with a serpent at her breast; here a man pushing a disc of sun up an endless incline; here a figure with wings of wax, falling, always falling, carved at the top of doorframes so that one passed beneath the fall each time one entered a house. *Remember*, the doorways said, in the language of a world none of these people had ever seen. *Remember what flying cost.* The market in the lower quarter smelled of fermented grain and lamp oil. The Tessel were everywhere — short, deep-chested, their skin the dull copper of high-radiation adaptation, their hands enormous and precise. They were not servile. A Tessel woman haggled down an Aulit cloth-merchant with cheerful brutality while her neighbors laughed; a Tessel man sat on a fountain rim reading aloud from a printed sheet to a crowd that included, Enwe noted, at least four of the tall, pale Aulit, listening with the particular stillness of people hearing something dangerous and true. "You're offworld," said a voice at her elbow. An old Tessel woman, selling roasted tubers from a brazier. It was not a question. "Is it so obvious?" "You walk like the ground might be taken away." The woman handed her a tuber, waved off payment. "And you look at the carvings. Nobody here looks at the carvings. They're just where the stories live." She turned the coals. "Tell your people the mines flooded in Derred and the Aulit councils say the water was an act of weather. Tell them we count our dead even if no one else does." Enwe ate the tuber walking back, and it sat in her like a stone, like an oath. --- The reprimand came before she had even removed the cloak. "You were observed," said Coordinator Ferenn's image, blue and flickering above the desk console, eleven light-minutes of delay flattening her anger into something worse: deliberation. "The Residence staff observed you. Likely Aulit intelligence observed you. You are an Envoy of the Stabile, Salas, not a tourist. You do not improvise." "The briefings are wrong," Enwe said, knowing the words would take eleven minutes to arrive and another eleven to be dismissed. "The Tessel are not content. There has been a flood at Derred—" She sent it anyway. The reply, when it came, did not address the flood. "Tomorrow you will call on Minister Othora Vey, Ministry of Science. The posting is political — she is the Aulit Council's eyes, not a researcher. She has requested you specifically. Be careful. Be correct. Be *nothing else*." --- The Ministry of Science was the oldest building in Sennorath, and over its doors the falling winged figure was carved larger than anywhere else in the city, life-sized, exquisite, the face serene in its descent. Minister Vey was old even for an Aulit, her white skin gone translucent at the temples, her eyes the gray of weather. She did not rise. She poured two cups of bitter tea herself, which Enwe understood was meant to be understood as significant. "You walked in the lower market yesterday," Vey said. "In a laundress's cloak." "I did." "Good. I despise being lied to in my own office. It wastes the tea." She sipped. "Tell me, Envoy: what does the Stabile want with us? The true answer, not the one in your credentials." "Stability. Trade. The usual." "The *usual*." Vey set down her cup. "Child, I have buried two Coordinators' worth of envoys, diplomatically speaking. They come, they recite, they leave, and the Stabile's reports say *harmony maintained*. You went walking. So either you are a fool who breaks protocol from boredom, or you are something rarer." Her gray eyes did not blink. "Which?" Enwe thought of the woman at the brazier. *We count our dead.* She thought of Ferenn: *be nothing else.* "I'll tell you what I want," she said slowly, "if you tell me first why there is a flooded mine at Derred and a Ministry of Science that calls it weather." Silence sat between them like a third guest. Then Vey smiled — a small, terrible, genuine smile, the first genuine thing Enwe had seen above the lower quarter. "Weather," the Minister said, "is what we call a decision when no one wishes to have made it. You knew that already, I think. Your grandmother's people knew it. Mine did. It is why we carve the falling boy over every door on this world: not to mourn him, Envoy. To remind ourselves that someone built the wings, and someone said *fly*, and someone watched from the shore and wrote it down as weather." She refilled Enwe's cup, unasked. "Now," said Othora Vey. "Tell me what the Stabile wants. And then, if you are still rarer than a fool, I will tell you what Derred actually was. We may," she added, almost gently, "be of use to each other yet." Enwe lifted the cup. Beneath the falling boy, eleven light-minutes from anyone who could forbid her, she began to speak the truth.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of the prompt, written with clear awareness of Le Guin's stylistic register: measured, anthropological, morally serious, with political tension carried through implication rather than action. The chapter hits all required beats — the divergent subspecies (Tessel/Aulit), the falsified briefings, the unauthorized walk through markets, the reprimand, and the testing conversation with the political Minister of Science. Strengths: The central symbol system (the falling winged figure carved over doorways, "weather" as euphemism for political decisions) is genuinely Le Guin-like — mythic, economical, thematically load-bearing. The dialogue with Vey is the highlight: it has real verbal chess, power asymmetry, and a satisfying reversal where the envoy answers a test with a test. The light-minute delay on the reprimand is a smart sci-fi detail that turns bureaucratic anger into something colder. Prose is controlled and mostly clean; sentences flow well; the world feels lived-in through small specifics (laundress's cloak, tuber brazier, syllabary glyphs). Weaknesses: The subspecies worldbuilding is somewhat thin and familiar — oppressed worker caste vs. pale ruling lineage is a well-worn colonial allegory without much novelty. The market scene, while effective, is brief and the old woman's speech ("tell your people...") edges toward exposition-as-convenient-stranger. Vey's "child, I have buried two Coordinators' worth of envoys" is slightly stock seasoned-operator phrasing. The ending is a touch neat — the envoy's "began to speak the truth" is a graceful fade-out but slightly easy, and the closing image is more polished than surprising. Some lines ("it sat in her like a stone, like an oath") flirt with over-neatness without tipping into purple. The piece is somewhat short of the ~1000-word target but close enough. Overall: a competent-to-excellent piece with authentic stylistic mimicry, strong dialogue, and coherent structure, held back slightly by familiar allegorical furniture and a few convenient expository moments. Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.

# The Azra Gambit ## Chapter Three: The Antares Proposition The transfer vessel *Diplomatic Courtesy*—Arthur had noted the name with grim amusement—accelerated at a steady one-third gravity toward a rendezvous point that no one had bothered to specify. He sat strapped into a couch of genuine leather, a luxury that would have cost six months of his mining stipend, and watched a small display screen on the wall cycle through system diagnostics in green text. REACTOR OUTPUT: NOMINAL. HULL INTEGRITY: 100%. CABIN PRESSURE: 14.2 PSI. The numbers scrolled past with bureaucratic indifference. Arthur found himself wishing the screen would display something useful, such as where he was going, or why, or whether he would ever see his little prefabricated dome on the Hellas slope again. The men who had come for him—six of them, in pressure suits of dove gray with the starburst insignia of the Antares Diplomatic Corps—had been impeccably courteous. They had wiped their boots. They had complimented his hydroponic tomatoes. The tallest one, who identified himself only as Attaché Voss, had said, "Mr. Neegan, you are cordially invited to a consultation of mutual benefit," while five flechette rifles remained pointed, with perfect politeness, at the floor near his feet. One did not refuse the Antares Corps. Everyone on Mars knew that "diplomatic" was a word they wore the way a knife wears a sheath. Now, ninety minutes out from Mars orbit, the hatch at the cabin's forward end sighed open, and Attaché Voss inclined his head. "The Minister will see you now." --- The compartment beyond was circular, paneled in dark wood—actual wood, Arthur thought dazedly, hauled across forty light-years or grown in some orbital arboretum at unthinkable cost. A viewport occupied one wall, and through it Mars hung like a rusted coin. Behind a desk of the same dark wood sat a small, neat woman of perhaps seventy, white hair cropped close, eyes the color of slate. "Mr. Neegan. Sit down. I am Minister Calyx Dann, of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. You will have tea." It was not a question. A steward materialized, poured, and vanished. "I'd rather have answers, Minister." "Naturally. You are an engineer; you believe the universe owes you explanations." She smiled thinly. "It owes you nothing, but I will pay you some anyway. Tell me, Mr. Neegan—what do you know about Azra?" "I know what every miner knows. It accelerates decay. Put a gram of it near a kilo of thorium and you get the energy output of a fission pile with no moderator, no critical mass, no waste worth mentioning. It makes torch drives possible. It makes—" he hesitated. "Say it." "It makes bombs possible. Small ones. A bomb the size of my fist that could crack a city dome." "Crack a *continent*, Mr. Neegan, if the geometry is right. Yes." Dann turned her teacup precisely ninety degrees on its saucer. "And what do you know about your own claim? Plot 44-Hellas-North?" "I know my assay came back three weeks ago. I know that since then I've had eleven purchase offers, four lawsuits, two marriage proposals, and now an abduction." "An *invitation*." "The rifles were very inviting." To his surprise, she laughed—a short, dry sound, like a page turning. "Good. You are not stupid, and you are not so frightened that you've gone servile. That improves your value considerably. Mr. Neegan, your plot does not sit on an Azra deposit. It sits on *the* Azra deposit. Preliminary deep-sounding suggests a vein structure massing perhaps forty thousand tons. The total Azra extracted by all parties to date, everywhere, is under six hundred kilograms." Arthur set his cup down very carefully, because his hand had begun to tremble. "That's not possible. The decay-acceleration field—a mass like that should have burned out every radioactive in the crust for kilometers—" "Should have. Did not. Which means the vein is *shielded* somehow, or inert, or—and this is the hypothesis that keeps better minds than yours awake—it is in some configured state we do not understand. Azra is not merely a resource, Mr. Neegan. It is a *question*. And whoever controls your forty thousand tons controls the answer." "And Antares wants it." "Everyone wants it. The Terran Directorate wants it. The Belt Combines want it. The corporations holding mining leases on Mars—who own, may I remind you, the indenture contracts of some two hundred thousand laborers—want it desperately, because their charters expire in six years and Azra is their argument for renewal." She leaned forward. "Some of those parties will offer you money. Some will offer you lawyers. At least one, by our intelligence, intends to offer you a shallow grave and a forged transfer of title. The Directorate's Bureau of Resources filed a sealed motion in the Hellas circuit court two days ago. We believe it is an expropriation order." "And what does Antares offer?" "Partnership. You retain title. We provide protection, extraction technology, and a royalty of eleven percent of refined yield—which will make you, within a decade, wealthier than most planetary governments. In exchange, Antares receives exclusive purchase rights." "And the laborers? The indentured?" Minister Dann regarded him for a long moment, and something shifted behind the slate eyes—calculation, or perhaps reassessment. "An interesting first question. Most men ask about the money." "I was born here, Minister. First generation. My father came out on an indenture and died with three years left on it. Ask your question differently: what happens to two hundred thousand people when the corporations lose their argument for renewal?" "That," she said softly, "would depend a great deal on who holds the Azra. Wouldn't it?" The diagnostic screen on the wall flickered: COURSE CORRECTION IN 00:04:00. Through the viewport, Mars had shrunk perceptibly. "I want it in writing," Arthur said. "All of it. Including the part about the laborers." "You shall have documents by morning, ship's time. And Mr. Neegan—do not mistake my courtesy for the absence of urgency. The expropriation order is real. So is the grave." She rose, small and immaculate. "Sleep on it. But sleep quickly." The hatch sighed open behind him, and Arthur Neegan walked out into a future that had, in the span of one teacup, become very large and very dangerous indeed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens exactly as instructed: Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, reflecting on his situation. The Antares diplomatic corps is rendered with the requested "polite but forceful" menace—wiped boots, complimented tomatoes, rifles pointed politely at the floor. The meeting with Minister Dann is dialogue-heavy as specified, with vivid scene-setting (dark wood, viewport, tea) and clear stakes: expropriation orders, forged titles, shallow graves, expiring corporate charters, and two hundred thousand indentured laborers. The Asimovian flavor is well captured: dialogue-driven intrigue, big-picture politics (Directorate, Belt Combines, Antares) interleaved with small human details (the father's indenture, hydroponic tomatoes), and a central scientific puzzle (why hasn't the Azra vein irradiated the crust?) that functions as a classic Asimov mystery hook. The retrofuturistic vibe—flechette rifles, teacups, PSI readouts—lands well. Weaknesses: Dann is somewhat familiar as a type (small, immaculate, sharp-tongued spymaster), and the negotiation follows a fairly predictable offer-refusal-counteroffer arc. The closing line ("very large and very dangerous") is a bit pat. Arthur's characterization is efficient but slightly convenient—his laborer-sympathy question, while thematically apt, is a touch on-the-nose. Prose is clean and controlled, dialogue crisp, pacing tight at roughly the requested length. No purple prose, no tonal missteps, coherent throughout. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 84.3
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations The red light makes everything look like the inside of a heart. That's what I think every time we lock ourselves into this developing room—that we're two figures moving inside some massive, slow-beating organ, and whatever we say in here doesn't count in the daylight world. Elliot is humming again. Something minor-key and meandering, maybe Cocteau Twins, maybe something he made up. He hums when he's nervous and when he's content, and after six weeks of late nights I still can't always tell the difference. He's bent over the chemical bath, watching one of his images surface like a ghost deciding to be seen. His silver rings—he wears four, all thrifted, all slightly tarnished—catch the safelight as he rocks the tray. "There she is," he murmurs, and I don't know if he means the photograph or something else. Here's what nobody tells you about being the assertive one, the one who always makes the first move, who pins people with eye contact across parties: it leaves you completely unprepared for someone like Elliot. Nineteen years old, wrists like a heron's legs, wearing a moth-eaten mohair sweater over a pleated skirt he started wearing three weeks ago without announcement or apology. He just showed up in it, hands shaking slightly, and I said *killer silhouette* and watched his shoulders drop two inches in relief. I've dated men with jawlines you could draft blueprints from. I've dated women who could break hearts with a smirk. I like definition. I like knowing the shape of what I want. Elliot is all soft edges and questions, and I am—against everything I know about myself—undone by it. "Dani?" He doesn't look up from the bath. "Can I tell you something weird?" "Weird is my whole aesthetic." He laughs, this small exhale through his nose. The image in the tray is one of his self-portraits—double-exposed, his face overlaid with lace curtain shadows, deliberately blurred at the jaw. We're calling the project *Liminal*, which felt pretentious until I saw his negatives. "When I look at these," he says, tongs hovering, "I keep thinking—that's the closest anyone's gotten to seeing me. Not the me in the mirror. The..." He gestures vaguely at his own chest. "The inside one." My instinct—God, my instinct is to *fix* it, to grab the moment by the collar, to say something definitive and bold that resolves his uncertainty into a shape I can hold. That's what I do. I take charge. I steer. Instead I make myself stand very still and say, "Tell me about the inside one." He's quiet long enough that I count three drips from the rinse tap. Then: "I don't think I'm—" His voice catches, restarts. "I've been wondering if 'boy' was ever the right word. Or if it's the right word *sometimes* and not others. Like a tide thing. Does that sound insane?" "It sounds like a tide thing," I say. "Tides aren't insane. They're just the moon doing its job." He looks up at me then, and in the red light his eyes are dark as developer fluid, and he's smiling like I handed him something fragile and didn't drop it. This is the part I haven't told anyone, can barely tell myself: I don't know what my attraction to him means. I've built a whole identity on knowing my own desire—loud, certain, categorized. And here's this person dissolving categories in front of me like a print left too long in the bath, and I want him *more* for it, not less. I want the tide thing. I want whoever surfaces. What does that make me? Some nights I lie awake genuinely confused, like my own internal labels have started peeling at the corners. "You're staring," Elliot says softly. "I'm always staring. I'm a photographer." "You're staring like I'm a print that's not done developing." "Maybe you are." I step closer—careful, slow, which is not my speed, my speed is collision—and look down at the image floating between us. "Maybe that's the best thing a person can be." His humming has stopped. The room is just chemical hum and tap drip and the two of us breathing in red light. He's so close I can see the chipped black polish on his thumbnail where he picks at it during critiques. "Dani." Barely a whisper. "Why are you nice to me? You're scary to literally everyone else." "I'm not nice to you." My voice comes out rougher than intended. "I'm—careful with you. There's a difference." "Why?" And here is where the old Dani would close the distance, take his face in her hands, decide for both of us. I can feel that version of me straining at the leash. But Elliot has spent nineteen years having the world decide things about him—what word he is, what shape he should hold—and I will not be one more person doing that, not even with a kiss. "Because you're in the middle of becoming something," I say. "And I don't want to develop you in my chemicals. I want to see what you turn into in your own." He sets down the tongs. The photograph drifts, finished, abandoned. When he reaches out, it's his hand that finds mine—tentative, deliberate, his cold rings against my knuckles. "What if," he says, "I want you in the room while it happens?" The leash snaps, but gently. I turn my hand over and lace our fingers together, and I let him pull me the last inch closer instead of pushing. "Then I'm in the room," I say. "Lights down. No rushing the exposure." He laughs—real, bright, startled—and starts humming again, that minor-key tune, except now I recognize it for what it always was. Something becoming. Something not finished. Something I'd wait in the dark for, as long as it takes.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of a very specific brief. It hits nearly every requested element: first-person Dani POV, darkroom setting with red light as confessional atmosphere, Elliot's tentative gender questioning, Dani's assertiveness complicated by restraint, her identity confusion about attraction outside her usual "defined presentations," tender awkwardness, and emerging chemistry. The darkroom metaphor—developing, exposure, chemicals—threads consistently through the piece, culminating in the line "I don't want to develop you in my chemicals," which is the story's thesis and its best moment. Strengths: The voice is confident and distinctive. Dani's characterization as someone who "takes charge" is established through concrete self-description ("I've dated men with jawlines you could draft blueprints from") rather than assertion. The central tension—her instinct to "fix" versus giving Elliot agency—is dramatized in real time rather than narrated, particularly in the moment she forces herself to stand still and ask "Tell me about the inside one." The dialogue is mostly strong: Elliot's "tide thing" is a fresh, believable way for a 19-year-old to describe fluidity, and Dani's "Tides aren't insane. They're just the moon doing its job" is a lovely deflection that validates without over-explaining. The ending—him initiating the hand-hold, her letting him pull her the last inch—resolves the power dynamic question physically, which is good craft. Weaknesses: The piece occasionally tips into preciosity. "Wrists like a heron's legs" is a striking image but borders on overwrought; "eyes dark as developer fluid" is a bit on-the-nose given the setting. The metaphor load is high—heart-interior, ghost prints, tide, leash, peeling labels—and a couple of these could have been cut for a leaner effect. Dani's internal monologue about her identity confusion ("What does that make me?") edges toward telling rather than showing in one passage, though it's brief enough to be forgivable as genuine confusion rather than exposition. The ending's final three lines ("Something becoming. Something not finished.") are slightly too neat, wrapping the theme in a bow when the preceding hand-hold had already earned the moment. The "leash snaps, but gently" line is a small contradiction that mostly works but shows the author straining to have it both ways. The transformation here is mutual and small-scale—a shift in dynamic, not a personality overhaul—so it feels earned. The positivity of the ending is congruent with the material; this is a tender scene and the story never pretends otherwise. Nothing meanders; the ~1000-word target is respected and the pacing is tight. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Stolen Moments in Roma **I. The Trevi Fountain, 9:47 a.m.** Ben Whitmore was reading about Bernini when the motorcycle nearly killed him. He heard it first—an angry mechanical snarl—then felt the wind of it as he stepped off the curb, nose deep in *Rome: A Scholar's Companion*. The bike swerved, tires shrieking against cobblestone, and came to rest inches from his shins. The rider tore off her helmet. A cascade of dark hair, a face like a thundercloud, and a stream of Italian so rapid and ornate that Ben caught only the word *cretino*. "I'm—terribly sorry—*mi dispiace*—" He fumbled the guidebook, dropped it, picked it up upside down. "*Sono molto... stupido?*" The woman stopped mid-tirade. Her mouth twitched. "At least you know what you are," she said in accented English. "Most tourists, they think the street is a museum. You think it is a library." "I was reading about the fountain." "The fountain is *right there*." She gestured at the roaring marble spectacle behind him. "You are reading about a thing you could be looking at. This is very British of you." "Yes, well. We do like our texts." She studied him—the rumpled linen jacket, the spectacles, the apologetic posture of a man who said sorry to furniture. Something wicked kindled in her eyes. "Alessandra," she said. "Ben. Benjamin. Ben is fine." "Ben-Benjamin-Ben." She kicked her bike onto its stand. "I have decided you are my problem now. Come. You are seeing Rome wrong." --- **II. Campo de' Fiori, 11:15 a.m.** She moved through the market like weather. Ben trailed behind, clutching his bag, watching her argue cheerfully with a fruit vendor about the morality of his apricot prices. When they walked away, she handed Ben an apricot. "I didn't see you pay for that." "Didn't you?" She bit into her own, eyes dancing. "You should pay more attention, professor." "I'm not actually a professor. I'm a research fellow. Medieval trade routes." "Trade routes." She said it like a diagnosis. "Ben-Benjamin-Ben. You study how things moved seven hundred years ago, and you yourself do not move at all." "I moved to Rome," he said, a bit wounded. "Rome moved you here. There is a difference." She tossed her apricot pit over her shoulder. "Today, you move." --- **III. Trastevere, 1:30 p.m.** She took him through alleys that existed on no map, up a fire escape ("It is allowed," she lied breezily) to a rooftop where all of Rome spread out beneath them, terracotta and gold. "This is technically trespassing," Ben said, breathless. "Everything good is technically something." She sat on the ledge, legs dangling over the abyss, and Ben's heart performed an arrhythmia that had nothing to do with the climb. "Sit." He sat. Several careful feet from the edge. "Why a courier?" he asked. "You seem—you could do anything." She was quiet for a moment, which seemed unlike her. "When I am on the bike, the city cannot hold me. Nothing can." Then the grin returned, deflecting. "Also, I am very bad at sitting in offices. I take things that are not mine." He laughed. He thought she was joking. She watched him laugh, and something complicated crossed her face, there and gone like a cloud's shadow. --- **IV. Near the Pantheon, 4:00 p.m.** "*Alessandra Moretti.*" The voice belonged to a heavyset man outside a café, espresso in hand, expression somewhere between affection and ancient grievance. A torrent of Italian followed. Alessandra answered in kind, laughing, unrepentant. The man turned to Ben. "You are the new friend? Listen to me, English. This one—" he pointed his tiny cup at her like an accusation, "—she will steal the watch from your wrist and the heart from your chest, and you will thank her for both. I know. She stole my scooter in 2019." "*Borrowed*," Alessandra said. "For six weeks!" "It came back." "With a dent!" "With *character*." She kissed the man's cheek and pulled Ben away by the sleeve. "Should I be worried?" Ben asked. "Always," she said cheerfully. "But you won't be. That is your problem and my fun." He checked his wrist. His watch was gone. She held it up between two fingers, glinting in the afternoon sun, grinning like sin itself. "You're a menace," he said, and realized he was smiling. "You're learning." --- **V. Gianicolo Hill, 7:50 p.m.** She drove him up the hill on the back of her bike—Ben clinging on, terrified, exhilarated, his scholarly life dissolving behind them at sixty kilometers an hour—and they arrived as the sun collapsed into the city, setting every dome on fire. They stood at the railing in silence. The first comfortable silence of the day. "Tomorrow you will go back to your library," she said. "Your trade routes." "Probably." He turned to look at her. The dying light made her unreadable. "Although I find I've developed a sudden academic interest in... local culture." "That is the worst flirting I have ever heard." "I'm out of practice. By approximately a decade." She laughed—a real one, not the performed wickedness of the afternoon—and for a moment she looked younger, less armored. Then she stepped close, and Ben's pulse forgot its job entirely. She reached up, and he thought, absurdly, hopefully— She straightened his collar. "Same fountain. Tomorrow. Nine o'clock," she said, pulling her helmet on. "Don't read the guidebook. You have a real guide now." "Is that a promise or a threat?" "Yes." The visor came down. The engine snarled to life. She was gone before he could answer, taillight vanishing into the Roman dusk. Ben stood alone on the hill, smiling like an idiot at a city on fire. It wasn't until he reached for his guidebook on the walk home that he realized she'd taken it. In its place, tucked into his bag, was a single apricot.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, well-structured piece that executes the prompt with notable confidence. The scene-by-scene structure (five timestamped vignettes) suits the "interconnected short scenes" requirement, and the day-in-Rome arc builds cleanly from collision to parting. The prose is economical and often witty ("a face like a thundercloud," "apologetic posture of a man who said sorry to furniture"), with a consistent comic-romantic tone that never slips. Characterization is the piece's strength. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled exactly as specified—never named outright, shown through the apricot, the watch, the guidebook, and corroborated by the café acquaintance's anecdote. The final image (the stolen guidebook replaced by an apricot) is a genuinely elegant callback that lands the "enigmatic but smitten" ending without overplaying it. Ben's transformation is modest and believable—he doesn't become a rebel, he just smiles more—so nothing feels unearned. Weaknesses: the characters flirt with archetype. Ben is a bundle of British tics (apologies, linen jacket, spectacles, awkward flirting), and Alessandra's "menace" is performed rather than felt—her dialogue occasionally tips into quip-machine territory ("Everything good is technically something"). The rooftop moment gestures at depth ("the city cannot hold me") but retreats quickly, keeping her interiority thin; the prompt asked for enigmatic, and the piece delivers enigmatic, though some readers may want a touch more substance beneath the armor. A few jokes are slightly familiar (the "promise or threat" / "Yes" exchange is well-worn). The Italian is used decoratively rather than authentically, and Rome itself is a backdrop of postcard landmarks rather than a lived-in place—more atmosphere than texture. Still, the pacing is tight, the dialogue is mostly sharp, the humor is earned, and the closing beat is satisfying. This is skilled commercial fiction: very good, not transcendent. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 80.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Last Outpost I've been wiping the same spot on the bar for three minutes now. It's a habit. Gives my hands something to do while my ears do the real work. "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." The stranger who says it has tentacled dreads hanging limp around her face, the kind that usually coil and shimmer when their owner is healthy. Hers look like they've given up. I pour the double and slide it across. "Rough cycle?" I ask, rag making its slow circle on the counter. "You could say that." She downs half the glass in one go. Her dreads twitch—a wince, maybe. "You could also say I'm a dead woman drinking, which would be more accurate." Behind her, old Marsten looks up from his card game with the Tellurian twins. I give him the look that means *mind your own hand, friend*, and he obliges. Mostly. "We get a lot of dead women in here," I say. "Most of them recover by last call." "Not this kind of dead." She finishes the glass, taps the rim. I pour again. "You know the Halcyon Combine?" The rag stops. Just for a second. Then it resumes its circle. "Mining conglomerate," I say carefully. "Owns half the processing rights in this belt. Why?" "Because as of sixteen hours ago, I have something they want back. And they are not the asking-nicely type." "And you brought it *here*?" "I brought *me* here. The something is..." She waves a hand vaguely at the ceiling. "Parked. Hidden. Doesn't matter. Point is, I needed a drink before I figure out my next move, and this was the only light on this side of the belt." Marsten has stopped pretending to play cards. The Tellurian twins are openly staring. Even Dovo, our resident drunk poet, has lowered his stylus. "What's your name?" I ask. "Calliope. Cal." "Cal. I'm Nettle. Nets to people who don't bring corporate enforcers to my doorstep." I lean in, keep my voice low, keep the rag moving. "What did you take?" She studies me. Her dreads lift slightly, tasting the air, reading me the way her people do. Whatever they tell her, she decides to trust it. "A survey core. Geological data from the Veil Cluster." She turns the glass in her hands. "The official survey says the cluster's barren. Worthless rock. The *real* survey—the one I was hired to courier and then quietly delete—says different." "Different how?" "Different like there are eleven thousand people in settlements out there who are about to get evicted from 'worthless' rocks that are actually sitting on the richest iridium deposits this side of the rim. Combine buys the claims for scrap, families ship out thinking they got lucky, and six months later—" She mimes an explosion with her fingers. "Profit." The rag goes around. Around. Around. "And you decided to grow a conscience mid-delivery," I say. "I decided I have a sister on one of those rocks." Her voice cracks, just barely. "Funny how fast a conscience grows when it has a face." Dovo raises his glass from the corner. "To faces," he slurs solemnly. Nobody toasts back. "Okay." I exhale. "Okay. So you run. Coreward, rimward, anywhere. Why are you still sitting in my bar?" "Because my ship's drive coil cracked coming through the belt. I limped in on thrusters." She smiles, and it's the most exhausted thing I've ever seen. "I need a coil, a mechanic, and about forty hours I don't have. Combine tracker pinged me at the Threshold relay. They're maybe a day behind. Maybe less." The bar has gone very quiet. The kind of quiet where everyone is listening while pretending to study their drinks. Marsten clears his throat. "Combine ships docked here last month," he says. "Asking questions. About traffic. About who passes through." "They asked you?" I say. "They asked everybody." He looks at me, level and old and knowing. "They'll ask again. And not everybody in this belt says no to Combine credits, Nets." He's right, and that's the problem. The Outpost survives on neutrality. We serve miners and merchants and smugglers and, yes, the occasional Combine survey crew. We don't take sides. Taking sides gets stations like ours starved out, license-revoked, or worse—and the Combine has a long memory and longer reach. I should tell her to leave. Tow her crippled ship out past our beacon range and let her be someone else's catastrophe. The rag goes around. Around. "There's a mechanic on Driftrock Nine," I hear myself say. "Owes me a favor. Big one." "Nets." Marsten's voice carries a warning. "I'm just making conversation, Marsten." "You're making a *target* out of this station is what you're making." "Eleven thousand people," I say, and the words come out sharper than I intend. "You heard her." "I heard a stranger tell a story." He sets his cards down. "Good story. Maybe true. You willing to bet all of us on it?" Cal raises both hands. "He's right. I shouldn't have—I'll finish my drink and go. Thrusters'll get me somewhere." "Thrusters will get you dead," I say. "Sit down." She sits. And that's when the comm panel behind the bar chimes—the long-range hail tone, the one we maybe hear twice a year. I turn and read the incoming transponder code, and my stomach drops through the deck plating. *Halcyon Combine Security Vessel Reliant. Requesting docking clearance. Routine inspection.* A day behind, she said. Maybe less. Try two hours. I look at Cal. Cal looks at the comm panel. Her dreads have gone absolutely still. "Nets," Marsten says quietly. "What are you going to do?" The rag goes around. Around. Around. "I'm thinking," I say.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This chapter executes the prompt's requirements with notable skill. It maintains first person, present tense throughout, delivers roughly 60% dialogue, establishes a clear central conflict (Cal's stolen survey core, the Combine's pursuit, and the Outpost's precarious neutrality), and ends without resolution — indeed escalating the stakes with the Reliant's docking request. The word count lands near the 1000-word seed. Strengths: The voice is confident and consistent. Nets's rag-wiping is an effective recurring motif — a physical beat that carries tension and doubles as characterization (hands busy while ears work). The worldbuilding is delivered economically through dialogue: the Halcyon Combine, the Veil Cluster settlements, the iridium deposits, the station's dependence on neutrality. Cal's motive (a sister on one of the rocks) is a grounded, humanizing detail that avoids melodrama. Marsten functions well as the voice of pragmatic caution, giving the conflict genuine internal stakes rather than a simple good-vs-evil setup. The ending cliffhanger — the tracker arriving in two hours instead of a day — is a well-judged escalation, and "I'm thinking" is a strong closing line. Weaknesses: Some elements are familiar to the point of predictability — the "dead woman drinking" line, the ragged stranger with a secret, the corporate-villain reveal, the conscience-stricken courier. The plot machinery (cracked drive coil, tracker ping) is functional but conventional. Dovo's "To faces" toast is a slightly forced bit of color. Cal's trust in Nets arrives a touch easily, and the eleven-thousand-settlers stakes are stated rather than deeply felt. The prose is clean but rarely transcendent; it prioritizes momentum over lyricism, which suits the piece but caps its ceiling. Overall this is a polished, professional genre chapter that does everything asked of it, with only mild derivativeness and a few stock beats holding it back from excellence. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 81.6
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South ## Chapter Two: The City That Care Forgot The strap slips off my shoulder again. Third time in ten minutes. I hike it back up and keep walking, because stopping feels like admitting I don't know where I'm going. Which I don't. But the trick — and I learned this from years of walking into classrooms where everybody already had opinions about me — is to move like you have a destination. Predators can smell lost. New Orleans smells like fried something, river mud, and last night's beer baking off the sidewalk. It's 9 a.m. and already hot in a way Tennessee never managed. Wet hot. Like the air is sweating on you personally. I have $63. I counted it twice in a Burger King bathroom, locked stall, backpack between my knees. Sixty-three dollars and a phone I'm scared to turn on because Mom might've reported it, or worse, might *not* have. *Don't think about Mom.* Too late. I'm thinking about Mom. About her face going flat and gray when I said the words, like I'd unplugged something behind her eyes. About Dad not even getting angry, just quiet, which was worse, because quiet is how he gets before — The strap slips. I yank it up. I find a park — Jackson Square, says a sign — and there are tarot readers setting up card tables and a guy painted entirely silver standing very still. I sit on the steps by the cathedral because steps are free, and that's when she sits down next to me. Doesn't ask. Just sits. "You're new," she says. She's maybe seventeen. Buzzed hair growing out uneven, an Army surplus jacket way too heavy for this heat, and a dog — a scruffy brown thing with one ear up, one down — leashed with actual rope. "I'm just visiting," I say. "Sure." She pulls a granola bar from her pocket, breaks it, hands me half without asking if I want it. I take it because I'm starving and pride is for people with more than $63. "Visiting. With a backpack you keep death-gripping and shoes you been walking in all night. Where from?" "Tennessee." "Mm. I'm Dez. That's Biscuit." The dog thumps its tail at its name. "You got a place to be tonight?" *Don't trust her. Don't trust anybody. This is how it starts in every after-school special — the friendly stranger, the favor, then suddenly you owe somebody something you can't pay back.* "I'm figuring it out," I say. "That's a no." Dez squints at the silver statue guy. "Okay, rules. You want rules?" "I didn't ask for —" "Don't sleep in the Quarter, cops sweep it. Don't take drinks you didn't watch get made. Don't go with anybody who offers you a 'place to crash' on day one — and yeah, I see the irony, I'm not offering, Biscuit doesn't share." A beat. "And if a guy named Marcus finds you and says he can 'help,' you run. He helps kids into things they don't come back from." I'm quiet, chewing granola bar, watching pigeons fight over a beignet. The fear in my chest is doing something weird — not shrinking exactly, but changing shape. Becoming something I can carry. "Why'd you leave?" she asks. And here's the thing. I came out once already this week and it detonated my entire life. Every instinct says *lie, deflect, invent some drama,* like the school counselor would predict. *Concerning behavioral patterns,* right? But I'm two states from anybody who knew the old version of me, and that fact suddenly feels less like falling and more like — "I'm trans," I say. Out loud. To a stranger. In daylight. "Told my family two days ago. It went bad." Dez nods like I told her the weather. "Taylor a chosen name or a keeping name?" "Keeping. It already worked." Nobody's ever asked me that. My eyes do something embarrassing and I blink it back. "Good name. Flexible." She stands, brushes crumbs off. "C'mon. Drop-in center on Rampart does lunch at noon, no ID, no questions, no church stuff. You can get on a list for an actual youth shelter. The good one, not the one that makes you pray the gay away first." We walk. The strap slips; I fix it. Dez talks the whole time — which streets flood, which gutter punks are okay, which busker spots are claimed turf — and I notice she never once mentions where *she's* from, or why a seventeen-year-old knows the shelter system like a subway map, or why she flinches, tiny but real, every time a police car rolls past. There's a story under that surplus jacket. She's not telling it, and I'm not asking, because apparently down here that's the etiquette: you get to be exactly who you say you are today. Which is, honestly, the whole reason I left. The drop-in center is a converted house with a rainbow sticker on the door, and the woman at the desk calls me Taylor without asking what's on my birth certificate, and writes *they/them* on the intake form like it's nothing, like it's normal, like it's *true,* and I have to go stand by the water fountain for a second and breathe. Past tense: yesterday I had a family and a town and a name everybody said wrong on purpose. Present tense: I have $63, half a granola bar in my stomach, a dog named Biscuit asleep on my foot, and a stranger with secrets teaching me the rules of survival. "You're doing the face," Dez says, sliding a tray of red beans and rice at me. "What face?" "The 'I might actually be okay' face. Don't get cocky. This city eats people." She steals my cornbread. "But yeah. You might actually be okay." The strap slips off my shoulder. This time, I let it hang.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong, controlled YA chapter that hits nearly every prompt requirement: first-person Taylor voice, mixed tense (explicitly leveraged in the "Past tense / Present tense" beat), one-day timeline, a runaway with secrets (Dez), internal monologue with conflicting emotions, and dialogue with an "interesting character." The prose is lean and voice-driven, with a distinctive recurring motif (the slipping backpack strap) that pays off in the final line — a well-earned, understated symbol of Taylor loosening their grip on fear. Dez is sketched efficiently with telling details (flinching at police cars, never explaining herself) that gesture at depth without over-explaining. The dialogue is naturalistic and character-revealing; Dez's "rules" monologue is both world-building and characterization. The emotional beats — the mother's flat face, the intake form moment at the water fountain — are shown through physical action rather than stated, mostly avoiding tell-don't-show. Weaknesses: the plot is somewhat familiar territory (wise street kid mentors naive newcomer; drop-in center as sanctuary is a touch convenient/idealized). Dez's dialogue occasionally tips into quippy, overly polished street-kid aphorisms ("Predators can smell lost" is Taylor's, but Dez's lines sometimes feel written). The shelter scene resolves a bit fast and gently for a first day in a dangerous city — mild incongruent positivity, though the "this city eats people" line and Marcus warning hedge it. The Marcus warning is a slightly stock Chekhov device. Some emotional summary lines ("changing shape. Becoming something I can carry") edge toward telling. Still, the voice is consistent, the pacing tight, and the ending lands.
