+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy The morning after the end of the world—which was now some forty years of mornings, give or take—dawned over the rubble of what had once been a retail park, and was now home to Midas and his koala. It is important to clarify, at this point, that the koala was not alive. It had never been alive. It was an animo-tronic Companion Friend™ from the Before Time, and its name was Chewy, and it had survived the collapse of technological civilization with the serene indifference of all truly useless things. "The water's gone green again," said Midas, peering into the rain barrel. "Greener. It's gone *more* green. It's achieving new frontiers of green." Chewy's eyes whirred open. "BECAUSE YOU'RE WORTH IT," he announced. "I'm really not." Midas had the kind of face that committees of trouble convened over. He wasn't unlucky, exactly. Unlucky implied randomness. Midas's misfortune had *direction*. It had ambition. If catastrophe were a river, Midas was the sea toward which it inevitably flowed. "Right," he said, consulting the map he'd drawn on the back of an ancient pizza menu. "The old pharmacy on Birch Street. Tuley swears nobody's cleared it. Water purification tablets, maybe iodine. In, out, home by dusk." "JUST DO IT," said Chewy. "That's the spirit. Probably. Nobody knows what your spirit is." He strapped Chewy to the top of his pack, where the koala served as a lookout in the sense that a garden gnome serves as a security system, and set off across the rubble. --- The thing about plans, Midas reflected three hours later, is that they are essentially prayers with diagrams. The pharmacy was exactly where Tuley said it would be. This should have been his first warning. Things being where they were supposed to be was, in Midas's experience, the universe winding up for the punchline. The second warning was the goat. It stood in the pharmacy doorway with the calm authority of a creature that had inherited the earth and found it adequate. Behind it, in the gloom, other shapes moved. Many shapes. Horizontal pupils gleamed. "It's a pharmacy," Midas told it, reasonably. "You don't even have a prescription." The goat regarded him with the flat yellow stare of middle management. "MEMBERSHIP HAS ITS PRIVILEGES," offered Chewy. The goat charged. What followed was less a battle than an itinerary of indignities. Midas went through the doorway sideways, over a shelf of expired vitamins, through what had once been the family planning aisle—the goats had eaten most of it, which raised troubling questions—and into the back room, where he discovered two things. The first was a sealed crate of purification tablets, miraculously intact. The second was that the back room had no other exit, and the herd was assembling at the door with the patience of creditors. "Okay," he panted, wedging himself behind a cabinet. "Okay. Tactical thinking. What would a clever person do?" "COLLECT ALL FOUR," said Chewy. "Four what? Four *what*, Chewy? Forty years and you've never once—" The ceiling, weakened by four decades of rain and the recent addition of several goats who had found their way upstairs, chose this moment to express an opinion. The opinion was: *down*. --- Midas came to in a fog of plaster dust, pinned under a beam, with a goat standing on his chest and eating his map. The crate of tablets had landed, intact, just out of reach, in the manner of all important things everywhere. "Chewy?" From somewhere in the rubble: "TASTE THE RAINBOW." "Good. You're alive. Functioning. Whatever it is you do." The goat finished the map and started on his sleeve. Midas, in a moment of inspiration born of desperation—the only kind he ever had—reached into his pocket and found his last strip of dried apple. He hurled it through the doorway. The herd departed with the unified suddenness of an opinion poll. It took him an hour to dig himself out, another to dig out Chewy—whose left ear was now somewhere in the pharmacy's foundations and whose voice box had developed a wet rattle—and a third to realize that the collapsed ceiling had pinned the crate under what used to be the second floor and was now simply *the floor, but angrier*. He got six bottles out. Six. From a crate of two hundred. Then it started to rain, because of course it did, and the rain woke up something in the old electrical substation next door, which sparked, which lit the dry weeds, which meant Midas spent the journey home jogging ahead of a modest but sincere grass fire while carrying a smoldering koala that kept announcing "NOW WITH 30% MORE." "More *what*?" Midas screamed into the wind, at the world, at the Before Time and all its unfinished sentences. Chewy, diplomatically, said nothing for almost a mile. --- They got back to the retail park at dusk, as planned, which Midas felt was a kind of victory if you squinted and had recently suffered head trauma. He was down one sleeve, one map, most of his dignity, and the skin off both knees. He was up six bottles of purification tablets, one new limp, and a goat—a small one, which had followed him home and now stood in the doorway with an air of tenancy. He set Chewy on the shelf by the rain barrel. The koala listed to one side now, ear gone, fur singed, one eye whirring at half speed. He looked, Midas thought, exactly like the world: broken, absurd, still inexplicably running. "Well," said Midas, dropping the tablets into the green water and watching it become merely greenish. "Could've been worse." Chewy's good eye clicked open. Somewhere in his ancient chest, a circuit board older than the apocalypse made its decision. "I'M LOVIN' IT," he said. And the terrible thing, Midas thought as the goat ate his bedroll, was that some days—not many, but some—he almost knew what that meant.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, confident piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that captures Pratchett's register well: dry asides, anthropomorphized misfortune, and a world where absurdity is treated with bureaucratic calm. The structure follows the prompt precisely—deliberation at home base, a mission that goes sideways in escalating stages (goats, ceiling collapse, fire), and a return home "worse for wear" in multiple senses (lost sleeve, lost ear on Chewy, new limp, plus a stray goat). Chewy is the standout invention: an animatronic koala spouting corrupted advertising slogans ("BECAUSE YOU'RE WORTH IT," "JUST DO IT," "TASTE THE RAINBOW") is both funny and quietly melancholic—a relic of a dead civilization that can only speak in its marketing. The story wisely never explains him, and the ending's "I'M LOVIN' IT" lands as a bittersweet punchline rather than a cheap one. Midas is a well-drawn hapless protagonist whose misfortune is characterized with wit ("his misfortune had direction. It had ambition"). The prose is elegant and controlled, with strong aphoristic lines ("plans... are essentially prayers with diagrams," "the patience of creditors"). The goat-as-middle-management imagery is a highlight. Dialogue is minimal but effective; Chewy's non-sequiturs are the joke engine and work consistently. Minor criticisms: the plot beats (trapped by animals, ceiling collapse, fire chase) are familiar survival-comedy tropes, and the emotional arc, while touching, stays within expected bounds. The "could've been worse" ending is earned but the final beat of near-understanding is slightly telegraphed. Some jokes ("the floor, but angrier") are excellent; a few ("garden gnome as security system") are more serviceable. Word count and tone requirements are met. No purple prose, no meandering, no amateurish tells. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 60.0
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Shelf Life The bell above the door of Pendragon Books jangled violently as a man in sunglasses and a flat cap practically fell through the entrance, slamming it shut behind him. "Sorry—sorry. Just—give me one moment." He pressed his back against the door, peering through the glass at the rain-slicked street of Aberdyfi. Rhiannon Pryce looked up from the counter, where she was repairing the spine of a 1923 edition of *The Mabinogion*. "We open at nine. It's ten past, so technically you're fine, but the dramatic entrance was unnecessary." "There are photographers," he said, breathless. "A whole pack of them. Like wolves. Wolves with telephoto lenses." "In Aberdyfi?" "They followed me from the film set in Harlech." He removed the sunglasses with a flourish that suggested he expected a reaction. She gave him a long look. "Am I supposed to know who you are?" His face flickered—a fascinating little collapse, quickly rebuilt. "Dylan Vaughn?" "Is that a question?" "No. It's—I'm Dylan Vaughn. The actor. *The Falcon's Reach*? *Midnight in Tangier*? I was nominated for a BAFTA." "Nominated," she repeated, returning to her book glue. "Hm." "That's a very loaded 'hm.'" "It's an entirely neutral 'hm.' You're welcome to hide here, but mind the display table. The wolves rarely venture past the chippy." He drifted toward the counter, watching her hands work the brush along the cracked spine. "You genuinely don't know who I am." "I genuinely don't own a television." "Everyone owns a television." "I own four thousand books and a kettle. I find it sufficient." He laughed—a real one, surprised out of him—and leaned against the counter with practiced casualness. "You know, most people are quite pleased to meet me." "I imagine that's terribly comfortable for you." "It is, rather." He grinned, deploying what three separate magazine profiles had called *the smile*. "And you are?" "The owner." "The owner has a name, surely." "The owner has work to do." But her hands, she noticed with some irritation, had stopped moving. She set down the brush. "Rhiannon." "Rhiannon. Like the song." "Like the goddess, actually. Fleetwood Mac came second." "I stand corrected." He picked up a book from the counter—then froze. "Hang on. Is this a first edition of *The Worm Ouroboros*?" She blinked. "You know Eddison?" "Know him? I spent an entire summer when I was fourteen reading nothing but pre-Tolkien fantasy. Eddison, Dunsany, Hope Mirrlees—" He turned the book over reverently. "I have a 1926 *Lud-in-the-Mist* at home. Found it in a stall in Hay-on-Wye before anyone cared. It's possibly my favourite object on Earth." Rhiannon stared at him. "You collect interwar fantasy." "Obsessively. Don't tell the tabloids; it ruins my image. I'm meant to collect vintage motorcycles and ex-girlfriends." He said it with a wink, but his eyes were still on the book, and the wink died halfway through, as if he'd embarrassed himself. "Mirrlees," she said slowly, "is criminally underread." "*Criminally*. The Duke Aubrey chapters alone—" "—the fairy fruit as forbidden art, yes—" "—yes! Exactly! Nobody ever wants to talk about this." He looked at her with naked delight, all the polish gone. "I once tried to discuss it with my co-star on *Midnight in Tangier* and she asked if Mirrlees was 'on Netflix.'" "Tragic." "It was genuinely the loneliest moment of my career, and I've done dinner theatre in Swindon." A laugh escaped her before she could stop it. She covered it badly with a cough. He noticed—of course he noticed—and his whole posture brightened like a plant turned to the sun. "She laughs," he said. "I was beginning to think you were carved from Welsh slate." "Don't get excited. It was at you, not with you." "I'll take it. I'm not proud." "You're entirely proud. You've checked your reflection in that glass cabinet twice since you came in." He had the grace to look caught. "Occupational hazard. My face is my mortgage." Then, quieter, oddly sincere: "It's exhausting, actually. Wondering whether people like you or the—the poster of you." "And which one wants me to like him right now?" The question landed harder than she'd intended. He was silent a moment, turning the Eddison over in his hands. "Honestly? I'm not sure I know the difference anymore." Then the grin snapped back into place, slightly crooked. "That was alarmingly candid. Forget I said it. I'm enormously well-adjusted and beloved by all." "Clearly." "You really aren't going to be charmed, are you?" "Not visibly." His eyebrows lifted. "*Not visibly.* Now there's an interesting choice of words, Rhiannon-like-the-goddess." She felt heat climb her neck and turned briskly to the shelf behind her. "The Eddison's forty pounds. The dust jacket's chipped, or it'd be twice that." "I'll give you sixty if you'll have a coffee with me." "That's not how commerce works." "Forty, then, and the coffee's a separate negotiation." She set the wrapped book on the counter, and for a moment neither of them moved, his fingers an inch from hers on the brown paper. "The photographers will have given up by now," she said. "They'll have gone to the chippy. The wolves, as you say, have simple appetites." "Right. Yes." He didn't move toward the door. "There's a book fair in Machynlleth next month. Antiquarian. I saw the poster on your window. Backwards, obviously, but I'm a quick study." "I'm aware of the fair. I have a stall." "Then I'll need directions. And possibly a guide. I'm hopeless with rural Wales—I once got lost between two sheep." "You're filming in Harlech for how long?" "Eight weeks." He paused at the door, cap back on, looking suddenly less like a film star and more like a boy hoping not to be turned away. "Long enough to develop a serious book-buying habit, I'd imagine. Daily, possibly." "We open at nine," she said, picking up her brush. "Try to arrive without the dramatics." "No promises." The bell jangled. "Goodbye, Rhiannon." She waited until the door had fully closed before she allowed herself to smile—and then noticed, with profound annoyance, that her hands were trembling slightly over the *Mabinogion*, and that she'd already begun calculating what stock to bring to Machynlleth.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, confident scene that fulfills nearly every instruction with precision. The premise (actor fleeing paparazzi into a Welsh bookstore) is executed briskly, and the setting is authentically Welsh without being decorative—Aberdyfi, Harlech, Hay-on-Wye, Machynlleth, the *Mabinogion* all ground the piece geographically and culturally. The dialogue is the engine here, as requested. Both voices are distinct and consistent: Dylan deploys celebrity patter ("wolves with telephoto lenses," "the smile" as a named commodity) while Rhiannon answers in dry, clipped deflections ("It's an entirely neutral 'hm.'"). The prompt's central dynamic—the rogue whose charm offensive is derailed by her immunity—is handled well: his "fascinating little collapse, quickly rebuilt" at not being recognized, and the moment his wink "died halfway through, as if he'd embarrassed himself," show the fragile ego economically. The shared-interest turn (interwar fantasy: Eddison, Mirrlees, Dunsany) is the scene's cleverest move. It gives the attraction a plausible, specific basis rather than relying on pure banter, and it lets Dylan drop the polish ("naked delight, all the polish gone"), which is exactly the derailment the prompt asked for. Rhiannon's interiority is rendered with restraint: the covered laugh, the heat climbing her neck, the trembling hands, the pre-planning of the Machynlleth stall—show, not tell, of her flustered state. Weaknesses: the banter occasionally tips into overly scripted quippiness—lines like "I once got lost between two sheep" and "dinner theatre in Swindon" feel written-to-impress rather than spoken, a touch too polished for naturalistic dialogue. The "plant turned to the sun" simile is a small cliché. The ending, while charming, is a touch neat—both characters resolve into tidy mutual anticipation with minimal friction or cost, and the scene risks being a well-execected romantic two-hander without much risk or surprise in its structure. The emotional beats, while genuinely complex, stay within comfortable genre territory. Still, this is skilled work: coherent, economical, well-voiced, emotionally layered without melodrama, with a satisfying and earned lightness. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Underhold The door swung inward on oiled hinges—too smooth, too silent for a door that should have been locked against them. Aya felt the wrongness of it crawl up her spine like a beetle beneath her corset. The underhold opened before them in a wash of gaslight, the brass fixtures hissing along walls of weeping stone. Whale-oil lamps burned in sconces shaped like krakens, their tentacles black with soot. And there, seated upon the very plinth where the Scythan artifact should have rested, was Madame Vexa Crowle—uncuffed, unbothered, and very much *un*-arrested. "Shut the door behind you, loves," Vexa said. "There's a terrible draught." In Simeon's waistcoat, his pocket watch ticked. *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Loud as a hammer on a coffin nail. Bodyguards peeled out of the shadows—six of them, maybe more, with pistols of brass and bone-handled cudgels, their faces lit ghoulish from below. Katra swore under her breath, a dockside oath involving someone's mother and a harpoon. "The raid," Aya said slowly, her voice disguised behind the mask in the low rasp she'd cultivated for two years. "The constabulary—" "Were paid handsomely to make a spectacle of dragging an empty carriage through the fog." Vexa rose, skirts rustling like dead leaves. The artifact hung at her hip in a cage of cold iron, pulsing faintly, like a heart cut out and kept beating from spite. "You'd be astonished what a power vacuum flushes out of the woodwork. Rats. Climbers. *Traitors*." She smiled, and her teeth caught the lamplight. "And my, haven't you three come scurrying." *Tick. Tick. Tick.* "Take them." It happened without violence, which was somehow worse. Hands like dock-cranes seized Aya's arms; she felt Katra thrash beside her and heard the meaty sound of a forearm across her friend's throat, choking the fight out of her. Simeon didn't struggle at all. Simeon never struggled. He simply went pale and rigid, watch ticking against his ribs like a second, smaller heart. *The shadows*, Aya thought, reaching inward to the cold place beneath her sternum, the door in herself that opened onto the immateria. *I could call them. I could—* A pistol's muzzle pressed cold beneath her jaw. "Ah-ah," said Vexa, drifting closer. "I know what you are, little shade-caller. Heard the whispers. Things with too many fingers, plucking purses from locked rooms." She tilted her head. "Brass and powder, dearie. The old reliable answer to the old unholy question. You'd not finish the summons before Mortlake here redecorates the ceiling with you." The cold place closed. Aya stood very still. "Now then." Vexa's gloved fingers found the edge of the mask. "Let's see what manner of rat wears silk stitching on a thief's hood." *No. No, no—* The mask came away. The silence that followed had texture, had *weight*, like the held breath before a hanging. One of the bodyguards actually stepped back. "Strike me blind," Vexa breathed. "Lady Aya Veltrayne. The Magistrate's own niece, slumming in my gutters." She laughed then, a sound like a saw through wet wood. "Oh, this is *Christmas*." Aya's face was bare to the lamplight and she felt it like a flaying. Two years of careful hours, of climbing through windows and back into ballgowns before dawn, of being *someone else*—gone, peeled off with a square of black cloth. She thought, absurdly, of her mother. The scaffold in Gallowmarket Square. The crowd's hunger. *They hang our kind twice, Aya. Once for the crime, once for the blood.* *Tick. Tick. Tick.* "You're calculating," she said. Her voice came out in her own accent now—the cut-crystal vowels of the Hill—and she let it. Leaned into it. "I can see it behind your eyes, Madame. So allow me to assist with the arithmetic." "Bold words for a woman with a barrel under her chin." "Pragmatic words." Her heart slammed against her stays but her voice, gods bless her breeding, stayed level. "Kill me, and you've a corpse. Corpses fetch nothing at market and the Veltrayne name buys a great deal of vengeance. My uncle would burn the Saltrow district to its pilings to be seen avenging me—not for love, you understand. For *appearances*. We are nothing if not concerned with appearances." Vexa's eyes narrowed. "And alive?" "Alive, I'm leverage. A magistrate's niece in your pocket. Charters un-revoked. Raids that knock politely first. Constables who develop sudden blindness." Aya swallowed against the pistol's kiss. "You bribed the law to fake your own arrest—so you already know the price of everything in this city. I'm telling you mine. It's considerable." "She talks pretty," rumbled Mortlake. "She talks *desperate*," Vexa corrected, but she was circling now, considering, the artifact pulsing at her hip like a tide. "And your friends? What's their exchange rate, your Ladyship?" *Tick. Tick. Tick.* Simeon's watch, counting out their lives in brass increments. "Package deal," Aya said. "Damage them, and I become remarkably uncooperative. I'll go to the gallows singing, and I'll sing every name and every den and every counting-house you've ever touched." "The gallows." Vexa stopped before her, close enough that Aya could smell lamp-oil and lavender water gone sour. "Aye, there's the rub, isn't it? Because the moment your fine uncle learns where you've been spending your evenings—the moment a single whisper of *Lady Veltrayne, guildswoman and shade-caller* slips these walls—you'll swing from the same beam as your sainted mother. They do so love a matched set, the Magistracy." Her smile was a wound. "So you're not negotiating your ransom at all, are you, pet? You're negotiating my *silence*. Which makes you not my hostage." She leaned in, breath warm and rotten-sweet. "It makes you my *property*." Aya said nothing. Beneath her sternum, the cold door trembled on its hinges, and the shadows in the corners of the underhold leaned in, listening, patient as creditors. *Tick*, said the watch. *Tick. Tick.* "Put them somewhere damp," said Vexa. "Her Ladyship and I shall take tea in the morning, and discuss the terms of her employment."
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of genre fiction that executes the brief with notable skill. The scene delivers every requested beat: the trio enters the underhold, confronts the un-arrested guild leader (Madame Vexa Crowle), is captured without a fight, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates on her hostage value while grappling with the exposure of her identity and her mother's fate. The prose is the standout element. The whalepunk/Victorian aesthetic is rendered through precise, era-appropriate detail: gaslight, whale-oil lamps in kraken sconces, corsets and stays, brass and bone-handled weapons, "cut-crystal vowels of the Hill." The recurring tick of Simeon's pocket watch works as an effective structural motif, counting out the tension in brass increments, and the "cold door" beneath Aya's sternum as a metaphor for her summoning ability is a nice gothic touch that pays off in the final image of shadows "leaning in, listening, patient as creditors." The dialogue is largely excellent. Vexa is given a distinct, theatrical menace ("There's a terrible draught," "my, haven't you three come scurrying"), and Aya's negotiation is sharp and character-revealing — she correctly identifies that her value is not ransom but silence, and Vexa's counter ("It makes you my property") lands as a genuinely chilling reversal that reframes the power dynamic. The mother's scaffold memory ("They hang our kind twice") is economical and effective. Weaknesses are minor. "Oh, this is Christmas" reads slightly off-register for the setting. The capture happens a touch conveniently — six bodyguards materialize and the trio is subdued with little resistance, though the prompt forbade a fight scene, so this is largely excused. Vexa's knowledge of Aya's shade-calling ("Heard the whispers") is asserted rather than earned, a small tell-don't-show lapse. The ending, with its "take tea in the morning" menace, is well-judged — dark, unresolved, consistent with the piece's tone, no false positivity. The piece is coherent, tightly paced, never meandering, and avoids both purple excess and amateurish flatness. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gunpowder Rendezvous The bar is called Mao's, which makes Spike laugh for reasons he doesn't explain to anyone. It squats at the rotting edge of a port city where bounty heads come to disappear and bounty hunters come to find them. The whiskey is watered, the lights are dying, and the woman three stools down has been watching him for ten minutes. Spike lights a cigarette with a lighter ringed in rust—it's been dropped in harbor water more than once, fished out, kept anyway. Some things you don't replace. "You're sitting on my mark," the woman says. She's got a dragon tattooed up her right arm and shorts that violate several climate considerations. "Funny." Spike exhales toward the ceiling fan. "I was about to say the same thing." Revy turns on her stool. "Chen Wu. Eighty grand, dead or alive. I've been tracking that fat bastard for a week." "Eighty? They told me sixty." He sighs. "Story of my life." "Then walk away, beanpole. Cut your losses." "Can't. I haven't eaten a real meal in three days." He signals the bartender. "Two whiskeys. She's paying." "The hell I am." "You've got eighty grand coming. I've got lint." Something in the sheer shamelessness of it makes Revy bark a laugh. She slaps money on the bar. "Fine. One drink. Then you disappear, or I make you disappear." "Whatever happens, happens." They drink. Then they drink again, because the first round was insulting and the second is principle. Revy talks with her hands, and her hands keep drifting toward the Cutlass pistols on her hips, and Spike notices she notices him noticing. She's fast. He can tell by the way she sits—loose everywhere except the shoulders. "You move like a guy who used to be somebody," she says. "I died once. Took the pressure off." "That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard." She knocks back her shot. "I like it." He studies her sideways with his good eye, the real one, the one that sees the present. The fake one sees the past, and the past has a woman in it, blonde and gone, so he keeps the good eye on Revy instead. "You drink like you're trying to kill something." "Yeah, well. It keeps coming back." She grins, all teeth and no warmth, except there's a flicker—just one—of something underneath. Spike recognizes it because he owns the same flicker. The look of someone who decided long ago that they're already dead and got cheated when the world kept turning anyway. That's when Chen Wu walks in. Eighty grand on two fat legs, flanked by four bodyguards, heading for the back room. Spike and Revy lock eyes for exactly one heartbeat. Then they're both moving. She flips the table; he kicks his stool into the first bodyguard's knees. Guns come out everywhere at once. Revy's Cutlasses sing in stereo—two muzzle flashes, two bodyguards down screaming about their shoulders. Spike flows through the third man like water, Jeet Kune Do turning the guy's own momentum into a face-first meeting with the bar. The fourth gets the Jericho's barrel against his temple before he clears leather. Chen Wu runs. They both fire at his legs. He drops. Two holes, one in each calf, perfectly symmetrical. Silence. Gunsmoke. The bartender, with the weariness of a man who's seen this before, points at a sign: YOU BREAK IT YOU BUY IT. "That's my bullet in his left leg," Revy says, breathing hard. "Right leg's mine. Guess we split him." "I don't split." "Neither do I." Spike holsters the Jericho. "But he's bleeding and the bar's about to be full of cops, so let's argue somewhere with fewer witnesses." --- The Sunrise Motel has neither sunrise nor much that qualifies as motel. Chen Wu is zip-tied in the bathtub, whimpering. The bounty office opens at eight a.m. It is currently midnight, and the room has one bed, one bottle of rum Revy produced from somewhere, and two people who don't trust anybody, least of all each other. They drink sitting on opposite ends of the bed, guns within reach, the bottle passing between them like a hostage exchange. "That shot you made," Revy says. "Through the fan blades. With one eye that works." "You counted my eyes?" "I count everything." She takes a pull of rum. "Could've shot you in that bar, you know. Crossed my mind twice." "Only twice? I'm losing my touch." He takes the bottle from her, and their fingers overlap a half-second longer than the transfer requires. Neither acknowledges it. Both file it away. The room is hot. She's close enough that he can see the old scars under the dragon ink. She's looking at his mouth the way she looked at the bounty—like something she wants and doesn't trust herself to take cleanly. "You got somebody," she says. It's not a question. "Some ghost. I can smell it on you." "You've got one too. Smells like cigarettes and bad decisions." "That's just me." "Exactly." She moves first—or he does, afterward neither will admit which—and they're six inches apart, and then her Cutlass is under his chin and his Jericho is against her ribs, both drawn so fast neither saw the other do it. They freeze. Breathe. Her eyes are amber and furious and amused. "Habit," she says. "Same." Neither lowers the gun. Neither pulls the trigger. The standoff stretches—steel and body heat, two people fluent in violence and illiterate in everything else. "This is the dumbest foreplay I've ever had," Revy mutters. "Speak for yourself. This is Tuesday." Slowly, simultaneously, like a treaty between hostile nations, the guns lower. They don't kiss. They don't touch. Revy takes the rum back and Spike lights another cigarette with his rust-ringed lighter, and they sit shoulder to shoulder against the headboard, not sleeping, waiting for eight a.m. "Fifty-fifty," she finally says. "Sixty-forty. I'm hungrier." "Fifty-fifty, cowboy, or we do the gun thing again." He smiles around the cigarette. "Maybe later." She doesn't say no.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a crossover premise that could easily have gone wrong. The writer clearly knows both source materials: Spike's fatalism, hunger, prosthetic eye, and "whatever happens, happens" philosophy are woven in organically rather than quoted as decoration; Revy's "Two Hands" skill, dragon tattoo, anger, and guarded vulnerability are all present and active in the plot rather than merely described. The prose is lean and confident, with a hardboiled rhythm that suits both franchises. Lines like "two people fluent in violence and illiterate in everything else" and "the bottle passing between them like a hostage exchange" are genuinely good—witty without straining. The dialogue crackles: the bounty-haggling opening ("You're sitting on my mark" / "Funny. I was about to say the same thing") efficiently establishes both characters and their dynamic in a few exchanges. The banter about counting eyes, smelling ghosts on each other, and "That's just me" / "Exactly" is economical character work. The bar fight is well-choreographed and uses both characters' distinct skill sets (Revy's dual-wielding, Spike's Jeet Kune Do flow). The motel standoff delivers the requested unresolved sexual tension without tipping into either romance-novel sentimentality or crude excess—guns drawn mid-lean-in is exactly the right image for these two, and "This is the dumbest foreplay I've ever had" / "Speak for yourself. This is Tuesday" is a highlight. Weaknesses: the piece leans on familiar beats—the "one bed" motel, the reluctant partnership, the mutual ghost-recognition—and a reader well-versed in either fandom will see most moves coming. The bartender's YOU BREAK IT YOU BUY IT sign is a stock gag. Chen Wu is a cipher, purely a MacGuffin, which is acceptable but leaves the plot machinery visible. The symmetry of the leg shots is a nice touch but slightly cute. Some of Revy's vulnerability is asserted ("a flicker—just one—of something underneath") rather than fully dramatized, a mild tell-don't-show moment, though the piece mostly shows well. The ending's "she doesn't say no" is a well-judged button, but the overall arc is more a well-executed vignette than a story with anywhere surprising to go. The tone is consistent throughout—dry, cool, smoke-and-whiskey—and the present tense is maintained without wobble. Length is on target. No purple prose, no overwrought passages, no unearned transformations (nobody softens too fast; the truce is transactional). The darkness (both characters' damage) is earned by their histories. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 58.7
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Útiseta Thirty years have passed, and I still cannot explain what happened on the mound that night. I've told the story so many times—to therapists, to a husband who listens with kind skepticism, to myself in the dark—that the words have worn smooth like river stones. But the fear underneath has never worn away. We met at the edge of Astrid's family's property at half past eleven, where the cultivated fields gave way to forest. October in Norrbotten, and already cold enough that my breath hung in front of me like something separate from my body. Astrid had told me to fast since noon, to wear nothing borrowed, and to bring a knife I'd never used to cut food. I'd taken one from the box of kitchen things my mother still hadn't unpacked, three months after the move. It felt right, somehow—an object as displaced as I was. "You didn't speak to anyone after sunset?" Astrid asked. She wore her grandmother's gray wool shawl over her jacket, which should have looked ridiculous on a fifteen-year-old and somehow didn't. "Just my mum. To say goodnight." Astrid frowned, considering, then shrugged. "Mothers don't count. Mormor said the rule is about strangers and enemies." She said it the way she said everything about her grandmother's teachings—flatly, practically, like reciting the rules of a card game. That tone was what made me believe her, I think. There was no theater in Astrid. The theater was all mine. We walked twenty minutes through the pines. The forest at night in that part of Sweden isn't dark the way Stockholm is dark; it's an older darkness, layered, and the wind moving through the high branches made a sound like a roomful of people murmuring just below the threshold of words. I kept turning my head. Astrid never did. The mound rose out of a clearing where the trees stood back in a rough circle, as if they too kept a respectful distance. It wasn't large—maybe my height, grass-covered, with a single flat stone embedded near its crown. In daylight, Astrid said, you'd walk past it without noticing. The county had never marked it. Her family had simply always known. "Iron Age, probably," she said. "Mormor calls it *farfarsfars hög*. Great-great-grandfather's mound. But it's older than anyone we have names for." She made me leave my shoes at the base. The grass was wet and shockingly cold through my socks. At the flat stone she had me sit facing north, and she sat behind me, back to back, her shoulder blades pressing against mine through our jackets. The contact was the only warm thing in the world. "The rules," she said. "We don't speak until dawn or until it's over, whichever comes first. We don't stand up. Whatever you hear, you don't answer it out loud—only in your head. And if something asks you a question, you don't tell it your name." "What would ask me a question?" I meant it to sound mocking. It came out small. "Sitting out is for receiving knowledge," Astrid said, as if that answered me. "You wanted to know about Petra. What she says about you. So hold her face in your mind and wait." A pause. Then, quieter: "Mormor only did this twice in her whole life. She said the third time, they know you." I wanted to ask who *they* were. The midnight hour arrived instead, unannounced, and Astrid's breathing behind me slowed into something deliberate and rhythmic, and the silence took us. I want to be honest about what happened next, which means being honest about what I cannot verify. I was cold, fasting, frightened, fifteen. Every condition for hallucination was met. I have read about hypnagogia, about sensory deprivation, about the suggestibility of adolescent girls. I know all of it. The wind came up from the north, and the whispering of the pines sharpened. That's the only word for it—sharpened, the way a radio sharpens when you find the station. The murmur of branches began to develop edges, consonants. I told myself: it's wind. It was wind. But it was wind that had learned the shape of my new schoolmates' dialect, that rolled and stopped the way Petra's voice rolled and stopped, and beneath my held breath I began to make out—or assemble, or invent—fragments. *The Stockholm girl. She thinks. She thinks she.* My heart was a fist against my ribs. Then the cold changed. It stopped coming from the air and started coming from below, up through the stone, up through me, the specific cold of a hand laid flat against the small of my back. Astrid's breathing hitched. She'd heard something too, or felt it—to this day she has never told me which, and I have never told her about the question. Because something asked me a question. Not in words, exactly. It arrived the way you remember a dream—already finished, already inside. A sense of attention turning toward me, vast and incurious and old, and the question, simple as a customs official's: *who*. I almost answered. That's the part that still wakes me. My name rose in my throat like a bubble, reflexive, polite, and I had to physically clamp my jaw to keep it down. I sat with my own name pressing against my teeth while the wind said Petra's syllables and the cold hand printed itself into my spine, and I understood—suddenly, completely—that Astrid's rules were not a game's rules. They were a wall. And we were sitting on the wrong side of it, two girls who had come to gossip with the dead. Astrid stood up. She wasn't supposed to stand up. She grabbed my wrist with fingers like winter iron and we ran, shoeless, down the mound and through the pines, and behind us the whispering rose and rose and then, at the treeline, stopped—all at once, like a door closing. We never spoke of it. We never went back. But sometimes, even now, even here, the wind finds me. And it knows the shape of my name.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that executes the brief with notable skill. The frame device (30-year retrospective narration) is handled transparently, as requested, and even becomes thematically productive—the narrator's adult rationalizations ("I have read about hypnagogia...") mirror the reader's own ambiguity-management. The ritual details are the piece's greatest strength. The specific, matter-of-fact rules (fasting since noon, nothing borrowed, unused knife, no speaking to strangers after sunset, don't give your name) feel authentically folkloric rather than invented-from-whole-cloth, and Astrid's flat, practical delivery—"Mothers don't count. Mormor said the rule is about strangers and enemies"—perfectly captures the requested mix of teenage casualness and eerie specificity. The detail of the unmarked mound the county never recorded, known only through family transmission, is exactly right for the genre. The ambiguity is well maintained. The narrator explicitly catalogs the psychological explanations (cold, fasting, fear, suggestibility) while the sensory escalation—wind developing "consonants," the cold hand at the small of the back—stays just plausibly deniable. The climactic non-verbal question ("who," arriving "the way you remember a dream—already finished, already inside") is an effective escalation that avoids the cliché of literal ghost dialogue. Weaknesses are minor. The ending's final two lines ("the wind finds me. And it knows the shape of my name") tip slightly toward the overwrought and conventional—a stock horror stinger that the rest of the piece has earned better than it delivers. Astrid's sudden standing and flight is slightly undermotivated; we're told she heard or felt something, but her breaking of her own rule reads more as plot necessity than character. Astrid herself remains somewhat thin—functional rather than fully realized—though this is partly defensible given the tight POV. The prose occasionally reaches ("my heart was a fist against my ribs," "fingers like winter iron") but these are within genre tolerances. A few phrases like "the specific cold of a hand laid flat against the small of my back" work; "an older darkness, layered" is a touch abstract. Dialogue is sparse but effective where present. The pacing is disciplined—no meandering, the 1000-word target is hit closely. Emotionally, the piece earns its dread through accumulation rather than cheap shocks, and the closing note of lifelong haunting is congruent with the darkness established. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Therapeutic Boundaries** The table is vinyl, the color of dried mustard, and I hate it the way I hate everything in this room: the foam wedges, the resistance bands hanging like surrender flags, the laminated spine poster curling at one corner. Mostly I hate that Dario Reyes is the one standing over me. "Supine," he says. "Left leg flat." I lie back. The reconstructed knee—my right, the one that ended me eleven months ago on a landing I'd stuck ten thousand times before—sits bent at maybe forty degrees, which is all the flexion my scar tissue will allow without my nervous system filing a formal complaint. He still wears the compression sleeves. That's the thing I can't get over. Forearm to bicep, both arms, that screaming geometric print—teal and orange chevrons—from our old training squad. On him they should look ridiculous. They look like he never lost anything. "Heel slides first," he says. "You know the drill." "I know the drill." I plant my right heel on the table and drag it toward my hip. The knee folds—forty degrees, fifty—and then the tightness arrives, a hot band across the front of the joint, the patella grinding faintly in its groove like a stone in a shoe. "Stop guarding." His hand settles on my quad, four inches above the kneecap, fingers spread. Warm through the fabric of my shorts' hem, warm on bare skin below it. "Your quad's firing. Let it go soft. The muscle's fighting me before I've done anything." *Before I've done anything.* I exhale and the quadriceps releases under his palm, and the heel slides another inch, sixty degrees, and the pain sharpens from band to blade. "There," he says. "Hold." I hold. My breath goes shallow and I make it deep again, deliberately, because he's watching my ribs and I know he can read me. We used to count each other's breathing during max-effort sets. He knows what my body does when it's lying. "Passive flexion now." He moves to the end of the table, cups my heel in his right hand, slides his left under the back of my knee—fingers in the popliteal crease, that soft vulnerable hollow, supporting the joint from beneath. "I push, you breathe. You don't help me. You don't fight me." "That's my whole personality you're ruling out." A flicker at the corner of his mouth. He doesn't take the bait. He starts to fold the leg, slow, his hand on my heel guiding it up the table while his other hand stabilizes the joint, and the knee bends past sixty, past seventy, and the blade becomes a wall, a full-body objection—heat flooding the joint capsule, my hip flexor twitching, my hands fisting in the vinyl. "Talk to me. Number." "Six." "Liar." "Seven and a half." "Better." He holds it there, at the wall, not pushing through it, just leaning his weight into the threshold so the tissue has to negotiate. His forearm—those absurd chevrons—braces along my shin. I can feel his pulse through the sleeve, or maybe that's mine, the whole leg one circuit now. "Twenty seconds. Breathe into it." The thing nobody tells you about pain at the edge of range is that it's intimate. It strips you. I'm staring at the ceiling tiles and my eyes are wet, not crying, just *responding*, the body doing its involuntary weather, and he's six inches from my face checking my pupils because that's his job now, reading me, and I used to want him to look at me like this for entirely different reasons. Still do. That's the humiliating part. The want didn't retire when I did. "Release." He lowers the leg back to forty degrees and the relief is obscene, a flood of warmth down the shin, my whole thigh trembling in small fasciculations I can't control. "That's normal," he says, watching the tremor. "Neuromuscular. It'll settle." "I know what it is." "Then stop looking embarrassed about it." I turn my head. He's already moving, professional, repositioning—"Side-lying, left side, I want your hip"—and I roll onto my left side facing the wall, knees stacked, and he stands behind me, and this is worse, this is so much worse, because now I can't see him, only feel: his left hand anchoring my pelvis at the iliac crest, thumb hooked over the bone, his right hand gripping my right ankle as he draws the leg back into hip extension, opening the front of the hip where everything has shortened from months of limping. The stretch lights up my hip flexor like a struck match—a long pulling burn from groin to mid-thigh. "Pelvis still," he murmurs, and presses down at the crest when I try to arch away, his palm flat and absolute. "You're cheating with your lumbar spine. The stretch goes here"—his thumb taps the front of my hip, precise, clinical, devastating—"or it goes nowhere." "You used to be nicer." "You used to be coachable." A beat. His grip on my ankle shifts, and he eases the leg back another degree, and I make a sound, low, involuntary, somewhere between pain and something I'd rather he not catalog. His hands go very still. The room goes very still. I can hear the HVAC. I can hear him swallow. "Number," he says, and his voice has dropped half an octave and he knows it. "Six," I say, and this time it's true, and the lie is everywhere else—in my heat-flushed neck, in the way I haven't pulled away from his hand on my hip even though the stretch released seconds ago. He sets my leg down. Steps back. I hear him roll his shoulders, the sleeves whispering against themselves. "Same time Thursday," he says, already at the counter, already writing notes, already a professional with appropriate distance and a clipboard. "Same time Thursday," I say, and lie there one second longer than I should, my knee aching at forty degrees, learning—both of us learning—exactly where the threshold is, and exactly how long we can hold it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong, controlled scene with genuinely precise physical therapy detail—heel slides, passive flexion, popliteal hand placement, hip extension with pelvic anchoring—all anatomically coherent and spatially trackable. The tension between professional touch and suppressed attraction is handled with restraint, largely through show: the dropped voice, the still room, the "lie is everywhere else" line. The voice is consistent—wry, resentful, self-aware—and the recurring motif of thresholds (pain, range, boundaries) ties theme and body together elegantly. Dialogue is sharp and character-revealing ("That's my whole personality you're ruling out"). Weaknesses: the prompt specified a female physiotherapist and male protagonist; the model reversed this, a clear instruction deviation. The "former training partner" backstory is thin—compression sleeves carry it, but the shared competitive history is more asserted than dramatized. The ending's "both of us learning" is slightly neat, and some images ("surrender flags," "involuntary weather") flirt with over-cleverness. The piece is also somewhat one-note in register—every line is polished quip or precise sensation, leaving little variation in rhythm. Still, it earns its tension honestly and never tips into purple or melodrama. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Tide That Takes I woke before the gun sounded from the flagship, which was the first wrong thing. A man who sleeps properly does not wake at four bells with his shirt soaked through and his hands performing their small, private rebellion against stillness. "You're grey as a gutted fish," said Pemberton, when I passed him on the factory veranda. He was eating congee with a spoon too small for his hand, the way all of us ate here, awkwardly, like guests who had stayed too long. "Hartley's asking after the survey reports." "Tell Hartley the survey reports are coming." I coughed then—the cough that lived in me now, that came up wet and left a taste of old pennies on my tongue. I turned my face toward the Pearl River and spat discreetly over the rail. "That cough of yours, Merrick." "Sea air. Eight years of it. The lungs object to land." "We're hardly at sea." "The damp, then. The river damp. It's all one water, Pemberton." He let me go. They always let me go, which I had begun to understand was its own kind of verdict. --- By eight I was through Hog Lane, where the smell changed every six paces—frying pork fat, then joss-stick smoke, then the green rot of vegetable water thrown into the gutter, then something sweet and dark that made my throat clench with wanting. A boy tried to sell me a songbird in a cage made of split bamboo. The bird was the color of a bruise. "No bird," I said. "Cheng. Where is Cheng today?" The boy's face closed like a fist. "No Cheng." "There's always Cheng." "Cheng gone Whampoa. You go see Old Wu." I did not want to see Old Wu. Old Wu's prices ran half a dollar higher and his pipes ran half as clean, but the morning was already turning on me, the light going hard and white, and my stomach had begun its slow folding-in, the cramping that announced itself like a creditor at the door. --- Old Wu's room sat above a chandler's shop, reached by a ladder that I climbed with the careful dignity of a drunk man pretending sobriety. The room smelled of the smoke gone cold in the walls—years of it, soaked into the plaster and the matting, so that the whole chamber was itself a kind of pipe. "Lieutenant." Wu never bothered with pretense. He knew my rank, my ship, likely my mother's maiden name. "You owe from Tuesday." "I'm aware." "Four dollars Tuesday. Today, four more." "I have three." I laid the coins out. Spanish dollars, worn smooth, one of them clipped at the edge by some previous thief. "And I'll have the rest by evening." Wu looked at the coins the way a physician looks at a tongue. "You say this Tuesday also." "There's a man at Jackass Point who wants cargo manifests. Copies. The Hoppo's runners pay well for knowing what the country ships declare and what they actually carry." My voice came out steadier than I deserved. "I have access. I have a fair hand. By six o'clock I'll have your dollar and more besides." He weighed it. The room ticked with heat. Somewhere below, the chandler was hammering at something, each blow arriving up through the floorboards and into my teeth. "One pipe now," Wu said. "You come back six o'clock with two dollar, or no more come back ever." --- I will not describe the pipe. Or I will say only this: that the first breath of it was like a hand laid flat against every screaming nerve in my body, a hand that said *hush, hush*, and that the shame arrived precisely four seconds after the relief, as it always did, punctual as the tide. I lay on the matting and watched a lizard cross the ceiling and thought, with the particular clarity the smoke lends to useless thoughts, that I had once stood on the quarterdeck of the *Andromache* in a Biscay gale and felt nothing but joy. --- The man at Jackass Point called himself Figueira, though I doubted it. Portuguese coat, Macao manners, eyes that did arithmetic on everything they touched. "The *Lady Hayes* manifest," he said. "And the *Falcon*, if you can manage it." "The *Falcon* berths under my own squadron's eye. You're asking me to copy out documents my own service is meant to safeguard." "I'm asking you nothing, Lieutenant. I'm offering. Six dollars." The cough took me then, doubled me over against a piling. When it passed I wiped my mouth and saw the rust-bloom on my handkerchief and folded it away quickly, the way one folds away a letter bearing bad news, as though unread meant unwritten. "You should see a physician," Figueira said, almost kindly. "It's the sea air." "Of course it is." He counted three dollars into my palm. "Half now. Half on delivery. We are all of us paying for something, Lieutenant. The trick is knowing the true price before the bill comes." --- I copied the manifests in the back room of the factory between five and six bells, my hand steady now, beautifully steady, the smoke still doing its work, my pen moving through columns of long-cloth and saltpetre and the forty chests of Patna that appeared nowhere on the official page. Forty chests. I had carried perhaps four hundred pipefuls through my own blood since spring. We were all of us in the same trade, I thought; I had merely cut out the middlemen. Pemberton found me at dusk on the veranda. "Hartley wants you at seven. The survey reports." "He'll have them." "You missed muster, James." It was the Christian name that did it—the small mercy of it, worse than any reprimand. I looked at the river, at the lanterns coming alight on the flower boats, gold smearing across black water, and I coughed, and tasted copper, and said what I always said. "It's only the sea air, Tom. A man can't be blamed for the air." The evening gun sounded from the anchorage. I had two dollars for Wu and an appetite already rising in me like the tide, and tomorrow, I told myself, tomorrow would be the day I did not climb the ladder. The lanterns burned on. The river took everything downstream.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of historical fiction that largely fulfills the brief. The prose is controlled and often striking: "the smell changed every six paces," "shame arrived precisely four seconds after the relief, punctual as the tide," "the bird was the color of a bruise." The sensory grounding in 1830s Canton is specific and convincing—Hog Lane, the Hoppo, Jackass Point, Spanish dollars, Patna chests, the flower boats—without tipping into travelogue. The dialogue carries most of the narrative weight as instructed, and it does real work: Pemberton's "You missed muster, James" lands as a quiet moral blow precisely because of the Christian name, a well-observed beat. The character is believable throughout. Merrick's rationalizations ("It's the sea air"), his self-awareness without self-reform, and the escalation into copying manifests for sale are all psychologically coherent with addiction. The supporting cast—Wu, Figueira, the bird-seller boy—are sketched economically but with distinct voices. Figueira's "We are all of us paying for something" flirts with aphorism but earns it in context. Weaknesses: the piece leans on a few familiar addiction tropes—the "tomorrow would be the day I did not climb the ladder" resolution, the rust-bloom handkerchief, the cough as shorthand for decline. These are competent but not surprising; the shape of the day (wake, deny, score, use, betray, deny again) is the expected one. The final image ("The river took everything downstream") is a touch neat. Occasionally the aphoristic density ("They always let me go, which I had begun to understand was its own kind of verdict") edges toward over-polish, though it never collapses into purple. The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed, and the "schemes and unsavoury jobs" element, while present, is a little thin—a single transaction rather than a web of dealings. Still, the voice is consistent, the time-sense precise (bells, hours, the evening gun), and the ending's refusal of redemption is honest rather than contrived. This is professional-grade work with minor lapses in originality. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 85.5
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# The Uphill Correspondent The boulder had a name, though Sisyphus had never told anyone what it was. You don't share a workspace with something for three thousand years without developing certain intimacies. "Right," he said, settling onto a flat rock at the bottom of the slope. "What's first?" Crow extracted a letter from the mailbag with the air of a bird who had opinions about people's handwriting and was prepared to share them. --- *Dear Uphill Correspondent,* *My husband chews with his mouth open. Twenty-two years. I have mentioned it perhaps four thousand times. I am beginning to fantasize about feeding him exclusively soup. Is this a sign the marriage is over?* *— Audibly Suffering in Thebes* --- "Dear Audibly Suffering," Sisyphus dictated, while Crow scratched away with a quill held in one foot, which should have been impossible but was the sort of thing one stopped questioning around year eight hundred. "The marriage is not over. If it were over, you would have stopped mentioning it around mention two thousand. People only keep correcting the people they intend to keep. What you are tired of is not him — it is the *mentioning*. So stop. Not forever. For one month. You will discover one of two things: either the chewing recedes into the general weather of your life, like a creaky door you've stopped hearing, or it doesn't, and you'll know the chewing was never really the problem. Either way, you'll have learned something, and you'll have had a month off. Also, there is nothing wrong with soup. Some of history's great marriages ran almost entirely on soup." He stood, brushed off his hands, and addressed the boulder. "Back in a bit," he told Crow. The push took forty minutes. He was not in a hurry. The boulder, as ever, came thundering back down with what an uncharitable observer might call enthusiasm, and Sisyphus walked back down after it, whistling. --- *Dear Uphill Correspondent,* *My employer expects me at the olive press from dawn until dusk, and now wants me to "check the vats" on rest days, "just quickly," which is never quick. I love my work but I am beginning to dream about olives. Last night an olive asked me where my quarterly figures were.* *— Pressed in Corinth* --- "Dear Pressed," said Sisyphus. "Your employer has discovered that you will say yes, and he is a man standing at a well that has never run dry, so why would he stop drawing water? He is not evil. He is simply not thinking about you, because you have made it unnecessary for him to do so. The next time he asks about the vats, say no, pleasantly, the way you'd decline a second helping. Do not explain. Explanations are negotiations, and you are not negotiating. He will be surprised exactly once, and then he will adjust, because people adjust to walls much faster than they adjust to doors. And Pressed — the olives in your dreams have no authority over you. Tell the olive the quarterly figures are *its* responsibility, and see how it likes that." Crow made a noise that in a less dignified bird would have been a snicker. --- *Dear Uphill Correspondent,* *There is a man at my bathhouse. We have, on three occasions, shared what I can only describe as a Significant Glance across the steam room. On the fourth occasion I panicked and asked him if he enjoyed steam. He said yes. I said "me too" and left. I have not been back in two weeks and I miss both the steam and the man. Advise.* *— Sweating It in Argos* --- "Dear Sweating It," Sisyphus said warmly. "First: 'do you enjoy steam' is, contextually, a perfectly respectable opening, and I'll hear no criticism of it. He said yes. That was an invitation, not a verdict. You are treating one awkward sentence as a closed gate when it was actually a door left ajar by a man who, I'd wager, has spent two weeks composing his own better answer about steam. Go back. Sit near him. Say, 'I left rather abruptly last time.' That's it. That's the whole strategy. The brave thing is rarely the eloquent thing. And if it goes nowhere — well. You'll be clean, and warm, and you'll know." It was at this point that a minor deity arrived, as minor deities do, in a puff of self-importance and lavender. "Sisyphus," said the god — Phrastor, deity of misplaced ladles and unsolicited feedback. "I've been *hearing things*. An advice column? In the *underworld*?" "Letter for you, actually," said Sisyphus mildly. "Bottom of the bag." "The optics are *terrible*. You're meant to be *suffering*. It undermines the whole punitive framework. Also, the crow lacks gravitas." Crow looked at him in the way crows do, which is to say like a small black auditor. "I'll take it under advisement," said Sisyphus, and went to push the boulder. When he came back down, Phrastor had gone, having achieved nothing, which was, after all, his portfolio. --- *Dear Uphill Correspondent,* *I am thirty-four and I do not know what my life is for. My brother breeds prize goats. My sister speaks four languages. I make sandals. Good sandals. But surely there's supposed to be more?* *— Unremarkable in Athens* --- Sisyphus was quiet for a moment. "Dear Unremarkable," he said at last. "I once knew a man who spent his whole life asking what it was *for*, and missed most of what it *was*. Your sandals carry people to weddings, to deathbeds, to bathhouses where they fail to talk to handsome men. You are in ten thousand journeys you'll never see. Purpose isn't a destination you arrive at — most days it's just the next thing done well, and the willingness to come back down and do it again." He glanced at the boulder. The boulder said nothing, but companionably. "Send that one first," he told Crow. "And then lunch, I think. We've earned it." Crow, who had earned at least half of it, agreed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece that hits nearly all the prompt's specific requirements. The epistolary format is maintained with light scene interjections; Sisyphus is warm, grounded, and zen without stoicism lectures; the advice is genuinely practical and insightful (the "people adjust to walls faster than doors" line, the soup marriage, the bathhouse strategy); the humor is understated and emerges from the letters themselves; the boulder routine is woven in naturally; and the single boulder metaphor is subtle ("the willingness to come back down and do it again"). The Pratchett voice is well imitated — the footnote-style asides ("which should have been impossible but was the sort of thing one stopped questioning around year eight hundred"), the minor deity Phrastor with his absurd portfolio ("misplaced ladles and unsolicited feedback"), and Crow's dry characterization ("a small black auditor"). The piece shows rather than tells: Sisyphus's contentment is demonstrated through his whistling, unhurried pushes, and mild deflection of the deity. Minor weaknesses: the Phrastor interruption, while funny, is a slight detour that resolves a bit too neatly and quickly. The final letter's answer edges toward the sentimental ("ten thousand journeys you'll never see") — the one moment where the prose risks being a touch too neat, though it's earned by the piece's tone. The ending is gentle but not falsely positive. Some letters could be slightly sharper; the risque element is present but mild. Overall, highly competent, funny, and humane with only small imperfections.
